pushed by _enable_extended_enter_keys), Shift+symbol keystrokes such as
Shift+- ('_'), Shift+= ('+'), Shift+[ ('{') are encoded as the tilde
form ESC[27;2;<produced_cp>~.

is the layout-resolved produced character, making this layout-safe.

inserted into the buffer instead of raw escape bytes.

fix(compression): probe aux feasibility before the first compaction; clear stale clamp notice on un-clamp

A fresh AIAgent whose main model already had the larger window still got
its first compaction at the main-window threshold, and only then did the
lazy probe in compress_context clamp the trigger to the aux window — so
the oversized compaction request was already sent (#114707 steps 1-6;
every instance recycle restarted the cycle).

ensure_compression_feasibility_checked(agent, estimated_tokens) runs the
probe once a request first reaches MINIMUM_CONTEXT_LENGTH — the smallest
window any summariser may have — from both compaction gates
(run_preflight_compression, compress_after_tool_results), so the clamp
lands before the main-window threshold fires. Requests below that size
stay probe-free, preserving the cold-start deferral of 6cb9917c73a
(#28957); a failed probe leaves the latch unset for the lazy probe.

Symmetric un-clamp: when a re-probe finds the aux fits again,
_compression_warning / _last_feasibility_notice are cleared so
replay_compression_warning does not resend an "auto-lowered" notice for
a session that is no longer clamped.

fix(compression): fallback/restore re-probe only refreshes an existing feasibility verdict

The eager aux feasibility re-probe ran on every fallback activation and primary restore, resolving an
auxiliary client inside the provider error path. Sessions that never probed gain nothing from that (the
compaction-time probe still owns the first verdict) and the extra client resolution broke the fallback
chain on stubbed resolvers (tests/agent/test_provider_fallback.py, test_fallback_api_mode_preservation.py,
test_fallback_429_after_timeout.py). Explicit /model switches keep the unconditional re-probe (#114707).

fix(compression): keep the aux ceiling and re-probe feasibility on every main-runtime change

The aux-window clamp installed by _lower_threshold_to_aux_context() was a one-time
assignment to threshold_tokens; ContextCompressor.update_model() recomputed the trigger
from the main model and discarded it, and the _compression_feasibility_checked latch was
never reset, so after a mid-session switch to a larger main model the trigger sat at the
main-model value (450K) while the pinned summariser accepted 272K (#114707).

- ContextCompressor holds the aux window as a durable _aux_context_ceiling that
  _apply_threshold_tokens_cap() honours on every recomputation; update_model() voids it
  only when the main runtime changes (an "auto" aux route follows the main model).
- revalidate_compression_feasibility(agent) resets the latch and re-probes eagerly at
  every runtime change: switch_model (outside the rollback guard), fallback activation
  and primary restore. Symmetric: a runtime whose aux fits restores the main trigger.
- Feasibility notices emit once per distinct verdict so /model --once restores and
  fallback cycles do not re-announce an unchanged verdict.
- Rewrites the switch-time hunk salvaged from #114710: unconditional, outside the
  rollback try, so a catalog hiccup never undoes a good switch. Test kept and extended.

fix(discord): backfill stops re-dispatching a message once its turn delivered, and bounds the rest

Three defects let the missed-message backfill re-run the same inbound message on
every reconnect (24 turns in 12 h for one message on the reporter's install):

- Completion was only ever recorded by the send-path ledger writer, keyed on the
  Discord reply anchor. With reply_to_mode "off", a streamed final delivered via
  edit_message(finalize=True), a fresh-final send or a media-only reply there is no
  anchor, so the row stayed processed/replied=0 and _should_backfill_discord_message
  re-admitted it forever. The adapter already learns the outcome per inbound id in
  _record_discord_processing_complete: on SUCCESS (base confirmed delivery, or the
  stream already delivered) it now writes status='responded', replied=1.
- The scan wrote status='discovered' over every candidate at the top of each pass,
  erasing the queued/processing claim so the 10-minute active-claim guard could never
  fire; two back-to-back scans dispatched the same message twice. The 'discovered'
  write no longer overwrites an existing row's status or updated_at.
- A stored per-channel cursor REPLACED the window floor (12-hour-old messages stayed
  candidates under window_seconds: 3600) and the parent's cursor object was passed
  down to child threads. after = max(cursor, now - window) and threads only see the
  window floor plus their own cursor.
- max_dispatches caps one scan, not one row. New missed_message_backfill.max_attempts
  (default 3; env DISCORD_MISSED_MESSAGE_BACKFILL_MAX_ATTEMPTS) is a lifetime ceiling
  on re-dispatch of a single message; `attempts` now counts dispatches only.

Live repro (real DiscordAdapter, temp HERMES_HOME ledger, fake client yielding the
same message per scan, fresh adapter per scan = reconnect): streamed final with
reply_to_mode=off 3 scans -> before 3 dispatches, after 1; turn that never completes
3 scans -> 3/1; turn that always fails 6 scans -> 6/3; 12h-old cursor with a 1h window
-> before 2 out-of-window dispatches (parent + thread), after 0; control: an
unanswered message still dispatches exactly once, and a cursor newer than the window
still narrows the scan.

profile-shaped HERMES_HOME without a flag is the home; otherwise the root is

process HOME, and the profile is the -p flag, else the root active_profile
unless the process has a fixed identity (supervised child, post-swap updater,

fix(dashboard): --stop and the update sweep resolve backend ownership tri-state, never guess

- `_hermes_home_for_pid` is tri-state. `None` now means ONLY "environment unreadable"

  with a `--profile X`/`-p X` argv flag selecting `<default>/profiles/X` because
  `_apply_profile_override` writes HERMES_HOME into os.environ AFTER exec and
  `/proc/<pid>/environ` never reflects it. Without this, the common default-home install
  (nothing exported) got a `--stop` that matched nothing — the regression flagged on

fix(desktop): pin the bootstrap marker with the probed git, not the first PATH hit

resolveCheckoutHead ran a bare `git`, which resolves by PATH order and
so hits the same existing-but-unlaunchable Intel git the update check
now skips; execFileSync threw, was swallowed to null, and the
bootstrap-complete marker fell back to whatever pin was already on disk.

runBootstrap accepts `gitBinary` and threads it to resolveCheckoutHead;
main.ts passes resolveGitBinary(), so both paths use the same binary.

fix(desktop): name the unlaunchable git instead of blaming the update server

When git itself cannot be spawned (ENOENT, EACCES, or Darwin's EBADARCH,
which Node surfaces as a bare errno -86 "spawn Unknown system error -86"),
the update check rejected with the raw spawn error and both the updates
overlay and Settings > About led with "couldn't reach the update server"
— a network diagnosis for a local Intel-only git that macOS refuses to run.

runGit now maps child 'error' events through describeGitSpawnFailure()
(pure, in select-runnable-binary.ts) to "Git on this computer cannot run
(<path>: Bad CPU type in executable). Install a Git build for this machine
(on macOS: `xcode-select --install`) and check again.", the IPC catch tags
the status error 'git-unusable', and the two renderer surfaces lead with
a new updates.gitUnusable copy for that tag. Nonzero git exits never fire
'error', so their existing wording is unchanged.

Closes the second expected-behaviour atom of #114718.

fix(desktop): gh PATH fallback goes through the runnability probe too

resolveGhBinary() still fell through to findOnPath('gh') — existence-only —
when none of the four fixed non-Windows locations existed, so an
unlaunchable gh earlier on PATH than a working one would be picked again
from an unlisted directory. Feed PATH hits into the same selectRunnableBinary
call; the bare findOnPath/'gh' fallback is now reached only when nothing
exists at all. Windows branch untouched.

fix(desktop): probe non-Windows git and gh candidates for executability

resolveGitBinary()'s non-Windows branch used findOnPath('git') || 'git',
and resolveGhBinary() used candidates.find(fileExists) || findOnPath('gh')
|| 'gh' — both existence-only. On macOS an Intel-only binary earlier on
PATH than a working native one still exists, so it wins and fails at spawn
time with "Bad CPU type in executable" (Darwin errno 86, EBADARCH); the
update check then reports the update server as unreachable.

Add a pure select-runnable-binary module (injectable fileExists/binaryRuns
seam): first candidate that exists AND runs (`--version` probe), falling
back to the first that merely exists so behaviour is unchanged where the
probe itself cannot run. Wire it into both resolvers; Windows branches are
untouched.

fix(telegram): slash-confirm card budgets the MarkdownV2 rendering; approval budgets count UTF-16 units

send_slash_confirm cut the RAW message to 3800 chars and only then ran format_message,
whose MarkdownV2 escaping expands text (3800 dots -> 7600 chars), so the button card could
still exceed the 4096 cap and fail exactly like the approval card this branch fixed. It now
fits the message with the shared _ea_fit bisection measured after format_message (the
suffix's own rendering is reserved from the budget).

_ea_fit takes an optional `escape` renderer (default _ea_escape) and measures in the
adapter's message_len_fn units, and the Telegram command budget sums the framing with
utf16_len, so astral chars (emoji) are budgeted the way the adapter's 4096 chunker counts
them (len() undercounted them by half).

Tests: slash-confirm preview for a 3800-char message and the approval card for an
emoji-dense command both stay <= 4096 UTF-16 units (red before, green after).

fix(telegram): approval button card fits the 4096-char cap after HTML escaping

Telegram truncated the command to 3800 RAW chars and only then html.escape()d it, so a
command heavy in `&`/`<`/`>` rendered far past 4096 chars; the framing (header, <pre>,
reason label, deadline, smart-deny line) sat outside that budget and the reason itself
was unbounded. Telegram answered "Message is too long" and the gateway fell back to the
text /approve prompt.

- `BasePlatformAdapter._ea_fit`: the shared exec-approval core now measures both the
  command preview and the reason after `_ea_escape` (bisection on the raw prefix; the
  escaped length is monotonic) — identity for non-escaping platforms.
- Telegram computes the command budget from `MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH` minus the rendered
  framing and escaped reason (the same idiom Discord and Slack already use) and bounds
  the reason at 500 escaped chars.

Live against a local fake Telegram Bot API (fake token) rejecting text > 4096:
before, 3700 x "&" sent 18670 chars → 400 → /approve fallback; after, 4093 chars,
inline keyboard delivered.

fix(cli): re-resolve reasoning after every startup model move, not just the auth fallback

_resolve_cli_reasoning's invariant is that every path moving self.model re-resolves
reasoning_config before the agent build. The previous commit covered only the auth
fallback swap; the custom-entry runtime.model swap, the provider-default fill and the
provider normalization in _ensure_runtime_credentials, plus the first-run picker

model's config (kanban passes it per task the same way).

`_read_script_for_scanning` returned a lifecycle-shaped sentinel ("hermes gateway
restart") when the job's OWN script was oversized, a device, or a SQLite database
open in this process, so `check_gateway_lifecycle` raised the misattributed
"cron job contains a gateway lifecycle command" error. It now returns
`(text, refusal)` via `_unreadable_reason` and the caller raises the existing

(#113944 atom 4).

scanner flagged bare write_text()/open() calls.

fix(cron): a data file only mentioned in an inert heredoc never fails the lifecycle guard closed

The referenced-script walk reads paths named inside a masked (provably inert)
interpreter body so `os.system('/x/restart.sh')` is still caught, but it
turned every "could not scan" outcome for those mentions into a block: a
<1 MiB JSON with one >64 KiB line exhausted the text budget at depth 1, a
markdown table of paths pulled 64 remote-read misses and exhausted that
budget, and a live SQLite database (`state.db` inside a running gateway)
failed closed via LiveConnectionError with nothing logged. 22 of 36
in-gateway terminal blocks in one deployment were this class (#113944).

Thread `executed` through `_contains_unsafe_gateway_action`: content reached
only through a mention is still scanned for a literal lifecycle command, but
budget/depth/size/device/live-DB/cloud there is "nothing to scan", never a

  entries immediately, mirroring daytona's PID-suffixed remote temp.

  while content streams into subdirectories, and the download bound is
  SSH/Modal-only), and concurrent gateway processes under different
  HERMES_HOMEs never sweep each other's transfers. Legacy (pre-PID)

fix(tools): stop socket-ignoring tars from failing sync-back and leaking GBs

Every SSH sync-back on a host with a live gateway.sock failed: GNU tar
cannot archive a Unix socket, prints "socket ignored", and exits 2 —
so the download raised, retried three times, and (when the process was
hard-killed mid-download, e.g. by the gateway's tool-subprocess kill)
left its multi-GB temp tar behind. With the stale-temp sweep window at
6 h, a crash loop accumulated 45 GB in /tmp and filled the rootfs
(#114437).

- Exclude *.sock from the remote tar up front; tolerate a rc=2 whose
  stderr is only "socket ignored" lines (defensive for tars without
  --exclude support or unmatched socket names) — anything else still
  fails the transfer.
- Shrink the stale sweep cutoff from 6 h to 30 min; the download is
  bounded by a 120 s subprocess timeout, so a live transfer is minutes
  old at most and the cutoff only has to sit above that.
- Make the 2 GiB extraction cap overridable via HERMES_SYNC_BACK_MAX_BYTES
  for synced trees that legitimately exceed it.

fix(profiles): clone re-creates NTFS skill junctions instead of deep-copying them

`hermes profile create --clone/--clone-all` copies the source home with
`shutil.copytree(symlinks=True)`. POSIX symlinks survive that (b7192b1cb02),
but an NTFS junction is a reparse point, not a symlink: `os.path.islink()`
is False and copytree descends into it, so a `skills/foo` junction into a
`skills.external_dirs` root became a physical copy in the clone. The clone's
copy and the external original are then two same-named candidates and
`_locate_skill()` refuses to guess ("Ambiguous skill name"), which also
aborts Kanban worker spawns carrying the name (`Unknown skill(s)`).

`_copytree_keep_junctions` wraps both clone copies: an `ignore` callback
excludes junction entries (`st_reparse_tag == IO_REPARSE_TAG_MOUNT_POINT`)
and the recorded targets are re-created with `_winapi.CreateJunction`. A
junction whose target is gone is skipped with a warning (CreateJunction
requires an existing target), so a dangling link never fails the clone.
Off Windows the predicate short-circuits and behaviour is unchanged.

The export staging copy deliberately keeps deep-copying: `_scrub_export_secrets`
rewrites staged files in place, and a preserved junction would let that
redaction write through into the user's external originals.

fix(gateway): /stop, /new and /reset keep a parked internal wake instead of discarding it

held ("consume and discard", 59575d6a917). That was right when the slot only ever carried the
user's stale follow-up text, but internal wakes (async-delegation completion notices,
kanban/cron notify+wake) now park in the same slot and are claim-settled the moment the adapter
admits them, so the pop lost them for good: the drain that runs after the command found an
empty slot and the session idled until the next user message (#114456, ~6 min stall in the
reported session).

Now the human follow-up is still discarded, but an internal wake stays parked (promoted out of
the overflow FIFO when a discarded human head occupied the slot) and the post-command drain
starts it immediately. Applies to every caller of the helper — /stop (busy fast path, handler,
pending sentinel, thread sibling), /new and /reset — since a wake that arrives a second after
/new runs against the fresh session anyway; whether a completion pinned to the closed session
may run stays with _resolve_async_delegation_session (fail-closed).

Salvaged from #114538 (@whyyagswhy, earliest filer): the pop-and-re-park mechanism is theirs;
widened here to the /new and /reset callers and the overflow promotion, and the invariant tests

independently; its stop-reason taxonomy and overflow analysis informed the class coverage.

and the resurrection still unarchived the row once the lock dropped.

fix(gateway): warn when a live gateway's heartbeat goes stale instead of printing `running`

The reporter's case in #113372 is "not a crash": the process stays alive,
`gateway_state.json` keeps saying `running`, and housekeeping, cron and the
kanban dispatcher are frozen. Nothing wrote `updated_at` periodically, so the
file was a stored status, not a heartbeat, and both `hermes gateway status`
and `/api/status` rendered a wedged gateway as healthy (the existing stale arm
only fires when the recorded PID is gone).

Make the housekeeping tick re-stamp `gateway_state.json` first thing every
tick (60 s), so `updated_at` is a heartbeat that stops when the thread — or a
chore blocked on the loop — wedges. Readers then warn on `running`/`starting`
+ stale stamp + live PID: `hermes gateway status` prints
`⚠ Gateway heartbeat stale: housekeeping has not refreshed gateway_state.json
for N s (event loop or housekeeping wedged; pid X alive)`, `/api/status`
carries `gateway_heartbeat_stale_s` (null when healthy) and the sidebar strip
shows "Heartbeat stale". Liveness (`gateway_running`, busy/drainable) still
keys off the PID, never the stamp. Draining is excluded: shutdown drains the
housekeeping thread before the process exits, so its stamp legitimately ages.

a fresh stamp; /api/status sets/clears `gateway_heartbeat_stale_s` the same way.

`degraded` + `exit_reason` of a dead PID became a bare `stopped` with the
reason nulled, so the sidebar strip and System page read "Stopped" while
`hermes gateway status` said "exited degraded: event loop stopped dispatching".

Retain `degraded` under the same rule as `startup_failed` (only while
`desired_state` still wants the gateway running, and only for the watchdog
reasons in the new `gateway.status.WATCHDOG_EXIT_REASONS`); the resolver
already keeps `gateway_exit_reason` for any non-`stopped` verdict. The sidebar
strip gains the `degraded` label (warning while live, destructive when the
process is gone) and the System page describes a dead `degraded` record as a
watchdog exit. `/api/messaging/platforms` keeps yielding `gateway_stopped` for
it — the channels really are down.

Invariant tests: retained_gateway_state keeps/drops the verdict by
desired_state and exit_reason; /api/status carries degraded + exit_reason for

fix(cron): render watchdog-degraded exits in `hermes gateway status`; degraded is the last writer

inside `_mark_exited_quietly`, so both out-of-loop watchdogs (loop liveness, shutdown)
publish before os._exit. This follow-up closes the class:

- Order: lifecycle ledger first, runtime status LAST, immediately before os._exit —
  the runtime record is the one housekeeping refreshes, so nothing may overwrite the
  degraded stamp after it lands (ordering delta from #113386 by @KoNit-K).

  shutdown watchdog's exit code 1 no longer clobbers a recorded restart intent to False.

  stamp would still have been invisible on the surface operators use; it now renders

  startup-time `degraded` (retryable platforms queued, exit_reason None) stays silent.
- Docs: the built-in loop liveness watchdog and what it writes/exits with.

Why: housekeeping, cron and the embedded kanban dispatcher share one asyncio loop, and
liveness was a stored status field written by that loop — a dead loop left the file at
`running` (#113372). The watchdog thread already detected the stall and exited; it just
never told the file or the status command.

fix(desktop): join split try/catch in Windows SSH probe for PowerShell 5.1

its Catch or Finally block', so every Windows host without PowerShell 7
failed the SSH probe and Desktop reported it as unsupported-platform.

remotes. Merge the two elements at both Assert-NoReparse sites

strips the constants with delattr so a cron.jobs that stops exporting them breaks the test's
premise loudly instead of silently, and the three-name facade import in unclaimed_pending_slot
no longer wraps now that the TTL left it.

test(cron): stale-facade probe strips both fire-claim constants and reaches the TTL path

The subprocess probe only exercised completed_occurrence (the skew bound); the TTL move in
unclaimed_pending_slot had no test that went red when its import was pointed back at the
cached cron.jobs. Strip both constants from the cached facade and restore a lapsed slot
stamped by another owner, so the _claim_is_live(..., FIRE_CLAIM_TTL_SECONDS) comparison runs.
Reverting either import line to the facade now fails this test.

fix(cron): move FIRE_CLAIM_TTL_SECONDS to the same leaf as the skew bound

FIRE_CLAIM_SKEW_SECONDS now lives in cron/constants.py so a sibling loaded from a newer
on-disk tree never resolves it through the cron.jobs object a long-lived process cached at
boot. FIRE_CLAIM_TTL_SECONDS is the other half of the fire-claim pair and
cron/occurrences.py::unclaimed_pending_slot reached it the same way, through the facade.
Move it too, so both bounds have one home and the next sibling cannot re-open the trap by
importing the TTL from cron.jobs.

jobs.py keeps importing both from the leaf because it uses them (claim TTL default, live-claim
checks, skewed early-fire ownership); that import is a consumer, not a re-export shim.

Salvaged from #114692 on top of #114675; only the TTL delta and the leaf docstring are kept.

test(desktop): launch the portal-session Electron fixture without the sandbox and surface its stderr

The js-tests lane runs on ubuntu-latest (24.04), which restricts unprivileged
user namespaces, and the npm-installed chrome-sandbox helper is not setuid, so
a sandboxed Electron aborts before the fixture's main script runs. The
Playwright lane already launches with --no-sandbox --disable-gpu for the same
reason; pass the same switches here, after the positional root so
process.argv[2] in the fixture is unchanged.

execFile's rejection carries only "Command failed", which is all CI showed.
Rethrow with the child's stdout and stderr attached so the next failure names
its cause.
fix(desktop): retain auth rejection across socket cleanup
fix(desktop): stop reconnecting rejected gateway sessions
fix(desktop): recover Cloud connections after team changes
fix(desktop): support Privy and NAS portal sessions in Cloud sign-in
refactor(desktop): extract portal session window driver

fix(gateway): match the chat id as text so ids containing ':' survive

The slot-splitting parse silently disabled BOTH fallbacks for ids that
themselves contain ':' — Matrix rooms (`!room:example.org`), a real shape
`build_session_key` emits raw. Only the fixed-shape head is split now; the chat
id and the tail are matched as text, which also removes the alias hazard by
construction (a trailing participant id can no longer be read as a chat id).

Also folded from the review pass: the sibling tier's thread slot comparison goes
through the same `_tail_has_slot` boundary helper as the chat tier (one str
conversion, one comparison shape), the handler comment no longer re-narrates the
shapes `_chat_scoped_run_keys` documents, and the test helper drops its unused
return.

Guards: a Matrix-id test (the regression), a chat-id-prefix test where the run
ends AT its chat id (the case the tail-bearing fixture could not show), and the
sentinel test now goes through the shared helper. Each was mutation-checked
individually — reverting the parse to slot-splitting fails the Matrix, Telegram
and workspace tests; dropping the id boundary fails the prefix test.

fix(gateway): chat-scope match must not alias a chat_id or a reply thread

Two defects found by the pre-arm review gate on the matcher above.

- The scope-slot branch ran on every platform, but only Slack ever emits that
  slot (build_session_key appends scope_id for Slack alone). A non-Slack DM keys
  chat_id as the USER id, so a per-sender group key `group:<chat>:<user>` parsed
  as "<user>'s chat": a Telegram user's /stop in her DM interrupted her group
  run in a different chat. The branch is now Slack-only.
- The thread boundary only fired for `thread`-typed keys, so a top-level channel
  turn — which keeps chat_type "channel" with the relay-stamped reply-thread ts —
  stayed reachable from a /stop in a DIFFERENT reply thread of the same channel.
  The boundary now keys on the caller's thread alone: a stop sent from inside a
  thread reaches only runs whose own first trailing slot is that thread, or that
  carry no trailing slot at all (the slotless rolling-DM shape).

Guards: one test per defect (Telegram DM vs group run ending in the same user id;
channel-keyed run belonging to another reply thread), and the workspace/profile
negative now keeps a same-chat run live so a matcher that returns nothing can no
longer satisfy it. Each guard was mutation-checked individually.

test(gateway): pin the /stop chat-scope contract and its bounds

- Negatives strengthened: the isolation tests now keep a same-chat run AND a
  foreign run live and assert exactly which one was interrupted (the previous
  version also passed on base and would have passed for any early return);
  added the chat-id prefix case ("C90") and the workspace-scope + profile case.
- New: a different thread of the same channel is never reached; a pending
  sentinel is never claimed as stopped; a peer's per-sender group run IS
  reached (documents the intentional widening of #113846).
- Assertions now read the real reply (`t("gateway.stop.*")`) and the invalidation
  reason instead of an English substring, so a locale or copy change can't
  silently satisfy them.
- Docs: `sessions.md` no longer claims interrupt handling is strictly per-user;
  `hooks.md` lists the new `stop_command_chat_scope` reason.

refactor(gateway): one structural matcher for the /stop fallback tiers

Folds the chat-scope fallback's review findings; no wiring change beyond the
thread boundary below.

- One shared scan (`_same_chat_runs`) feeds both tiers, so the enumerate-and-
  filter block is no longer duplicated and `_snapshot_running_agents()` (which
  already drops the pending sentinel) replaces the hand-rolled filter.
- Key shape is compared by slot, not by an enumerated prefix list: the
  `{"dm","group","channel","thread"}` list was incomplete against the real
  values (forum/private/room/webhook) and is gone, along with the prefix build.
- The namespace now comes from the caller's own key in BOTH tiers (the thread
  tier previously re-derived it from `source.profile`, which disagrees with the
  session store whenever multiplexing is off) — one derivation, and the
  unreachable `"agent:main"` literal is gone.
- `chat_type == "thread"` runs in a DIFFERENT thread are no longer reachable:
  another thread is another conversation. The caller's own thread, a slotless
  run (top-level channel turn, rolling DM) and non-thread keys (group/channel
  participant slots) stay reachable — the two documented shapes are unaffected.
- The two handler blocks merge into one tier selection with a single
  authorization check and one log line.

fix(gateway): /stop falls back to any running turn in the same chat

A /stop whose session key misses the running turn's key replied 'no active
task' while the turn kept running. Two supported shapes produce the miss
(found via Slack's native stop button, gateway-gateway#286): a turn triggered
by a top-level channel message keys chat_type 'channel' while an in-thread
/stop normalizes to 'thread'; rolling-DM configs key the DM session without
the thread slot the stop carries.

/stop means 'stop what's running in this chat': after the exact-key and
thread-sibling misses, _handle_stop_command now falls back chat-wide via
_chat_scoped_run_keys (same platform[, Slack scope], same chat_id, ANY
chat_type/thread/participant slot), gated on authorization, never crossing
chat_id. Namespace is derived from the caller's own key, profile-aware.
docs: setup UX a standalone memory provider keeps; catalog migration note for users

feat(memory): a configured provider that left core is installed from the catalog automatically

Built-in memory providers are moving to their maintainers' repos and the plugin catalog. Their
name, memory.<name> config section, data directory and tool names stay the same, so the only
thing a user on the built-in form loses is the code path. Two hooks now fetch it:

- hermes update: every profile home sharing the venv whose memory.provider resolves nowhere gets
  the catalog plugin installed at its reviewed pin (kill list, dependency constraints, enable).
- agent init: when the provider resolves nowhere, one attempt per process (Desktop users never
  run `hermes update` by hand); honours security.allow_lazy_installs.

Offline / not in the catalog: a warning with the exact one-liner instead of DEBUG-only silence.
Also accepts `owner/repo#subdir` for plugin installs (the catalog's spelling; honcho ships its
plugin in a subdirectory of its main repo).

Live: bundled honcho removed, memory.provider=honcho, catalog entry staged → AIAgent() installs
plugins/honcho from plastic-labs/honcho#hermes-plugin-honcho with deps and loads it; config kept.

test(slack): expiry tests raise a shape-compatible error without importing slack_sdk

CI stubs slack_sdk as a bare module, so `from slack_sdk.errors import
SlackApiError` fails there. The adapter only reads exc.response["error"];
the tests now raise a local exception with that shape. Verified with
slack_sdk blocked from import.

fix(slack): reopen a native task card when Slack seals the stream mid-turn

Slack seals a native stream server-side after a few minutes (live-observed
at ~5m20s on three independent long turns, 2026-09-15/16; the lifetime is
not documented). The next chat.appendStream on the card fails with
message_not_in_streaming_state. The adapter returned a bare failure, the
TurnRunner latched native_failed, and the rest of the turn rendered as an
edited text bullet list. Long autonomous turns lost the card UX exactly
when it mattered.

On message_not_in_streaming_state from appendStream, drop the dead
stream_ts and chat.startStream a fresh plan-mode card in the same thread,
then append the current frame there. Every frame already carries the full
visible task projection, so no task state is lost. One reopen per update;
a second rejection surfaces as a real failure. The sealed card is a plain
message now, so no stopStream is sent to it; the turn-final stop targets
the reopened card. Error matching reads SlackApiError.response["error"],
never the message text.

Tests assert the wire sequence (start, append, rejected append, start,
append on the new ts), the reopened frame's task states, the cache pointing
at the new card, and the stop targeting it; plus the one-reopen bound.
Mutation: forcing the expiry branch off turns both tests red.

fix(plugins): an installed directory plugin keeps its identity over a same-name pip entry point

The pyproject wrapper shape (#113851) depends on a pip package that often ships its own
hermes_agent.plugins entry point under the same name. Discovery appended entry points last with
"later wins", so after a catalog install the plugin row became source=entrypoint with no install
dir or catalog provenance: Desktop lost "installed from catalog @ version / update to ..." for
exactly the shape the catalog now recommends. Entry points no longer displace a directory plugin
of the same key, in the loader and in the CLI/RPC listing.

Live: catalog install of mnemosyne, row before = entrypoint / mnemosyne_hermes:register / no
catalog fields; after = user / ~/.hermes/plugins/mnemosyne / catalog 0.7.0 @ 95ef3be2; provider
still discovered. Test red on base.
docs(bedrock): specify persisted URL for cache invalidation
fix(bedrock): restore Grok context with provider-confirmed cache provenance

fix(bedrock): cache only probed context windows, memoise probe failures

`_resolve_bedrock_context_length` means to persist only probe-derived context
windows -- its comment says "Only persist probe-derived values (region present);
a pure table fallback must not poison the cache" -- but the code under it cannot
tell the two apart. `get_bedrock_context_length(model, region=region,
probe=bool(region))` returns the probed window when the probe succeeds and the
static table (or the 128K default) when it does not, in the same int, and the
guard `if ctx and region:` tests the region, not the probe. The region is never
empty: `resolve_bedrock_region()` ends in `or "us-east-1"`.

Observed on a Bedrock deployment whose SSO session expires every 8 hours: the
first turn after expiry probes without credentials, `probe_bedrock_context_length`
returns None, and

    context_lengths:
      '<opus-5 global inference profile id>@bedrock:': 128000

is written (the synthetic `bedrock://` key lands on disk as `@bedrock:`, since
`_context_cache_key` strips trailing slashes) -- `BEDROCK_DEFAULT_CONTEXT_LENGTH`, because that model has no
`BEDROCK_CONTEXT_LENGTHS` row (#74263, addressed by #75824). The resolver returns
any cached value before it considers probing, so the probe never runs again for
that model and the compressor works from a 128K window on a 1M model.

The resolver now asks the probe itself and persists only what the probe said:

  probe returned a window   persist under model@base_url (or model@bedrock://), return it
  probe returned None       return the static table / default, persist nothing,
                            memoise the failure in memory for 5 minutes
  cached value present      serve it, as before

The memo keeps this cheap. `probe_bedrock_context_length` pads prompts of 1.3M and
2.2M tokens and attempts up to two `converse` calls (`_BEDROCK_PROBE_TIERS`; the
second tier is sent only when the first yields no parseable limit, i.e. on the
failure path), and `_cached_client` is a bare `boto3.client` that never validates
credentials, so a model whose probe keeps returning None WITH working credentials
(un-enabled model, opaque InternalServerException, unparseable length error)
would otherwise re-send both on every resolution -- and resolution is not memoised
per instance (model switch, every turn containing '@', each fallback candidate,
each /models API call). `_BEDROCK_PROBE_FAILURE_CACHE` /
`_BEDROCK_PROBE_FAILURE_TTL_SECONDS` follow the file's existing convention for
this shape (`_ENDPOINT_PROBE_FAILURE_TTL_SECONDS`, `_LOCAL_CTX_PROBE_CACHE`):
negative results in memory only, bounded, so credentials that come back are
noticed. A successful probe drops the entry, and
`_invalidate_cached_context_length` clears it for the model alongside the
local-probe memos, since a dropped entry is the reason to probe again.

Prior report: #68049 (open, 2026-07-20) fixes the same persistence defect with
the same core replacement (probe directly, persist only a probed window, return
`get_bedrock_context_length(model, probe=False)` otherwise). Its hunk targets the
inline code in `get_model_context_length` that has since moved into
`_resolve_bedrock_context_length`, so it no longer applies to main. This commit
adds, on top of that mechanism, the in-memory failure memo, its clearing on
invalidation, and a test of the memo's TTL.

Deliberately unchanged: the cached-value path of `_resolve_bedrock_context_length`
(a persisted value is served as on main; the step-1 table floor is not applied
to the `bedrock://` key, because a probed window may legitimately be below the
table and flooring it would re-probe every second call);
`get_bedrock_context_length` (signature, `probe=` parameter, table lookup and its
tests); `BEDROCK_CONTEXT_LENGTHS` (the missing Opus 5 row is #75824);
`save_context_length` / `get_cached_context_length`; the step ordering in
`get_model_context_length`.

tests/agent/test_model_metadata.py::TestBedrockContextCachePersistence, 2 cases:
a failed probe for a model with no table row persists nothing, and a failed probe
is memoised so a second resolution inside the TTL costs no probe and writes
nothing, then once the memo lapses the probe runs again and its window is what
gets persisted. Both fail on main, which persists 128000 on the first call.

test(rust): property and parametrized tests for legacy callback contracts

The payload boundary of callbacks-legacy gets a model-based proptest: for any
JSON body, caller keywords and callback edit, keywords the route sends unchanged
reach pre_call as the caller's own objects, and the wire is the body pre_call
received as the callback left it. A parametrized test pins that a keyword the
bridge never reads keeps its identity through setup, the deployment hook,
check_limits and prepare.

Behaviour owned by the real Logging object is pinned end to end in the OCR
tests: a hypothesis version of the body property over HTTP, sync hooks seeing no
running event loop, retained payloads staying intact after the call, success
callbacks sharing one standard logging payload, and state stashed before a
blocking deployment hook raises reaching both failure callback families

refactor(rust): route-neutral callback contract

Every legacy callback call from callbacks-legacy now goes through one typed
Python shim, litellm.rust_bridge.legacy_callbacks, the only Python module
the crate reaches. Before, the crate called Logging methods, litellm.utils
hooks, the logging worker, the executor and several litellm globals
directly, and its tests retyped those signatures by hand, so an outdated
fake could accept a call the real code rejects. python_contract.json lists
each shim function's parameters: a Python test pins it to the real
signatures and a Rust test pins it to the Rust enum.

The lifecycle contract changes to match the Python @client wrapper:
- the driver emits CallEvent::Started before begin, so every host sees one
  start time
- RequestContext carries the route-resolved api_key, so legacy pre_call and
  post_call receive it, and post_call's additional_args match the Python OCR
  path
- Passthrough and its re-aliasing are gone
- async deployment hooks always run, and the "no callbacks" shortcut that
  skipped the logging payload is removed, as in the Python path

The OCR api_key is a SecretValue from the wire request onward, so Debug
output upstream of the callback contract cannot leak it.

host-python's RouteHost now classifies native failures once through

* feat(proxy): limit repeated failed Admin UI sign-in attempts

The Admin UI sign-in endpoints accept an unbounded number of password attempts.
All three call authenticate_user, and none of them keeps any record of how many
times a given caller has already been refused, so a misbehaving or misconfigured
client can retry indefinitely at full speed.

A LoginThrottle is now a required argument to authenticate_user, so the accounting
lives at the one function all three endpoints share and a fourth endpoint cannot be
added without deciding what to pass. Failures are counted per username and source
address over a fixed window and further attempts are refused with 429 and a
Retry-After header. The check runs before the database lookup and before the
password comparison, so a refused caller does no further work.

Only genuine credential rejections count. Configuration errors do not, a refused
attempt does not extend the window, and a successful sign-in clears the bucket.
The username is case folded because the user lookup is case insensitive, so casing
cannot multiply the allowance. Both credential rejections now return one identical
message. SSO is unaffected; it never calls this function.

max_failed_login_attempts (10) and failed_login_window_seconds (900) are read from
config.yaml, with LITELLM_DISABLE_LOGIN_RATE_LIMIT to turn the accounting off. They
are deliberately not database backed, so editing YAML always wins and an operator
refused by a bad value can recover.

refactor(proxy): make the config file win over the database

The precedence used to vary per key: some keys let a stored row win, some
let the file win, some merged the two. That meant an operator could not
answer "which value is live?" without knowing the key.

Now file presence decides ownership. A key the config file declares is
config-owned, whatever the database holds, and a key the file omits falls
back to the stored row. KeyRule no longer carries a RuleKind, only which
row the stored value lives in.

Writes to a config-owned key are refused at the two surfaces that reach
the database instead of being stored and silently ignored: save_config
and /config/field/update both 400 naming the key and the config file path.

Both read endpoints now report source and editable off the same
SettingsStore, so /config/field/info and /config/list can no longer
disagree inside one process.

Replaces the 786-case checked-in JSON fixture with cases generated from
the rule table, so the matrix tests no longer assert that resolve() agrees
with a snapshot of resolve().

BREAKING CHANGE: a dashboard or /config/field/update write to a setting
the config file declares now returns 400 instead of being stored. Remove
the key from the config file to let the database own it.

lifecycles are gone

reworks: an inlined remote document no longer counts as the caller's value, so the legacy
adapter never hands the caller's URL back into the body. core/tests/ocr/passthrough.rs pins

fix(matrix): keep startup storage SQLite off the Gateway thread (#151994)

Related: #151845

## What Problem This Solves

Matrix client startup still runs storage-root selection, initial metadata, and legacy crypto imports through SQLite on the Gateway thread.

## User Impact

These startup operations now use the existing SQLite worker while preserving token-rotation selection, device identity, saved sync state, and migration recovery. Device backfill remains nonblocking at startup, and shutdown joins its admitted writes. No configuration, schema, or minimum host-version change is required.

Credential-readiness and package auth-presence probes retain their synchronous SDK contracts.

## Why This Change Was Made

The client factory awaits root selection, migration, and metadata before returning a client. Metadata comparisons preserve concurrent token claims and learned device IDs. The existing monitor task runner owns backfill cancellation and settlement, including disposal of its temporary identity client. Backfill rechecks credential lineage before publishing credentials after metadata persistence.

Claimed canonical roots still skip token-history scans. Rotated tokens reuse only active roots with matching devices; archived roots stay excluded. Imports still finish before archival, and interrupted archival preserves completed imports and unrelated files. Hosts without comparison support retain the named native compatibility path; a worker failure never selects it.

## Evidence

- The real client factory restored the seeded cursor but recorded 501 host SQLite `prepare` calls for a canonical root and 516 for token rotation before this change.
- Candidate factory tests record zero host `prepare`, `exec`, `get`, `all`, `run`, or `iterate` calls for canonical roots, rotated roots, and legacy crypto imports.
- Focused storage, Doctor, client factory, auth, startup verification, thread-binding, and monitor tests passed. Race tests cover initialization and token claims against a concurrently learned device, with explicit device inputs remaining authoritative. Other cases cover capability selection, worker failure, stale or cancelled backfill, and retirement settlement.
- Actual SDK HTTP fixtures on loopback verify that retirement closes an in-flight identity request and that token-only login disposes its identity client before returning. Request and cleanup failures remain available together.
- `pnpm build`, the changed-scope gate (including production/test typechecks and full extension lint), and the isolated built Matrix import profile passed. Fresh independent review found no actionable P0–P2 issues.
- No external Matrix account or live Gateway was used.

migrateLegacyMeetingTranscripts disposed of its private stage database in a
bare finally, so a failed close, a failed unlink of the disposable stage file
(force suppresses only ENOENT, not the EPERM/EBUSY an indexer or scanner
produces on Windows) or a failed lock release threw out of the function and
replaced the MigrationMessages it was about to return.

By then the migration had already committed: rows imported and verified, the
legacy tree moved to the archive root, the run recorded completed. Doctor
recorded the step as refused with no changes, so the operator never saw the
import or the archive path their files had just moved to, every later state
migration and repair was marked blocked and skipped, and doctor --fix exited 1.

failure into a warning next to the real outcome, and mark a result whose only
warnings are that disposal recoverable so Doctor reports it and continues. A
lock release that fails still refuses, matching state-migrations.lock.ts.

refactor(transcripts): run stored lookups in the shared SQLite worker (#146547)

Related: #144592
Related: #147375
Related: #147246
Dependency: #151816

## What Problem This Solves

Stored transcript detail and note lookups return promises but still execute SQLite on the Gateway event loop.

## User Impact

Transcript identity, descriptor, note, summary, and utterance lookups execute in the shared SQLite worker. Existing selectors, content, ordering, limits, and error responses are preserved. No schema migration or configuration change is required.

Chronological list queries and streaming/export snapshots retain their current owners. Capture appends are a separate stacked change in #151760.

## Why This Change Was Made

Eleven typed commands call the existing read kernels through the canonical shared-state worker. Compound enumeration, matching, and library reads keep one deferred snapshot. First-use schema creation finishes before those reads, canonical close drains accepted work, and existing-only task inspection stays non-creating. Meeting fixtures stop producers before asynchronous database cleanup, and canonical test routing keeps worker consumers in their owning processes.

The composition preserves Doctor's device-token dispatch alongside all eleven transcript commands, shared transaction-settlement checks, plugin-reload ownership, and current test-routing changes. Chronological reads preserve their parent-timezone date function; exports preserve their snapshot lifetime.

Qualified dependency history from #151816 is incorporated through normal merge ancestry. It pins the deprecated message facade at its published exports, aligns three global surface limits with the resulting smaller counts, and carries the canonical catalog-materialization prerequisite with its strict 18-read assertion. The per-entry SDK compatibility limit remains unchanged. This does not claim that dependency PR #151816 has merged.

fix(matrix): keep sync-cache SQLite off the Gateway thread (#151845)

## What Problem This Solves

Matrix sync-cache restore, persistence, and deletion run SQLite on the Gateway thread even though the cache methods return promises.

## User Impact

These cache operations now run in the existing SQLite worker while preserving restart replay, clean-shutdown markers, and failure reporting. No configuration, schema, or minimum host-version change is required.

Matrix credentials, storage-root selection, and initial storage metadata remain separate work; this does not move every Matrix database operation off-thread.

## Why This Change Was Made

The client factory awaits the loaded cache before publishing the client, so the monitor's pre-start replay decision sees the persisted cursor. The live cache reuses the async keyed-store operations and chunk writer. A storage-root queue keeps a reader's generation intact until its chunk reads finish, while the client still owns debounce, flush, deletion, and quiescence. The obsolete synchronous cache helpers are removed, and QA Lab uses the same prepared-store path.

## Evidence

- The original cold-load/persist/restore/delete regression recorded 2,128 host SQLite `prepare` calls. The migrated flow records zero host `prepare`, `exec`, `get`, `all`, `run`, or `iterate` calls.
- A two-store regression reproduces a lost cursor when a writer removes chunks while another reader is paused after reading metadata; the storage-root queue preserves the reader's generation.
- 79 focused tests passed, including real `matrix-js-sdk` sync/crypto behavior against synthetic HTTP fixtures, published-schema Doctor repair, storage migration, and QA Lab. Final adjustments were rechecked with 26 cache/factory/SDK tests and 18 shutdown cases.
- `pnpm build`, the changed-scope gate, extension production/test typechecks, and `git diff --check` passed. The gate reported only a nonblocking max-lines warning in an untouched memory-manager file.
- No external Matrix account or live Gateway was used.
- Fresh independent review of the exact final diff found no actionable P0–P2 issues.
- Initial CI failed on the shared catalog test expecting 20 SQLite reads while observing 18. The follow-up reuses the canonical strict 18-read correction, qualified locally with 3 binding-authority reads and zero worker operations per list; all zero-I/O checks and the CPU bound remain intact. Matrix runtime code is unchanged.

fix: retain model refresh failure after catalog worker recovery (#151597)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes lost refresh-failure status and repeated background discovery when the shared catalog worker exits during a provider renewal.

## User Impact

Last-good models stay usable. Passive reads do not repeat the failed renewal. Healthy providers can refresh, and explicit Retry can recover without switching the selected model, runtime or account.

## Why This Change Was Made

Record the active request's failure before recovery replaces its prepared owner. Failure status has one writer: the existing source-bound attempt reporter. Early notification and later rejection settle once; the caller still receives the original error.

## Evidence

- The registered `models.list` regression fails on the original code: rows survive, but `refreshFailed` is missing.
- All 64 focused behavior cases pass, including the real Gateway worker crash, provider scope, account replacement, native separation and shutdown. The corrected routing assertion and eight-file format check also pass.
- A controlled Gateway crash kept the picker usable; three passive reads made no extra provider request. Before/after images show retained usability, not a warning banner.

Registered red/green command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/server-methods/models-list.worker-recovery.integration.test.ts`.

[Inspected before/after picker images](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/151597#issuecomment-5726894039).

## Compatibility

No config, schema, public API or credential-precedence change. No new timer, automatic retry or account-access policy. This does not claim private-account discovery or updater fixes.

## Consumers

Gateway model-list requests and active catalog-worker borrowers retain the existing published model inventory and failure status.

## Invalidation

An admitted renewal failure expires the affected committed inventory before worker recovery. Account, plugin and source replacement still use existing owner checks; explicit refresh remains the recovery action.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes missing skill-use counts when tool diagnostics are disabled and missing directly created Workshop skills.

## User Impact

Status reports current Workshop files and recorded use. No skills are removed. Missing use is not proof of inactivity; native reads outside OpenClaw tools remain untracked.

## Consumers

The tool wrapper, Gateway and CLI use the existing owners. Public schema exports and existing Swift response types remain compatible.

## Invalidation

Status rereads configured roots and joins history by file path. Deleted files disappear; moving a skill does not transfer usage by name.

| Baseline prompt-budget 402 | 2 | 2 | Cancelled after reproduction; billing invariant fails |
| Fixed prompt-budget 402 | 1 | 0 | Billing error |
| Fixed output-budget 402 | 1 | 0 | Billing error |

fix(agents): keep a waiting reply when delegated work yields (#151032)

Related: #101656; completes the waiting-reply behavior from #125106.

## What Problem This Solves

An interactive parent could delegate work, yield without an acknowledgment, and leave Telegram silent until the final answer.

## Why This Change Was Made

One shared reply mechanism now selects the waiting text for implicit continuation and explicit yield. Runtime execution supplies facts instead of competing presentation. This state has one writer. Removes 18 lines overall, including 4 production lines.

## User Impact

A waiting reply remains without requiring the model to supply it. Explicit text overrides still work; quiet turns stay quiet. The parent still owns the final answer. No new timers or progress-notification defaults.

## Evidence

Real Telegram Test Server: before, no waiting reply at 30 seconds; after, the default reply arrives at 3 seconds and remains. Final delivery is automatic. Scripted responses control the wait. 314 tests pass on fresh main; 43 queued tests and 237 registration checks pass.

![Before: no waiting reply](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/387101c7-6be3-4c57-a091-2f6cf52ce6ec)
![After: waiting reply remains](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5d780555-e0bd-442b-a8ef-b73a107ac007)

## Compatibility

No configuration, schema, or public tool-field changes.

## Consumers

Direct and queued replies use the same waiting-text owner.

## Invalidation

Existing turn, silence, and delivery ownership remain unchanged.

## Tests

Missing acknowledgment, explicit override, quiet contexts, visible replies, and continuation settlement.

feat(provider-registry): add Moonshot AI global endpoint (#18835)

Add a built-in moonshot-global provider serving the international
endpoint (https://api.moonshot.ai, plus the /anthropic mirror) with the
international console links. It folds under the existing moonshot
preset, mirroring the minimax/minimax-global pair: shared reasoning
format, web-search server-tool declaration, and K2.6/K3 reasoning
overrides are extracted in moonshot.ts so the two endpoints cannot drift
apart. The English label of the CN entry is disambiguated to "Moonshot
CN" (same pattern as "MiniMax CN" / "MiniMax").

<!-- Template from
https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md?-->
<!--  Thanks for sending a pull request!  Here are some tips for you:
1. Consider creating this PR as draft:
https://github.com/CherryHQ/cherry-studio/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md
-->

> ### Branch strategy
>
> - Active development targets `main`.

### What this PR does

Before this PR:
The built-in Moonshot provider only ships the China endpoint
(https://api.moonshot.cn) with links to the CN console
([platform.moonshot.cn](http://platform.moonshot.cn/)). Users who signed
up on the international console (platform.moonshot.ai) hold API keys
that only work against https://api.moonshot.ai, so they have to
hand-create a custom OpenAI-compatible provider and copy the base URL
from the docs.

After this PR:
A new built-in moonshot-global provider serves the international
endpoint (https://api.moonshot.ai, plus the /anthropic mirror) with the
international console links. It folds under the existing moonshot preset
(same sidebar group, same icon, same runtime extension), mirroring the
existing minimax / minimax-global pair. The English label of the CN
entry is disambiguated to “Moonshot CN” (same pattern as “MiniMax CN” /
“MiniMax”).

<!-- (optional, in `fixes #<issue number>(, fixes #<issue_number>, ...)`
format, will close the issue(s) when PR gets merged)*: -->

Fixes #

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way
Moonshot operates two separate consoles and key pools:
[platform.moonshot.cn](http://platform.moonshot.cn/) (CN) and
[platform.moonshot.ai](http://platform.moonshot.ai/) (global). Keys are
not interchangeable across hosts; the global host is the one documented
to overseas users.

The following tradeoffs were made:
- `moonshot-global` reuses the exact connection behavior of the CN
preset — the reasoning format (`thinking.type` wire), the Kimi
`$web_search` server-tool declaration, and the K2.6/K3 reasoning
overrides are extracted to shared exports in `moonshot.ts` and
referenced by both, so the two endpoints cannot drift apart.
- `presetProviderId: 'moonshot'` routes runtime config through the
existing Moonshot extension (`matchesPreset`), so no new adapter code
was needed; the extension declares `aliases: ['moonshot-global']` like
`MinimaxExtension` does.
- The provider icon reuses the existing `moonshot` mark via
`PROVIDER_ID_ALIASES`.

The following alternatives were considered:
- Changing the existing provider's default host to `.ai`: rejected, it
would break every existing CN user.
- A host dropdown inside one provider entry: larger UI change; the
registry already has the dual-entry precedent (`minimax-global`, also
`zai`→`zhipu` folding), so this PR follows it.

Links to places where the discussion took place: <!-- optional: slack,

fix(seeding): lint-ban overwriting upserts in seeders (#20729)

### What this PR does

Before this PR: the seeding directory had no guard against
overwrite-style upserts. The legacy web-search preference upgrade
shipped an `onConflictDoUpdate` that force-wrote `!legacy` over the
already-renamed key on every seeder re-run (#20686 fixes the instance) —
and nothing in CI would have stopped the next seeder written the same
way.

After this PR: `no-restricted-syntax` fails CI for any
`onConflictDoUpdate` under `src/main/data/db/seeding/**` unless it is
exempted inline with a reason. The two sanctioned overwrites are
exempted explicitly:

- `SeedRunner.ts` — upserts the internal journal key (`seed:<name>` in
app state), not user state.
- `miniAppSeeder.ts` — refreshes preset display fields only, scoped by
`setWhere` to preset-seeded rows; custom rows are untouched.

Tests and `__tests__` fixtures are out of scope for the rule.

Fixes #

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

A seeder re-runs whenever its journal `version` changes, so "write the
migrated value" and "write the default" are only safe as
insert-if-absent. Today that invariant lives only as a per-seeder
authoring convention — every other seeder obeys it, but nothing enforces
it, so a future upgrade seeder can reintroduce the same clobber with CI
green.

An ESLint `no-restricted-syntax` override (the same local-warn /
CI-error pattern the console rule uses) turns the convention into a gate
at the exact construct that caused the bug, while leaving legitimate
scoped upserts available behind an explicit, reviewable exemption
comment.

Alternatives considered: a shared insert-if-absent helper (nothing left
to convert — the audited seeder set is already compliant, so the helper
would be dead code), and a run-all-seeders-twice idempotency test
(clobber-style bugs are idempotent — they set the same wrong value on
every run — so it would not have caught #20686).

### Breaking changes

None. Lint-only: one new restriction scoped to the seeding directory;
two inline exemptions for the existing sanctioned upserts.

### Special notes for your reviewer

- The rule is scoped to the seeding directory only. The v2 migration
engine (`src/main/data/migration/v2/**`) is deliberately not covered:
its upserts run once behind a one-shot status marker, a different risk
profile.
- The rule reports at the start of the insert chain, which is why the
two exemption comments sit above the chain rather than on the
`.onConflictDoUpdate` line.
- Stack note: the first commit is #20686's fix; the guard rides on top
so the banned construct is absent from the tree when the rule lands. It
merges after #20686 and retargets automatically.

feat(agent-session): add native checkpoint forks (#20340)

[Architecture
decision](https://github.com/CherryHQ/cherry-studio/pull/20340#issuecomment-5676521846)
| [Behavior and
ownership](https://github.com/CherryHQ/cherry-studio/blob/feat/agent-session-fork/docs/references/ai/agent-session-fork.md)

## Why the change

Let users branch a Pi, Claude Code or DSH Agent conversation from a
completed turn, preserving its visible messages and native context in an
independent session that waits for new input.

## Special things to note

- Fork requires a valid native checkpoint and available history; Cherry
does not reconstruct context from UI messages or manage harness
summaries. Claude and DSH also surface ordinary resume failures instead
of restarting with empty history.
- User workspaces remain shared; system workspaces copy their current
files without restoring historical versions. Queued inputs, running
tasks, approval authority and usage statistics are not inherited.
- No SQL migration is added: checkpoints use private message JSON. Files
are published before the child database transaction; ownership manifests
support cleanup after failure or restart. Successful forks retain
manifests and staged snapshots, including Pi lineage files.

## Change outline

Capture the native boundary when a turn completes; keep it inside Main.

```text
Runtime adapter: turn-complete(checkpoint)
  -> AgentSessionMessageBackend
     -> message.data.runtimeAnchor { checkpoint, excludedMessageIds }
        -> stripped from public message reads
```

Fork through the existing runtime owner, then open the committed child.

```text
Agent assistant message menu -> Fork
  ai.agent.session.fork({ sourceSessionId, messageId }) -> { sessionId }
    AgentSessionRuntimeService [admission, drain, cancellation]
      AgentSessionForkOperations
        1. AgentSessionForkService.read: selected message prefix + checkpoint
        2. Record owned resources; prepare workspace and staging directory
        3. Runtime driver.fork: native files + child resume token + remapped checkpoints
        4. Clone visible messages with new IDs; remove execution state
        5. Publish native files
        6. DbService.withWriteTx
             recheck source prefix, Agent and workspace
             create child session and messages atomically
        7. Notify read models -> UI opens child, ready for input
```

Each adapter owns its checkpoint and native fork behavior; Fork does not
start or interrupt the source.

```text
Pi       newest matching history file -> SessionManager.createBranchedSession(leafId)
Claude   transcript through assistant UUID -> isolated worker -> SDK forkSession
DSH      live snapshot or stored events -> isolated worker -> seeded SessionStore
           live source: wait for startup, or shutdown flush, before reading history
           each wait supports cancellation and a 60-second timeout

Child's next input -> existing runtimeResumeToken path -> normal native resume
```

feat(agent-heartbeat): restore heartbeat schedule provisioning on the JobManager stack (#20055)

### What this PR does

**Before:** the heartbeat switch and interval in the agent edit dialog
round-trip to `agent.configuration` while nothing produces a run. v1's
producer (`SchedulerService.ensureHeartbeatTask`) was dropped in the
JobManager migration, so no `agent.task` schedule carrying the
`__heartbeat__` sentinel is ever created (#19203) — and v1-migrated rows
point at a system workspace that `runAgentTask`'s heartbeat branch
rejects, so they skip forever too. The execution path is fully intact
and waiting on a schedule that has no producer.

**After:** the producer is restored on the v2 stack, aligned with the
sentinel-only identity introduced by #19568:

- **`syncHeartbeatSchedule`** (new
`src/main/ai/agents/heartbeatSchedule.ts`) — the config→schedule
translation, idempotent and converging:
- no row → create (`heartbeat_<agentId>`, interval trigger,
`skip-missed`); a drifted row → repair **in place** preserving its name
(this is what fixes migrated system-workspace rows); already correct →
no-op;
- a disabled heartbeat **pauses** the row (zero timer ticks) instead of
deleting it; the run-side `heartbeat_enabled === false` gate stays as a
backstop;
- invalid intervals (0/negative/non-numeric mean "unset", per the
renderer's `|| DEFAULT` form fallback) fall back to the 30-minute
default and clamp to the form's 1–1440 range;
- runtime capability gating mirrors the edit dialog — dsh agents get no
schedule.
- **Heartbeat home:** the heartbeat session runs in a user workspace
over the agent **data directory**, where `heartbeat.md` is seeded with a
comments-only template beside SOUL.md/USER.md. `readHeartbeat` now
treats a comments-only file as effectively empty, so an
enabled-by-default heartbeat skips the model call entirely until the
user writes a real checklist — default-on stays free.
- **Wiring:** agent creation provisions the schedule (failure logged,
not fatal — the v1 contract); a configuration save carrying either
heartbeat key re-syncs, so switch/interval changes take effect on the
next tick, not after a restart; a startup repair pass converges every
agent once (per-agent failures isolated).

### Why we need it and why it was done this way

- Identity by sentinel prompt + template agentId, never the schedule
name: the v1→v2 migration disambiguates names under the `(type, name)`
UNIQUE index (`task_<v1Id>`), so the name is the one marker it cannot
guarantee — same conclusion as #19568.
- The data directory as heartbeat workspace: system workspaces are
per-session ephemeral directories, which is exactly why migrated rows
never fire; the data directory is the one stable per-agent home.
Registered via `findOrCreateByPath` (idempotent on the path unique
index) with a "Heartbeat — <agent>" display name.
- Pausing instead of deleting on disable: no timer churn, no re-create
cost on re-enable, and the UNIQUE(`heartbeat_<agentId>`) name doubles as
the guard against duplicate rows if two syncs race.
- The comments-only template + effectively-empty skip follows the same
cost-gate principle as the HEARTBEAT.md mechanism in comparable agent
platforms: an idle heartbeat must cost zero model calls.

### Breaking changes

None. The run side (`runAgentTask`) is untouched; agents whose heartbeat
is off behave exactly as before (the row, if any, just stops ticking).

### Testing

New `heartbeatSchedule.test.ts` (real file-backed DB + real
JobManager/SchedulerService, mirroring `AgentJobsService.test.ts`):
create/seeds-file, never-touches-existing-file, idempotent no-op, custom
interval, invalid-interval default, **migrated-row in-place repair
preserving the name**, pause on disable, resume+repair on re-enable,
capability skip (dsh), missing-agent, two distinct agents, and the
startup repair pass. `heartbeat.test.ts` gains the comments-only skip
cases. Full `main` project: 925 files / 14,467 tests green; `pnpm lint`
clean.

Credit: #19214 attacked the same producer gap on the pre-#19568 codebase
(name-based identity); this PR is an independent implementation on
current main and supersedes it.

> ### Branch strategy
>
> - Active development targets `main`.

### What this PR does

Before this PR:

- The MCP SDK opens the browser during `client.connect()`, but Cherry
Studio only created the localhost OAuth callback server afterwards, when
`connect()` threw `UnauthorizedError`. A redirect landing before
`listen()` completed was refused with a `127.0.0.1` connection-rejected
page.
- A callback bind failure (e.g. port `12346` already in use) was stored
as a rejected promise nobody awaited, so nothing ever listened and the
flow hung until the 5-minute auth-code timeout — matching the reported
`netstat` output showing the port never open.

After this PR:

- The OAuth callback server is started and awaited **before** the first
`connect()`, so the browser redirect always lands on a listening port.
- A bind failure rejects immediately with an actionable message (`OAuth
callback could not listen on 127.0.0.1:<port> (<code>): free the port
and retry`) instead of hanging for 5 minutes.
- `CallBackServer.close()` tolerates a failed listen and double-close
(timeout + finally), so error paths no longer produce unhandled
rejections.

<!-- (optional, in `fixes #<issue number>(, fixes #<issue_number>, ...)`
format, will close the issue(s) when PR gets merged)*: -->

Fixes #20624

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- The pre-started server is owned by `connectWithFallback` (closed in
`finally` on every path, including non-auth success) rather than by
`finishOAuth`, so no listener leaks when auth turns out not to be
needed.
- Concurrent OAuth flows still share the fixed port `12346`: the second
one now fails fast with a clear message instead of hanging. Per-server
ports would require re-registering `redirect_uri` per flow and is out of
scope for this fix.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Retrying `listen()` in a loop until the redirect arrives: hides real
bind failures and keeps the port-open race.
- Picking a random free port per flow: breaks the `redirect_uri`
registered via dynamic client registration.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

Doctor detects and guides. The only repairs are boot-config recovery,
permission requests, and targeted MCP restart. Storage cleanup, update
installation, and hardware-acceleration changes stay in existing
user-controlled settings flows. This PR adds no new Doctor UI.

Runs and fixes are mutually exclusive; fixes validate report identity,
expiry, and matching actions again after re-probing. Partial selections
include transitive prerequisites, invalid tiers fail before publishing
running, and initialization or execution failures cannot leave a
misleading running/healthy state. Passing checks never offer actions,
and only MCP restart accepts a required target.

Log reading, diagnostic measurement, MCP resolution, and runtime probes
propagate cancellation, with 20-second Doctor budgets for expensive
checks. Logs are scanned once per run; truncated/unreadable evidence
stays explicitly incomplete. Model IDs and custom tool names remain
local-only; raw MCP errors and native causes require consent for
export/upload.

The following alternatives were considered:

Automatic deletion/retention policies and expanded trusted deletion
roots were not adopted for V1. The unsafe cleanup fixes and public
logs-cleanup group were removed instead. Hardware enable is navigation
rather than a new fix. A new account settings entry and broader
native-module probes are outside this scope; account login already lives
in the sidebar profile popup, and the native probe explicitly covers

feat(doctor): System Doctor infrastructure, NetworkService and entry points (#19982)

> ### Branch strategy
>
> - Active development targets `main`.

### What this PR does

Before this PR:

Diagnostics lived in scattered places (bundle export/upload, log-scan
rules, the assistant's `diagnose` MCP tool, per-settings-page checks).
There was no shared contract for "a health check with a result and a
repair action", nothing could answer "is it DNS, TLS, the proxy or the
server?" for the app's own endpoints, and the System Doctor had no entry
point.

After this PR (three stacked PRs merged into this branch:
infrastructure, #19985 NetworkService, #19987 entry points):

**System Doctor infrastructure**
- `src/shared/types/doctor.ts`: a catalog-driven contract.
`DOCTOR_CHECK_CATALOG` declares every check (domain, tier, fixes with
risk metadata, detail variants, prerequisites); check ids, fix ids,
detail variants, actions and results are all derived types. Report data
carries `dataClass` (`public` / `local_only` / `consent_required`) and
`projectDoctorReport()` builds the display / copy / export / upload
views.
- `src/main/services/diagnostics/doctor/`: a pure engine (prerequisite
layering, per-check timeout via `AbortSignal.timeout`, run cancellation,
skip cascade, per-lane concurrency via `p-queue`), an exhaustive
registry typed as `{ [Id in DoctorCheckId]: DoctorCheckDefinition<Id>
}`, a per-run `DoctorContext.share()` memo, and `DoctorService`
(lifecycle, `WhenReady`) that publishes progress and the final report on
the shared cache key `doctor.state`.
- IpcApi routes `diagnostics.doctor.run` / `.cancel` / `.fix`. `fix` is
bound to a `runId`, re-probes before executing and answers `stale` when
the run was superseded or the finding changed.
- `doctor/README.md` documents the three edits needed to add a check and
how the renderer consumes `doctor.state`.

**NetworkService** (`src/main/services/network/`)
- Lifecycle service owning online/offline state (shared cache
`network.online`), the proxy Chromium actually uses for a URL
(`session.resolveProxy` + the new read-only
`ProxyService.getAppliedSnapshot()` with apply convergence), the
built-in endpoint list (constants exported by their owning services),
and `diagnoseEndpoint()` with the DNS → TLS → proxy → HTTP cascade. Pure
probes and the error classifier (walks `error.cause`) live in
`probes.ts`; the code table and result types in `types.ts` (main-only
until a renderer consumer exists).
- `tests/helpers/http/server.ts`: reusable loopback HTTP and self-signed
HTTPS servers; `probes.e2e.test.ts` exercises the probes over real
sockets.

**Checks shipped** (10): `config-boot-config-valid` (with a `repair`
fix), `storage-userdata-location` (detects the silent fallback to the
default data directory), and eight `network-*` checks (online, DNS, TLS,
proxy, four built-in endpoints) sharing one diagnosis pass per run.

**Entry points**
- Help menu → "System Diagnostics" (`appMenu.doctor`, 13 locales)
navigates the main window to `/settings/about?doctor=checks` via
`openSettingsInMainWindow`; `doctorSettingsPath()` in
`@shared/types/doctor` is the contract the About page mounts the dialog
on.
- Assistant `diagnose` tool: `health` now returns NetworkService's
layered verdict (endpoint origin only); new `doctor` action runs
`DoctorService` and returns the report's `upload` projection so nothing
local-only reaches the model.

Domain checks and the dialog land in follow-up PRs against this
contract.

Fixes #

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- Checks are declared in a registry (same pattern as
`diagnostics/scan/rules`), not via decorators: no import-order side
effects, no metadata reflection, direct unit tests. Only the two
lifecycle services use decorators.
- Run state goes through the shared cache instead of IpcApi events:
every window sees the same run, the report dies with the process
(time-bound via `expiresAt`), and the IPC surface is three routes.
- Route outputs use `z.custom<T>()` (outputs are not parsed; precedent
in `schemas/ai.ts`); the `fix` input is validated by a catalog guard.
- Network probes are a general service, not doctor-internal: the
assistant tool and the coming proxy-settings test button consume the
same cascade. The `network.diagnose_endpoint` route was dropped until
that button exists.
- Log-scan rules were not rewritten to generate anchors from the code
table (`scan/rules/README.md` requires evidence-driven anchors); the
table is the superset they draw from.

The following alternatives were considered:

- A `@DoctorCheck()` decorator per check: rejected for the reasons
above.
- Loose `string` ids / fix ids: rejected; a 9-case negative typecheck
confirmed the catalog turns each misuse into a compile error.
- Mocking `net.fetch` only for the probes: rejected; the E2E against a
real server found a classification bug (undici buries errno under
`error.cause`) the mocks would have hidden.

(internal Feishu doc); review of #19985 (19 findings addressed in
`bdeeb7e8b9`, `df0c0f6001`, `d010ed5452`).
