fix(html-to-markdown): convert a fetched table into a table (#20644) ### The bug Turndown ships **no table support at all**. Both places that convert fetched HTML build a bare `new TurndownService()`, so a `` is flattened into one paragraph per cell. Measured on `main` (6ffa760): ``` input:

Specs

ProductPrice
Cable9 EUR
Hub29 EUR
output: Specs ===== Product Price Cable 9 EUR Hub 29 EUR ``` `9 EUR` is no longer attached to `Cable` in any way, and `Hub` sits between them. Whatever reads this — the fetch MCP tool's caller, or the browser tool's — has nothing left to join a value to its row or its column by. Every fetched page with a pricing table, an API parameter table or a comparison matrix arrives like this. ### The change One new `src/main/utils/htmlToMarkdown.ts` exporting `applyTableRules(turndown)`, applied at both call sites: - `src/main/ai/mcp/servers/fetch.ts` — the fetch MCP server's `markdown` tool - `src/main/features/browser/mcp/BrowserPageController.ts` — `format: 'markdown'` The rules: - `th`/`td` → a cell; a `
` inside it folds to a space, since a newline would end the row halfway through; - `tr` → a row; the **first** row of the table also emits the `| --- |` separator, because a GFM table has to open with a header and on a page written without `` the first row is the header anyway; - `thead`/`tbody`/`tfoot` → pass through, so no blank line lands between the header row and the body and ends the table; - `caption` → its own paragraph above the table; - `table` → the surrounding blank lines that make it a block. A pipe inside a cell is escaped, so `USB-A|USB-C` stays one cell. Turndown already escapes backslashes in text, so only the pipe is left to escape and a cell holding `a\|b` still reads back as `a\|b`. **Why not `turndown-plugin-gfm`** (the library-first option — it is even already in `devDependencies`, unused): I measured 1.0.2 before writing this, and it would trade one bug for three. A table that carries no `` is emitted as **raw HTML**; a pipe in a cell is not escaped; a `
` in a cell leaks a hard line break that breaks the row. For fetched web pages, header-less tables are common enough that returning raw HTML is not an acceptable outcome. ### One call site deliberately left out `src/main/services/readableContent/readableContentWorker.ts` has the same bare `new TurndownService()`, and I did **not** change it. It is started as a real worker thread from a `.ts` path (`ReadableContentService.integration.test.ts` spawns `new Worker('…/readableContentWorker.ts')`), so it runs under Node's own type stripping, where a relative import needs an explicit `.ts` specifier — which `tsconfig.node.json` rejects (`TS5097`, `allowImportingTsExtensions` is off). Measured: `@main/utils/…` gives `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` in the worker, `…/htmlToMarkdown.js` fails at runtime, `…/htmlToMarkdown.ts` passes the tests and fails `tsc`. That is why the worker keeps no local imports today. Happy to include it in whichever way you prefer — enabling `allowImportingTsExtensions`, giving the test's `Worker` a loader via `execArgv`, or something else. I did not want to pick a repo-wide config change on your behalf. ### Tests `src/main/utils/__tests__/htmlToMarkdown.test.ts`, 8 cases. They read the produced table back the way a reader does (split on unescaped pipes, resolve the escapes) and assert on the cells: - a header table keeps every value in its row and column, and stays a block of its own; - a table written with no `` takes its header from the first row; - `USB-A|USB-C` stays one cell; - a cell's own `a\|b` survives the escaping; - bold and a link still convert inside a cell; - `
` folds to a single space; - a caption lands in its own paragraph; - markup with no table converts byte-identically to a plain service (the guard). Measured: | | result | |---|---| | with the change | 8 passed | | `applyTableRules` reduced to a no-op, tests kept | **7 failed**, 1 passed | `vitest --project main` over `src/main/utils`, `src/main/ai/mcp`, `src/main/features/browser` and `src/main/services/readableContent`: `777 passed, 4 skipped`, no failures. `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` clean; `tsc -p tsconfig.node.json` reports only the pre-existing error in `src/main/ai/runtime/dsh/DshRuntimeConnection.ts`. --------- Signed-off-by: L4XB

fix(file): silence EPERM/EACCES dir-fsync errors on Windows (#20705)

> ### Branch strategy
>
> - Active development targets `main`.

### What this PR does

Before this PR: on Windows, every atomic file write warn-logged
`fsync(dir) failed after atomic rename; durability not confirmed` with
`EPERM`, because `shouldSilenceFsyncDirError` only silenced
`EINVAL`/`EISDIR`/`ENOTSUP` while Windows directory fsync always fails
with `EPERM`.

After this PR: `shouldSilenceFsyncDirError` takes an optional platform
parameter (default `process.platform`) and additionally silences
`EPERM`/`EACCES` on `win32` only. Non-Windows behavior is unchanged —
`EPERM`/`EACCES` still warn there to catch real ACL regressions.

Fixes #20689

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

On Windows, `fsync()` on a directory handle returns `EPERM`
(`FlushFileBuffers` on a directory handle → `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` → Node
maps to `EPERM`), not the `EINVAL`-family errnos the classifier assumed.
Since the code deliberately kept `EPERM` loud to detect ACL drift, every
Windows atomic write produced noise and a genuine regression would be
indistinguishable from it.

The following tradeoffs were made:

- Gating on `platform === 'win32'` preserves the ACL-drift signal on
Linux/macOS instead of globally silencing `EPERM`/`EACCES`.
- `EACCES` is silenced alongside `EPERM` on Windows as the same
access-denied family; both are routine there, neither is routine
elsewhere.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Globally silencing `EPERM`/`EACCES` on all platforms — rejected, it
would mask real ACL/sandbox regressions on POSIX systems.
- Downgrading to a one-time warn — rejected as unnecessary once the
classification is correct; the warn path still fires for genuinely
unexpected errnos (`EIO`, `ENOSPC`, …).

Links to places where the discussion took place: #20689

### Breaking changes

None. `shouldSilenceFsyncDirError` gains an optional second parameter
with a default; all existing call sites behave as before on non-Windows.

locally; please rely on CI for it. The change is an optional parameter

fix(sub-window): apply persisted zoom factor to detached tab windows (#20696)

## Description

Detaching a tab into its own window always opened at 100%, regardless of
the user's persisted `app.zoom_factor` (e.g. 130%). The stored
preference was never applied to the detached window, and one press of
`Cmd+=` then jumped straight to ~140% instead of 110% — because
`handleZoomFactor` computes `stored + delta` and writes it back, on top
of a window that was visually at 100%.

Two gaps combine to produce this:

1. **Fresh-window path**: `SubWindowService.createWindow` injected no
`webPreferences.zoomFactor`, unlike `MainWindowService` (which both
injects it at construction and re-applies it on resize/restore as the
electron#10572 workaround). The registry comment on `WindowType.Main`
even documents the convention ("zoomFactor depends on PreferenceService
→ injected via args.options"), but SubWindow never honored it.
2. **Pooled-standby path (the common one)**: the SubWindow pool keeps a
pre-warmed standby (`standbySize: 1`, `warmup: 'eager'`), and `open()`
usually pops that standby instead of constructing a window — so even a
correct per-call `options.webPreferences` would not reach it. The
standby is constructed at app startup with Electron's default zoom.

### Fix

- Inject `app.zoom_factor` via `options.webPreferences` in
`SubWindowService.createWindow` (mirrors `MainWindowService`).
- Re-apply the factor on the window after `open()` so a popped standby
is covered too (no-op for fresh windows).
- Re-apply on `will-resize` / `restore` (+ plain `resize` on Linux) via
`onWindowCreatedByType(WindowType.SubWindow, ...)`, mirroring
`MainWindowService.setupWindowEvents`'s electron#10572 workaround.
Subscribed in `onInit` per the Window Manager guideline ("attach
listeners in `onWindowCreated`"); the SubWindow pool is
destroy-on-close, so each `BrowserWindow` instance is opened exactly
once and the listeners never accumulate.

Zoom changes made from the settings page already reach sub windows via
`app.adjust_zoom` → `BrowserWindow.getAllWindows()` (hidden standbys
included), so no additional preference subscription is needed.

## Motivation & context

Repro on `main` (zoom factor set to 130% in Settings → Display):
1. Drag a tab out of the main window into its own window → the detached
window renders at 100% while the settings slider still shows 130%.
2. Press `Cmd+=` in the detached window → zoom jumps to ~140%.

After this PR, the detached window opens at the persisted zoom factor,
and `Cmd+=` moves it to the next step (140%) as expected.

Verified with unit tests (`pnpm test:main
src/main/services/__tests__/SubWindowService.test.ts`, 26 passed):
options injection + post-open application, `will-resize`/`restore`
re-application, Linux-only plain-`resize` re-application,
destroyed-window guard. `pnpm run typecheck:node`, eslint and oxfmt pass
on the changed files. (I did not capture a screenshot of the manual
repro — happy to add one if useful.)

## Note on related behavior (unchanged here)

`handleZoomFactor` intentionally derives the new zoom from the stored
preference rather than `webContents.getZoomFactor()`; with the detached
window now actually rendering at the stored factor, that arithmetic
lines up and no change to it is needed.

Signed-off-by: UIJM <uijm2004@gmail.com>

* fix(logmanager): portable rewrite mode and directory sync

os.fchmod is Unix-only, so Windows rewrites crashed before replacement.
Apply the preserved mode before fsync via fchmod, with chmod-by-path as
the fallback. Restore the containing-directory barrier after replace so
direct rewrite callers (fork/undo/edit) cannot acknowledge an unsynced
namespace.

Git-Session-Id: 6091b3f7-b6b1-5f8d-924b-888c45c1b6bc

* fix(logmanager): keep barrier failures proportionate

Two ways the new barrier could make things worse than the durability gap it
closes:

Directory fsync was made fatal, and the test asserting the opposite
(test_unsupported_directory_fsync_does_not_fail_save) was deleted along with
it. Some network, overlay and FUSE mounts reject fsync on a directory fd
outright; on those, every turn would now die with correct data on disk. Warn
once per directory for the errnos that mean "no barrier available" and
continue; genuine I/O errors (EIO, ENOSPC) still propagate, because those mean
the write did not land. Restores the deleted test alongside an EIO counterpart.

sync_directories() guarded its walk with a bare `path.relative_to(root)`, so a
branch or view directory symlinked outside the logdir turned into a ValueError
out of write(sync=True) and a failed turn. Sync the resolved target instead of
walking to the filesystem root.

Also replace through a symlinked transcript rather than over it: os.replace on
the link path leaves a regular file where the link was and orphans the real
transcript, which may be on another disk. The temporary file now goes in the
target's directory so the replacement stays on one filesystem, matching what
the append path already did by following the link.

Git-Session-Id: ef3cdde3-e933-5fe2-8980-96c819b20f9b

* fix(server): keep generation_complete early, acknowledge with turn_persisted

Moving generation_complete behind the TURN_POST hooks and the fsync barrier
reversed a deliberate decision, and the comment explaining that decision was
deleted with it: the frontend was made to wait on arbitrary hook code plus a
disk barrier before it could finish rendering a turn.

Split the two meanings instead. generation_complete keeps its old position and
its old meaning (generation finished, message is appended and written); the new
additive turn_persisted event follows the barrier and is the durability
acknowledgement, for clients that must not lose a turn. A barrier failure
emits error plus a visible system message and no turn_persisted, so nothing is
acknowledged that did not land.

The ACP path gets the same shape, so both paths mean the same thing by the same
event.

Additive contract change: CONTRACT_REVISION 2 -> 3.

Git-Session-Id: ef3cdde3-e933-5fe2-8980-96c819b20f9b

* fix(subagent): identify subagents by resolved logdir

LogManager.logdir is now resolved, but spawn sites build subagent logdirs from
get_logs_dir(), which is not. Any symlink in the logs path (a symlinked data
dir, macOS /tmp -> /private/tmp) therefore made `s.logdir == manager.logdir` in
the STEP_PRE control hook silently false: the in-memory cancel fallback stopped
working and agent_id fell back to logdir.name, which the comment directly above
that lookup says is wrong for thread-mode subagents.

Normalize logdir and parent_logdir in Subagent.__post_init__ so the registry
and the running manager agree regardless of how each side spelled the path.

Git-Session-Id: ef3cdde3-e933-5fe2-8980-96c819b20f9b

* docs: move the transcript persistence contract to docs/design/

A filesystem persistence contract does not belong in the sessions command
reference, above the click directives that page exists for. Move it to
docs/design/, which is where cross-cutting contracts with a stated status and a
list of non-guarantees already live, and rewrite it around the problem, the
barrier, and the two server events.

Git-Session-Id: ef3cdde3-e933-5fe2-8980-96c819b20f9b

* Revert "fix(server): keep generation_complete early, acknowledge with turn_persisted"

This reverts commit 69cfa58ba.

Greptile is right, and my reasoning for the reorder was wrong on the part that
matters. I argued the early emit protected frontend responsiveness, but what
gates responsiveness is `session.generating`, not `generation_complete`: the
reservation is released in step()'s finalizer, and no event announces it. The
WebUI infers the release from generation_complete (`setGenerating(false)` 100ms
later, in useConversation.ts), and ChatInput flushes its queued message on that
inferred idle, dequeueing unconditionally whether or not the send is accepted.
A send that lands before the finalizer gets 409 "Generation already in
progress" and the user's queued message is simply gone.

So emitting early does not buy interactivity; it buys an earlier chime and
final-content set, and it pays for that by widening a message-loss window.
Emitting after the barrier is the better trade. The window is pre-existing and
not fully closed by either ordering (auto-naming still runs inside it) — see
the follow-up issue for the root cause.

Reverting also removes the turn_persisted event, its contract bump, and its
WebUI case: with generation_complete back behind the barrier, a second
acknowledgement event has nothing left to say.

* fix(logmanager): propagate permission denials from the directory barrier

EACCES and EPERM were in the tolerated set on the reasoning that opening a
directory read-only can fail on unusual setups. That conflates two different
things: a permission or policy denial is not evidence that the filesystem lacks
a barrier, and tolerating it lets write(sync=True) return having done nothing
the caller asked for. Only the errnos that actually mean "no directory barrier
here" stay tolerated.

Docs updated to match the reverted event ordering.

* fix(webui): authenticate sandboxed panel postMessage by frame identity

Sandboxed panels run with an opaque origin: resolveSandbox drops
allow-same-origin whenever allow-scripts is requested, so browsers deliver
their messages as event.origin === "null" and no concrete targetOrigin can
address them. The strict origin-equality gate therefore rejected every
gptme:ready/gptme:resize, leaving the bootstrap and auto-resize protocols
inactive for every scripted panel -- including the /preview/{port}/ panels
this branch fixes.

Address such frames with targetOrigin "*" and pin identity with the
existing event.source === contentWindow check instead. Frames that keep
their origin (unsandboxed, or allow-same-origin without scripts) still
require an exact origin match, and a "null" origin from those is rejected.

Also reword the server-side opaque-origin warning, which claimed the
handshake could not work at all.

* fix(webui): bootstrap-once guard prevents navigation-bypass re-bootstrap

An opaque-origin sandboxed panel shares the same contentWindow WindowProxy
across document navigations. Before this fix, a panel that navigated to an
attacker-controlled opaque-origin document (e.g. data:text/html,...) could
send a second gptme:ready and receive the conversation_id bootstrap payload,
since both event.source and event.origin === "null" checks would still pass.

Add a bootstrappedRef (reset each effect run / src change) that lets the
bootstrap fire only once per iframe lifecycle. Subsequent gptme:ready messages
are silently ignored.

Add a regression test: 'does not re-bootstrap after gptme:ready fires a second
time (bootstrap-once guard)'.

* fix(webui): key SandboxedIframePanel by conversationId to force remount on switch

  already carry the instance base path, or that are host-qualified

  instance prefix added a second time.

origin-preserving cases now use `allow-same-origin` (a bare empty sandbox does
not preserve the origin); already-prefixed and host-qualified srcs do not double
the prefix. 46 webui assertions pass; typecheck, eslint, prettier clean.

Stop one test's app settings answering another test's read (#11309)

* Stop one test's app settings answering another test's read

test_chat_absent_model_with_only_resolver_withheld_checkpoints fails as
`assert 500 == 404` in the (Python 3.13, l-r) shard and nowhere else. This is the
half of #11241 that stayed open all session because nothing reproduced it.

The CI traceback named it:

    Error loading model: '_B' object has no attribute 'load_model'
      File "studio/backend/routes/inference.py", line 16213, in _load_model_impl

`_B` is the withheld tests' own backend double, reached through _load_model_impl --
a LOAD path those tests must never take.

_wire_unloaded_chat pins every input for determinism (local catalog, resolver,
auto-switch, both backends) and misses auto-download. get_openai_auto_download_enabled
is `stored AND auto_switch`, and auto_switch IS pinned to True there, so the answer is
whatever `stored` says. `stored` comes from _cached_setting, a module-level memo with
_CACHE_TTL_S = 2.0 and no test isolation, so a neighbouring test that read that setting
hands this one its value and the refusal becomes a fetch-and-load.

Reproduced by seeding the memo the way a neighbour would:

    seeded True  -> not 404, takes the auto-download path
    seeded False -> 404, as the test expects

That is why no amount of reordering found it. It is not an ordering bug, it is a clock:
only tests landing inside a two second window are affected, which is why it shows up in
the full shard and never in a single-file run, and why CPU contention, a leaked managed
account and a stranded waiter all came back clean.

Two independent layers:

- _wire_unloaded_chat pins auto-download off, which is what line 6190 of this same file
  already does for the one test that thought to.
- an autouse fixture clears the memo around every test, so no process-wide settings cache
  can carry across tests at all.

Sabotage, each hitting its own test: remove the wiring pin and the new regression test
fails; drop the fixture's entry clear or its exit clear and the fixture test fails, each
with its own message. The fixture test drives the fixture directly rather than relying on
two tests running in order, since under --dist loadgroup that pair can land on different
workers and pass by luck.

* Disengage FBCache on the word of whoever owns it

test_video_backend.py::test_video_step_cache_auto_toggles_on_actual_steps is red on
main. Bisected: it passes at 9cf1f6e24^ and fails at 9cf1f6e24 (#11174). CI's captured

    removed); running uncached

#11174 made the auto disengage refuse to clear the marker until the private-name hook
sweep confirms the hooks are gone. That is right for the case it was written for: an
ADOPTED low-level cache, installed through apply_first_block_cache, leaves _cache_config
None, so diffusers' own disable_cache removes nothing and trusting it would clear the
marker over live hooks. Clearing it there would let the CUDA graph wrapper capture across
them, so "cannot verify" has to mean "still engaged".

But the veto was applied unconditionally. When diffusers owns the cache, disable_cache
returning without raising IS the evidence: it removed both hooks and cleared the config
itself. Requiring the sweep on top makes every disengage depend on
diffusers.hooks.first_block_cache staying importable, and where it is not, FBCache stays
engaged on short trajectories forever -- the quality regression the auto policy exists to
prevent. The veto now applies only where the code's own comment says it is needed.

The test's diffusers stub was wrong too, and in a way that hid this: FirstBlockCacheConfig
was a lambda returning ("fbcache", threshold). The cache layer matches on
type(...).__name__ to tell its own config from a MagCache / PAB one, so a plain tuple read
as "some other cache" and made the teardown unverifiable by construction. It is now a
class named FirstBlockCacheConfig, as test_diffusion_cache.py already does, and the fake
DiT records _cache_config the way diffusers does.

Two regression tests cover both directions, since #11174's 618 lines of tests never
reached this: its harness always makes the sweep succeed.

* Desktop: run one managed repair at a time

start_managed_repair guarded itself with the install and update child handles,
which are empty while it stops the backend and between the update child and
the installer. Five Retry clicks two seconds apart after a backend crash each
passed the guards, each ran their own `studio update`, and then raced for the
bundled installer: one won and the other four surfaced "Installation is
already running." over its progress.

The install state now carries a repair_in_flight flag taken at the top of the
command and released by a guard on every exit; update and install refuse while
it is set. The frontend stops the fan-out at its source: one preflight and one
repair in flight at a time.

* Keep one repair flag, the one already on main

#11226 landed the same single-flight while this was in review: UpdateProcess.repair_in_flight, a
RepairInFlight guard with the same RAII shape and the same poisoned-lock release, claimed at the
top of start_managed_repair. Rebasing onto main left two flags for one invariant, so this drops
the copy in InstallProcess and keeps main's.

What main does not have, and this keeps: start_install and start_backend_update refuse while a
repair is in flight. They now ask update::is_repair_running, which is the flag main already keeps,
rather than a second one. start_install gains the UpdateState parameter that needs; Tauri injects
state by type, so no caller changes.

start_managed_repair keeps its original "installation is in progress" refusal ahead of the claim,
which is where main has it.

The two unit tests that covered the removed flag are dropped: update.rs already tests the guard it
kept, including the poisoned-lock release, and duplicating that against a deleted type is not
coverage. The frontend single-flight and its test are untouched.

* Hold the preflight flag over the probe, not over what the probe starts

The guard spanned the whole of checkInstallAndStart, including the managed_ready arm's
await startManagedServer(), which parks in waitForManagedServerPort's 500 ms poll. The
server-start-timeout handler clears startingRef and shows Retry from inside that wait, so a click
arriving before the poll next wakes cleared the error and then returned on the flag, leaving the
screen in error with nothing running until the user clicked again.

Released as soon as desktop_preflight returns. The dispositions it leads to are re-entrant on
their own account: startManagedServer takes startingRef, startRepair takes repairInFlightRef.
What the flag exists to stop, five Retry clicks fanning out into five preflights and five repairs,
is unchanged.

The test now pins the release point between the probe and the switch, and that no long await runs
while the flag is held. It fails on the previous shape.

* Tighten the comments this change added

* Give the managed-environment harness the flag the hook now reads

managed-environment-wait.test.ts evals checkInstallAndStart's body in a scope it builds by hand,
so the preflight guard this PR adds resolved to nothing and all six cases died with
ReferenceError: preflightInFlightRef is not defined. Landed on main after this branch was cut,
which is why the branch was green when it was opened.

* Release the preflight flag only while this call still owns it

Releasing early at the probe left the finally clearing the flag unconditionally, and by then it
may belong to someone else: A releases, A is still awaiting startManagedServer, Retry starts B
which arms the flag, A finishes and its finally clears B's, and a third Retry runs a preflight
concurrently with B. That is the fan-out the guard exists to stop.

releasePreflight() is a no-op once this call has handed the flag on, and both the early release
and the finally go through it. The test pins that shape and fails on an unconditional clear.

Same window as the preflight one, one flag along. runRepair awaits startManagedServer after the

Carry over five temp-scanner fixes that landed after #11217 merged (#11280)

* Recheck existence inside the retry, and stop a failed watcher counting as cover

Two ways the previous version still reported a clean run over a hole.

The deletion race can land INSIDE the retry window. The first read fails,
Test-Path says the directory is there, and it is gone by the time the retry
runs; the inner catch then recorded it as unread, and an unread directory under
an unwatched root voids the measurement. That is the ordinary temp deletion this
change exists to tolerate, so existence is rechecked in the inner catch too.

A FileSystemWatcher that overflows its buffer raises Error and drops the
creations it could not queue, and its handle stays in the list looking exactly
like a working one. The coverage check therefore counted an overflowed watcher
as covering its root and withheld the unread directories beneath it, so an
artifact could be missing from the live stream AND from the listing at once,
which is the only combination that turns a real compile into a pass. The Error
event is now subscribed, drained in Stop-StudioTempWatch as FailedRoots, and
those roots are excluded when $watchedRoots is built. Any Error at all condemns
the root: the event carries the exception, not the list of creations it dropped,
so a watcher that raised once cannot say what it missed.

* Classify the enumeration error instead of probing the path

Test-Path cannot tell a deleted directory from an unreadable one, so using it to
decide meant an ACL-denied directory was called deleted and dropped silently out
of the comparison. Pre-existing files under it then read as new in the other
snapshot, and where its root had no watcher the coverage guard was skipped
entirely, so an incomplete scan could report clean.

Measured under pwsh with $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop':

    missing directory  ->  ItemNotFoundException, Test-Path returns $false
    denied directory   ->  Test-Path THROWS 'Access to the path ... is denied'

which is worse than it first looks: the probe could raise from inside the catch
that was meant to contain the failure.

Test-StudioPathIsGone walks the exception chain for ItemNotFoundException,
DirectoryNotFoundException and FileNotFoundException, and is used for the first
failure and the retry alike. It fails safe: anything not positively identified
as a missing path is reported as still present, so the directory is recorded as
unread. Over-reporting a gap costs a withheld path or a voided run;
under-reporting one drops a directory out of the comparison, which is the defect
this file exists to prevent.

* Match the raised message however PowerShell chose to wrap it

Windows staging caught this and nothing else could: the two rows asserting the
void message did a plain substring match, and on Windows a throw reaches the
caller through PowerShell's error formatter, which wraps at terminal width,
interleaves ANSI colour codes and gutters each continuation line:

    ...so this run cannot
         | say whether a compiler ran.

so the sentence is never contiguous. Linux pwsh does not wrap that way, which is
why both rows passed everywhere they could be run locally while failing on the
one platform this script actually executes on.

Colour codes, then the gutter, then whitespace collapsed. The gutter is the part
worth naming: stripping ANSI alone leaves a '|' in the middle of the sentence and
the match keeps failing for a new reason, which is what happened on the first
attempt at this fix.

* Raise the incomplete-scan verdict last, not over the action's own failure

The void-the-run throw sat before the evidence write and before the captured
action failure was rethrown. So an installer that genuinely died, on a run where
the final sweep also hit an unreadable directory with nothing watching its root,
was reported as a scanner problem and never produced the <name>-error.txt this
function promises.

The uncovered directories are collected into $uncovered now and raised at the
very end: evidence first, then the action's own failure, then the incomplete
scan. An incomplete sweep is worth failing on; it is not worth failing on
INSTEAD of the thing being measured. $uncovered reaches the evidence either way
through <name>-unread-dirs.txt.

Ordering is the whole claim, so the tests assert offsets taken from the shipped
function, and pin that the coverage loop collects rather than raises.

* Say what Windows actually covers in the temp-scan tests

A skip reason claimed the Windows half of the denial question was "the
ACL-based control below". There is no such control and there never was, so the
file promised a guarantee it did not provide.

Three rows here are POSIX-only and skip on Windows, and nothing replaces them:
on a Windows runner the denial behaviour of this walk is not exercised. That is
now stated, along with why an ACL control is not being guessed at from a Linux
host - the failure worth catching is a control that denies nothing and passes,
which is what happened when an ACL denial was first tried as a stand-in for the
race.

The eight platform-neutral rows do run on Windows and do drive the real
PowerShell. The DirectorySeparatorChar bug is the class they catch, which is why
they are written against Windows-shaped literals.

* Void the measurement when a watcher raised, not only its coverage

Excluding a failed watcher's root from $watchedRoots changes the verdict only
when $unread also holds something beneath that root. With two otherwise clean
sweeps, $uncovered is empty and the run is accepted.

That is the wrong way round for this detector. The live half exists for
artifacts that never reach the listing at all: CodeDom deletes its intermediate
directory once the assembly is loaded, so a compile can be invisible to the
before/after diff and present only as events. An overflow drops those silently,
so two clean scans plus a failed watcher is the exact shape of a missed compile,
with nothing unreadable for the coverage check to catch.

A non-empty $watchFailedRoots is now an incomplete measurement in its own right.
Both reasons are collected into $incomplete and raised in one throw, so the
caller is told everything wrong with the sweep at once rather than fixing one
and meeting the other. Still after the action's own failure is rethrown, and

Studio: stop a Windows update deleting the venv it is running from (#11248)

* setup.ps1: stop a stale-venv rebuild deleting the venv it runs from

`unsloth studio update` runs setup.ps1 from the managed venv's own python.exe.
When the torch flavor no longer matches the host (here: cu130 installed, an
AMD GPU now in the machine, so rocm required), the direct-update branch did
Remove-Item -Recurse on that venv. Windows will not delete a running image, so
the delete emptied Lib\ and failed on Scripts\python.exe, leaving a venv with
no unsloth_cli and no rollback copy; the desktop's update and repair both start
from that interpreter, so neither could recover it.

setup.ps1 now knows when it runs from inside the venv (the CLI names its
interpreter as UNSLOTH_SETUP_HOST_PYTHON; a bounded Win32_Process walk covers
an older CLI) and takes the in-place PyTorch reinstall install.ps1 already uses
for the same situation. A rebuild that does run renames the venv aside first,
so a lock fails whole instead of after deleting most of the tree.

* setup.ps1: order the in-place route last, and make the venv probe separator-correct

The new direct-update escape sat ahead of the nvidia-smi cu* preservation guard. Its
condition is true for every stale direct update, because the desktop always runs setup
from the venv's own python.exe, so it consumed $shouldRebuild before the narrower guard
was tested and that guard could never fire.

That guard does two things: it keeps the venv, and it publishes
$script:PreservedInstallerTorchTag, which is what holds the index selection on the cu*
arm. Shadowed, the tag stayed null while the in-place route set
$script:PinChangedForceReinstall, and the pair reached the CPU arm. Replaying the
shipped ladder over 320 enumerated cells, base and head agree on 289; the one cell that
is neither an intended fix nor a match is an unpinned direct update with a cu128 venv
and a silent nvidia-smi:

  base: uv pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url .../whl/cu128
  head: uv pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --force-reinstall --index-url .../whl/cpu

which is the CPU-only update #9857 added that guard to stop. Moving the block below the
guard leaves all 30 intended fixes and restores that cell; base and fixed now differ in
0 cells where the venv is kept on both sides.

Get-SetupHostInterpreterInVenv built its containment prefix with a literal backslash.
.NET returns '/'-separated paths from GetFullPath off Windows and treats '\' as an
ordinary filename character, so the prefix matched nothing and the helper answered null
for every input. Only Windows runs setup.ps1 for real, but the shipped pwsh tests run
everywhere, and test_the_cli_hint_names_the_venv_interpreter was red on every non-Windows
runner while its sibling passed vacuously. Build the prefix from
DirectorySeparatorChar instead.

Also move the stale-venv sweep out of the rebuild branch, so an install that renamed a
venv aside, failed to delete the copy under a lock, and thereafter only ever repairs in
place still collects it, and give the destination a pid suffix so two rebuilds inside
one second cannot collide on a name.

* setup.ps1: let the stale-venv sweep prove a directory is ours before deleting it

Moving the sweep out of the rebuild branch put it ahead of the custom-root ownership
guard, so that guard can no longer cover it, and "$_venvLeaf.stale-*" is a wildcard
rather than a proof of ownership: a user's own unsloth_studio.stale-backup matches it and
was deleted on an ordinary healthy update.

Validate the way install.ps1 already validates its own rollback sweep
(Test-StudioVenvRollbackMustBePreserved): refuse anything outside the generated
timestamp-PID shape, refuse reparse points, and spare a copy whose owning process is
still alive, which is a concurrent setup's rescue copy rather than our litter. Enumerate
with -Force too, so a leftover that picked up the hidden attribute is not skipped
forever by the sweep meant to collect it.

test_setup_ps1_stale_sweep_only_removes_its_own_litter runs the shipped sweep under pwsh
against real directories rather than reading it: an abandoned copy in the generated shape
goes, a stale-backup directory and a live owner's copy stay, and the live venv is never
touched. It fails on the unvalidated sweep with "a directory outside the generated name
shape must be left alone".

Routing is unchanged: replaying the ladder over the same 320 cells still gives 30 fixes,
0 violations and 0 newly wiped cells against base.

* studio.py: say that UNSLOTH_SETUP_HOST_PYTHON is a hint, not a promise

sys.executable is the managed venv's python.exe on the path that matters, where the
desktop spawns the managed CLI. It is not on the others: a pip-installed CLI, a repo
checkout and a staged run all put an interpreter here that lives nowhere near $VenvDir.

That is already safe, because setup.ps1 tests containment itself and a value outside the
venv reads as 'not inside', which keeps the pre-existing rebuild. The comment asserted
the guarantee as fact, which is the kind of thing that later justifies dropping the
containment test as redundant. Say which path it holds on and who checks.

* setup.ps1: read the stale-venv pid from an explicit Match, not $Matches

The sweep decided what to delete from a capture group it reached through $Matches after
a -notmatch. Which of -match and -notmatch populates $Matches, and on which result, is
version-sensitive in exactly the way #9857's empty-string-vs-null was, and a read that
comes back empty here feeds [int]::TryParse and skips the entry. Failing safe is the good
case; a wrong pid is not. Take the group off a [regex]::Match whose semantics do not
move between Windows PowerShell 5.1 and 7.x.

* Tighten the comments added by this change

Opening comment-reduction pass over this PR's own additions only, not the surrounding
file: 62 added comment lines to 43. Every surviving line names a mistake the next reader
would otherwise make, which is why the ordering rationale and the ownership rationale
keep a line each. AST-verified comment-only against b30af0c38.

* Second comment sweep over this change's own additions

The in-place-route block restated the undeletable-running-image mechanism the function
header above it already gives, so it keeps only what is local to the decision: the issue
number, and that a hand-run checkout still rebuilds. setup.ps1 additions 32 comment lines
to 27. AST-verified comment-only against 7d0b1da8e.

* Make the stale-copy sweep prove ownership before it deletes

Three things found while simulating this PR, all in the new code rather than in what it replaced.

The sweep runs on every qualifying setup, including one that rebuilds nothing, and it runs ahead
of the custom-root guard. Its only authority for a recursive delete was a name, so a directory
named unsloth_studio.stale-<14 digits>-<pid> next to the venv was deleted on a run that otherwise
changed nothing, and also on a custom UNSLOTH_STUDIO_HOME whose venv the rebuild then refused to
touch for want of an Unsloth sentinel. Both are now refused: the guard predicate is hoisted so the
sweep asks the same ownership question the rebuild asks, and a candidate must carry pyvenv.cfg,
the studio-owned marker, or the new .unsloth-studio-stale marker that the rename drops into the
copy it moved. A copy too far gone to carry any of the three is named and left alone rather than
deleted blind. The marker is rewritten when the delete after the rename fails, so the litter that
branch announces is still litter the next run can identify.

Get-SetupHostInterpreterInVenv accepted a hint that named nothing. The hint is an inherited
environment variable and can outlive what it names, and a stale one pointing inside the venv would
route a venv that genuinely needs rebuilding into an in-place repair with no interpreter to
perform it. It must now name a file that is there. The parent walk also compares creation dates
before following ParentProcessId, which is what Microsoft's own Win32_Process guidance says to do
about reused process ids.

The rename destination took the timestamp and the pid but had no retry, while install.sh's
_start_studio_venv_replacement, which this mirrors, appends a numeric suffix until the name is
free. One process can reach this twice inside a second, and a copy it left earlier can still be on
disk because its delete failed. A taken name now takes a bounded suffix, and the sweep's shape
recognises it, or the copy it names could never be cleaned up.

Tests: the sweep test now drives the shipped sweep over six directories, including one that wears
the name and holds no environment and one whose name took a collision suffix; a new test refuses
an unclaimable custom root and then, as a negative control, sweeps the same tree once the owned
marker is present; the helper test adds a hint naming a deleted path, a directory, and Scripts
itself, with the real interpreter as its control.

Make the Colab pip cache able to shrink, which #11270 assumed it already could (#11271)

* Make the Colab pip cache able to shrink, which #11270 assumed it already could

#11270 removed 39 pins from the Colab freeze replay and freed nothing. The
cache is still 7,486,845,334 bytes. Two independent reasons, both of which
predate that PR.

The mapping was not a cache key input. The job keyed on
colab_pip_freeze.gpu.txt and notebooks-ci.yml, so editing
colab_to_cpu_pin.json -- where the skips, spoofs and index rewrites actually
live -- changed what the job installs while the key hash stayed put. The
restore then hit exactly, and pip-cache-save is gated on `cache-hit != 'true'`,
so the entry holding the removed wheels was never rewritten. The existing
comment shows the reasoning was one step short: it explains that the workflow
belongs in the key "because the seed step rewrites those pins in place -- CPU
index mapping, skips, spoofs", and those three things are all read out of the
mapping file it omitted.

And pip's HTTP cache is cumulative. pip never evicts from it, the save step
saves the whole directory, and restore-keys means a run that misses its exact
key still restores the previous generation's wheels into that directory and
saves them straight back out. So dropping pins cannot shrink the entry even
once the key does move. The two live generations are the proof:
7,486,810,247 bytes on 2026-09-15 against 7,486,845,334 on 2026-09-18, 35 KB
apart, because the second run inherited the first rather than re-downloading
5 GiB of wheels it no longer installs.

Adding the mapping to key-files fixes the first. The second needs the prefix
retired once, so this renames the family to notebooks-colab-cpu: the next run
on main starts from an empty pip directory and saves only what the trimmed pin
set downloads. Costs one cold install, once.

Renaming this job rather than bumping the shared `v2` segment is deliberate.
v3 would invalidate all 13 pip families at once, and it would fall outside
cache-janitor.yml's `pip-v2-` glob, so the new entries could never be pruned.
The janitor's keep=1 rule matches by prefix and so covers the new name and the
retired one both, which drains the orphan to a single entry for the 7-day idle
timer to finish.

Expected: about 2.6 GB for this family against 13.95 GB before #11270, once a
run on main writes the first clean entry.

Guarded by a mechanical rule -- every repo file the seed step opens must be a
key input -- plus explicit checks that the mapping is named and that every
key-files path exists, since a glob matching nothing makes hashFiles return
empty. All four verified to fail when inverted.

Contain a temp-scan failure to the directory that raised it, and refuse a partial scan (#11217)

* Stop the no-compiler detector failing on a temp directory it did not create

windows-no-compiler-ci has been red on main since this afternoon, and not because anything
compiled. The positive control died inside the detector itself:

    Get-ChildItem : The system cannot find the file specified
    + CategoryInfo : NotSpecified: (:) [Get-ChildItem], Win32Exception

Get-StudioTempArtifacts listed each temp root with one recursive Get-ChildItem. A temp root is
shared with everything else running on the machine, so a directory can be removed or stop being
openable partway through the walk, and the Windows provider raises a Win32Exception for it.
-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue does not cover that: it governs non-terminating errors, and the
step sets $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop', so the whole job went red while the installer under
test had done nothing at all.

The walk is by hand now, one directory at a time, so an unreadable directory costs that
directory and nothing else and the rest of the subtree is still reported. Reparse points are
not followed, which a recursive listing would have done.

The new tests drive the walk rather than reading it, since the question is what happens when
enumeration throws. The control that proves the old shape really does end the run is Windows
only and says why: the POSIX provider reports an unreadable directory as an ordinary
non-terminating error, which -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue does suppress, so on Linux that
control would assert something untrue. It runs in the parity matrix, which covers
windows-latest.

* Filter the temp scan as it walks, and refuse to report a partial one

Three corrections to the walk added in the previous commit.

The POSIX permission test ran on the windows-latest parity row, where os.geteuid does not exist
and chmod sets the read-only attribute rather than making a directory unopenable, so it could
only fail there and would not have denied anything if it had run. It is marked POSIX-only, and
the Windows half of the same question is the ACL-based control beside it.

The walk collected every path it met and the caller selected the six interesting extensions
afterwards, using += on a PowerShell array, which allocates and copies on every append. A temp
root can hold an extracted toolchain or a package cache, and this sweep runs before and after
every measured action. The patterns are matched during traversal now, and both the results and
the pending list are generic lists.

The ceiling stopped the walk silently. A truncated snapshot is indistinguishable from a clean
one to the caller, and this listing is exactly what stands in when the watcher cannot attach, so
stopping short turns a missed artifact into a clean verdict. It raises instead, which declares
the measurement void, and the ceiling is 200000 rather than 20000 so an ordinary busy runner
never reaches it. Driven by re-declaring the shipped function with a smaller limit, so the test
runs the real body rather than a retyped one.

* Trigger both lanes when the temp scanner or its tests change

The parity job runs the deliberate unreadable-directory and traversal-limit cases and nothing
else does, and neither the scanner nor its test file was in that workflow's path filters, so a
PR touching only the scanner would have regressed the new error handling with nothing red. The
no-compiler workflow already triggered on the scanner and now triggers on the tests too, since
their Windows-only ACL control can only run on a Windows runner.

Both the pull_request and the push lists, in both workflows.

teeth and they hold in all three cases, that nothing got through the proxy and that nothing on

The Windows control asserted that the shape this replaced ends the run, and it would have passed

disappears partway through a recursive enumeration and the provider raises a Win32Exception,
which -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue does not suppress because it governs non-terminating errors.

A POSIX chmod is the same story, which is why the first version of it failed here.

Reproducing the race means deleting directories under a live walk and hoping the timing lands,
which is a flaky test rather than a control, so what is pinned is the shape: enumeration is

where the control used to be rather than left as an absence.

reported as having compiled. Unread in the final sweep hides the reverse: a real

* Trim 2.59 GiB per generation from the Colab smoke job's pip cache

The repo's Actions cache sat at 49.44 GB of its 50 GB ceiling on 2026-09-18,
which means GitHub is evicting live entries by last-access date and every
family is paying for it in missed restores. One job held 30% of the budget:
pip-v2-notebooks-colab, at 6.97 GB per generation across two generations.

That job replays the whole 697-pin Colab freeze to reconstruct a Colab-shaped
venv, so its cache is all of Colab's package set rather than unsloth's
dependencies. Pricing every pin against PyPI puts 5.16 GiB of downloads in the
cached set, and two classes of it can never be used by this job:

  * CUDA wheels a CPU runner cannot load. The skip list already covered the
    nvidia-* runtime wheels and triton, but missed the entire RAPIDS stack
    (libcudf 652 MiB, libcuml 443 MiB, cudf, cuml, rmm, raft, ucxx, dask-cuda,
    numba-cuda), cupy-cuda12x, the jax-cuda12-* plugins, and six further
    nvidia-* wheels including nvshmem and cuda-nvcc.

  * Large wheels nothing in the job's import graph reaches: pyspark and its
    connector, the Intel math runtime (CPU torch links its own BLAS), and
    xgboost, which declares nvidia-nccl-cu13 unconditionally on Linux and so
    drags 241 MiB behind it.

Chosen as a dependency closure over the freeze, not as a list of names. The
seed step installs bare `name==ver`, so pip re-resolves any dropped package a
retained pin still requires and downloads it anyway, unpinned -- a saving that
is not one, and invisible because the install still succeeds. That is why the
parents come too: cuml and dask-cudf for cupy, pylibcudf and cudf-polars for
libcudf, ucxx and distributed-ucxx for rmm, dataproc-spark-connect for pyspark,
xgboost for nvidia-nccl-cu13. Verified against metadata for all 697 pins, so
the graph has no holes; nothing retained pulls any of the 39 back.

TensorFlow, Flax, JAX, keras-hub, ydf and dopamine-rl are deliberately kept,
though they are 761 MiB nothing here imports. Transformers imports the TF and
Flax backends merely because they are installed, via processing_utils ->
image_transforms, so their presence changes what `import unsloth` does, which
is the subject of tests/test_broken_tf_does_not_break_import.py. Colab ships
them. Fabricating .dist-info without the wheel would be worse than either
choice: a find_spec hit whose import fails is the broken-TF path, not Colab's
healthy TF, so the job would assert against a condition that is not real.

Also gives the janitor a per-family keep of 1 for this one prefix, using the
fkeep mechanism already there for CodeQL. An older generation here answers only
an exact revert of the freeze or of notebooks-ci.yml, which is rarer than the
eviction pressure a second 7 GB copy puts on every other family.

Net: the family goes from 13.95 GB to about 4.4 GB, and pyspark leaves
no_binary, where it was dead config once skipped.

Four invariants are now tested, each verified to fail when inverted: the
CUDA-only classes stay skipped, the detected-if-installed backends stay
installed, the skip list stays closed under the freeze's own dependencies, and
no pin sits in both skip and no_binary.

Studio: bring the picker's Connected rows up to the On Device rows (#11196)

* Studio: match the roundness of Connections settings boxes to the rest of Settings

The Connections panels were built with literal radii -- rounded-[6px], rounded-[8px],
rounded-[14px] -- so every box in there was flatter than the same box on any other Settings
tab. Tailwind's --radius is 1.1rem, which puts rounded-lg at 17.6px, and that is what the rest
of Settings uses.

Swap the literals for the scale: rounded-lg for the panel sections and the connection list,
rounded-md for the nested model lists and the provider logo tile, rounded-full for the model
count pill, and nothing at all on the icon buttons, which already carry a radius from the
button variant they were overriding.

* Studio: bring the picker's Connected rows up to the On Device rows

A Connected row was a name and nothing else. Every On Device row beside it carried modality
badges, a pin, a gear and a row menu, so the same model reached over the wire told you less
about itself than one on disk.

Rows now render through the shared ModelRow, which is what gives them the same badges, the
same hover gutter and the same alignment rather than a second set that drifts:

- Modality badges and a Vision mark, resolved through the layers the app already has: the
  backend capability registry, the connection's cached catalogue, then the name fallback.
- A context window chip ("400K ctx", "1M ctx"), which is usually what choosing between two
  models from one connection comes down to.
- Pin to top, with drag reordering inside the pinned group.
- A gear that opens that model's own system prompt, output cap and reasoning effort.
- Model info, and Copy model ID.

Above the rows, the list gets a sort (by connection or by name) and a modality filter
(vision, audio, generates images), and each provider heading gets a fold chevron and a gear
for that connection's settings, which deep-links into Settings -> Connections with the form
already open.

Notes on the pieces that are not just UI:

Connected pins keep their own localStorage list. An external id is
external::<connection>::<model>, and the On Device store reads the "::" in it as its
repo/quant separator, so a pin filed there comes back out of pinnedQuantEntries as a phantom
pinned quant on the On Device tab.

The per-model system prompt and output cap are not a new store. Chat has remembered both per
checkpoint for as long as "Remember settings per model" has been on; the editor writes into
the same paramsByModel through a new setRememberedParamsForModel, which merges per key and
also patches the live params when the edited model is the loaded one. Reasoning effort is the
one genuinely new value, since the chat's own is a single global level.

Reasoning read as "Not published" on every ChatGPT/Codex model while the composer showed the
same model thinking. openai_codex has no namespace in the models.dev snapshot, so every
catalogue lookup for a Codex connection resolved to null, while
getExternalReasoningCapabilities has always aliased codex to openai. Alias it at the snapshot
lookup so both agree, and have both dialogs read reasoning and the output cap through the same
resolvers the composer uses.

Context length is new to the catalogue: ModelCatalogSnapshotEntry gains context, the generator
emits limit.context, and since the live provider response carries no context window, a live
entry backfills that one field from the snapshot instead of reporting a model that has one as
having none. Regenerating the snapshot also refreshed the rest of the models.dev data, which
is the documented catalog:refresh workflow.

* Studio: send the context window with the served catalogue, and line up the group heading

Three fixes on the Connected rows.

The context window read "Not published" for every model models.dev covers, gpt-6-astra's
1,050,000 included. The served catalogue from /api/providers/model-catalog is merged over the
bundled snapshot per model, and the backend's trimmer never emitted a context field, so the
served entry replaced the bundled one and took the window with it. The backend now sends
limit.context, which is what the frontend's own generator has always read, and the merge keeps
a bundled window when the served entry carries none, so a backend older than the field or its
cached payload inside the TTL does not erase it either.

The heading gear now hides until the heading is hovered, like a row's own gear.

The fold chevron now sits in the column each row's dots menu does. The heading's px-2.5 put it
8px inside that column, so -mr-2 takes the cluster out to the rows' mr-0.5 and both buttons
take the row gutter's box and overlap.

* Studio: address the review on the Connected rows

Three fixes from the review on #11196.

Clearing the max output field could not remove a remembered cap. The patch omitted the key,
setRememberedParamsForModel merges per key, and the server deep-merges the settings row, so the
old cap survived in memory and on disk while the field looked empty. Nothing in the data model
can express "forget this key", so the field no longer offers a blank: it is seeded from what the
model runs at now, which is its remembered cap or the chat's, and always holds a number.

Editing reasoning effort for the model already loaded did nothing until the user switched away
and back. The pin is read in handleCheckpointChange, which returns early for the model already
loaded, so the edit never reached the chat's own level. Saving now sets it directly when the
edited model is the live one, matched against the levels on offer so a level the model does not
accept cannot get through.

A row drawn with no heading over it did not say which connection it came from. The pinned group
and the flat list the name sort produces have no provider heading, and two connections can serve
the same model id, so those rows were indistinguishable. They now carry the connection's logo in
the slot the format dot would have used, which keeps the names on one line, and name the
connection in the row tooltip, which is what tells two connections of one provider type apart.
Rows under a heading are unchanged: the heading is still the only place their connection is
named.

* Studio: one resolver for an external model's reasoning effort, and fence the per-model edit

Three more fixes from the review.

The pin was only ever read on a model switch, so a reload put the provider default back over it,
and so did any provider resync, since the normalization effect recomputes the effort from the
catalogue and provider defaults alone. The two computations were already duplicated line for
line between that effect and handleCheckpointChange, with only the second consulting the pin.
Both now go through one resolveExternalReasoningEffort in provider-capabilities, which takes the
pin first, then the catalogue default, then the per-provider default. Same policy as before;
the only behaviour change is that the effect honours the pin.

Clearing a live model's pin back to Follow chat removed the pin but left the chat running at the
level the pin had put there, so the cleared value stayed in force. The dialog now resolves
through the same function with pinned: null, which recomputes the default the model would have
had, rather than special-casing concrete levels.

A per-model save made while the initial /api/chat/settings request was still out was discarded.
The write was gated on settingsHydrated, and trackParamsByModel files nothing into
locallyRememberedModels before hydration, so the response in flight rebuilt paramsByModel from
the server without the edit. The write is no longer gated, since the patch can only set the keys
it names and the server merges per key, and the model is filed as locally remembered so
hydration lays the edit over the server's copy. This is the same reasoning setParams already
states for its own thread-scoped capture.

* Studio: hold a pre-hydration per-model edit as a patch, not as a row

locallyRememberedModels is overlaid wholesale, which is right for a row built from a hydrated
entry but wrong for one typed before there was an entry: that row names only the keys the dialog
touched, so it replaced the server's entry and dropped that model's temperature, top-p and seed
for the session.

An edit made before the settings response lands is now held in its own map as a patch and merged
over the server row, which is the idiom the checkpoint overlay two lines below already uses. Once
merged the row is complete, so the model is promoted into locallyRememberedModels and any later
response takes the wholesale overlay again.

The same save on the live model had the matching hole: it patched params without bumping the
mutation versions, so hydration put the global set back over those keys until the next switch.
It now fences them through getChangedInferenceParams, the way a slider edit fences its own.

* Studio: save only what the editor touched, and bound the cap the way every request is

Two more fixes from the review.

The dialog can open before chat settings hydrate. Its useState initializers then held the empty
store's values after the response landed, and Save wrote both back, so a save that only changed
reasoning effort could wipe the system prompt and cap the server already had. Each field now
holds null until the user types in it, so an untouched field keeps reading the store, and Save
sends only the fields that were touched. It is a patch, and that is what a patch should carry.

The cap accepted any positive number while the chat's own Max Tokens control bounds itself with
getExternalMinOutputTokens and getExternalMaxOutputTokens, and the adapter clamps every outbound
request to exactly those. A model capped at 64k would store and display 200,000 while every
request sent 64,000. The editor now reads the same bounds, shows them in the label, clamps on
save rather than trusting the input's attributes, and takes the connection's own cap override,
which lowers the model's documented one.

Both dialogs also subscribe to the model catalogue now. An OpenRouter cap arrives with the live
catalogue, which can land after the dialog has rendered, and it is what these bounds and the
reported figures are read from. Same subscription chat-settings-sheet keeps for the same bound.

* Studio: an untouched reasoning effort writes nothing either

The prompt and cap stopped writing when untouched, but the effort select kept its mount value and
saved it unconditionally. Another tab can change this model's pin while the dialog is open, since
the store listens for the storage event, so a save of an unrelated field put the value the select
opened with back over the newer one. It also reset the composer's own Think level for no reason.

The select now holds null until the user picks something, the same as the other two fields, and
nothing reasoning-related is written unless it was touched.

The normalization effect reads the active model's pin through pinnedReasoningEffort, a getState
