Persists the selection in localStorage (same pattern as the model picker)
and moves the WorkIn type into lib/work-in-selection.ts.

Co-authored-by: Saoud Rizwan <saoudrizwan@users.noreply.github.com>

* feat(desktop): remove a task's worktree when the task is deleted

delete_chat_session now force-removes the ~/.cline/worktrees/<id>/<repo>
worktree (discarding uncommitted changes), deletes its cline/<id> branch
and the <id> directory, unless another session still lives in it. The
session_deleted event carries the removed path and parent repo so the
page can fall back to the repo when the worktree was the active
workspace.

Co-authored-by: Saoud Rizwan <saoudrizwan@users.noreply.github.com>

* fix(desktop): tighten worktree cleanup guards

Only remove worktrees of the exact ~/.cline/worktrees/<id>/<repo> shape
(the cleanup also deletes the <id> parent), treat sessions rooted in a
subfolder of the worktree as still using it, and validate the session
config before creating a worktree so an invalid config cannot orphan one.

Co-authored-by: Saoud Rizwan <saoudrizwan@users.noreply.github.com>

* fix(desktop): new threads return to the repo after a worktree task

A task worktree is never remembered as the last workspace, and reset()
re-seeds the workspace from that memory when leaving one, so "New"
lands back on the original repo and branch. This also covers reopening
an old worktree session, and replaces the session_deleted fallback.

Co-authored-by: Saoud Rizwan <saoudrizwan@users.noreply.github.com>

* fix(desktop): only delete the generated cline/<id> branch on worktree cleanup

Cleanup derived the branch from 'git branch --show-current', so a task
that switched branches in its worktree had that branch force-deleted
along with its commits. Derive the generated branch from the worktree
path instead. Also add remove_git_worktree so the webview can roll back
a worktree whose session never started.

* fix(desktop): serialize worktree allocation with the pending session start

Worktree creation ran before the prompt claimed its submission slot, so a
second prompt sent during allocation cut a second worktree and session.
Fold allocation into the pending start promise so follow-ups queue
behind it, and remove the worktree when the session fails to start in
it.

* feat(desktop): explain Local vs Worktree in the Work in picker

* chore: drop pre-commit hook regeneration of state.proto from the merge

The hook regenerated the proto from main's state-keys while committing
the merge; that file is unrelated to this PR.

* fix(desktop): identify task worktrees by the sidecar's worktree root

The webview matched task worktrees with a literal '.cline/worktrees'
segment, so with a custom CLINE_DIR it missed the worktrees the sidecar
actually creates (the transient checkout got remembered as the last
workspace and reset() stayed on it), while a real project under a
'.cline/worktrees' folder was wrongly treated as transient.

The sidecar now reports its CLINE_DIR-aware worktree root through
get_process_context and the webview matches only the exact
<root>/<id>/<repo> shape under it.

* fix(desktop): warn that deleting a worktree task removes its worktree

All three delete confirmations (thread pane, sidebar, sessions view)
said the session is only removed from local history, but for a task
that ran in a generated worktree the sidecar also force-removes the
worktree and its cline/<id> branch, discarding uncommitted files. Each
dialog now says so when the session's workspace is a task worktree.

* fix(desktop): keep a failed first Worktree launch eligible for retry

On a worktree creation or start failure the hook withdraws the
optimistic user message but appends an error message, so
messages.length was non-zero and the restored prompt retried with
inNewWorktree: false, silently starting in Local while the chip still
said Worktree. "New thread" is now derived from accepted state (no
session and no user/assistant message) rather than transcript length.

* fix(desktop): offer Worktree only for the local environment

main added remote (SSH) environments after this branch. Worktrees are
created by the local sidecar's git against a local path, so the Work in
picker is hidden and the choice falls back to Local for remote
environments.

commits.message:
The skip-blocker guard measured whatever data root the machine had (#1113)

* The skip-blocker guard measured whatever data root the machine had

`tests/skip_blockers.py` says a skip condition has to be a property of the CI
fixture, and rejects `ML4T_ARTIFACT_ROOT` as an instrument for exactly that
reason. Its own file half then took `_resolve_data_path()`, which returns
whatever this machine holds: on a workstation with the full dataset that is
`/home/stefan/Dropbox/ml4t/data`, which carries the raw ITCH and IEX captures
and the futures contract definitions that three declarations say the fixture
lacks. The guard called all three expired and told the reader to un-skip
notebooks that red CI, and the evaluator's own negative control asserted a real
fixture path was absent while the file was there.

`_fixture_root` now returns a root only when it is a checkout of
`ml4t/third-edition-test-data`, which is what every site mounting the fixture
checks out, and raises `NotTheFixture` otherwise. That is a subclass of
`UndecidableHere`, so a notebook run honours the skip - an unmeasurable
condition is not evidence the blocker has gone - while the guard test reports it
as a skip rather than erroring. The rest of `UndecidableHere` stays uncaught:
"the fixture is here and the seeding produced no registry" is still loud.

Nothing silently disables the guard in CI. `test-unit-data` checks out the
fixture and fails the job on any skipped test, so a discriminator that stopped
recognising it turns the whole file red there instead of passing quietly.

Local run goes from 4 failed, 74 passed to 76 passed, 7 skipped, each skip
naming the root it refused to measure.

* Test the refusal itself, not only the discriminator it calls

The two tests added with the previous commit exercise `is_ci_fixture` against
synthetic checkouts, and nothing reached `_fixture_root`: deleting the
`raise NotTheFixture` left the whole file green while restoring the failure the
commit fixes. Four tests now cover the wiring, all independent of which machine
runs them - `_fixture_root` refuses a non-fixture root and still returns None
when no root resolved at all, `honoured_skip_reason` keeps an
`absent_fixture_path` skip standing on a root that holds the named file but is
not the fixture, and reports the expiry when the same file appears inside a
fixture checkout. Replacing the refusal with a no-op now fails six tests, two of
them machine-independent.

Also: `test_holdout_selection_is_single_sourced.py` pointed at
`tests/skip_blockers.py:158` for the deliberate `NoSelectableCandidates` catch,
which the previous commit pushed to line 223. It names the function now, so the
next insertion does not stale it again.

A reader bundle can ship without the training sweep's per-epoch dumps (#1110)

The v3.1 artifact bundles are 15.5 GB against 3.1 GB for v3.0, and two of the
nine land past GitHub's 2 GB release asset limit. 6.5 GB of that is per-epoch
prediction dumps under training/<hash>/diagnostics/: all_predictions.parquet,
which holds every epoch of every fold and reaches 1.45 GB for one
nasdaq100_microstructure run, plus the <model>_fold<k>_ep<N>.parquet files
beside it. ARTIFACT_SCOPE.md never promised them, and the bundles carried them
only because the builder copies whole directories.

Nothing reads all_predictions.parquet. _cached_research_run() listed it as
required, then parsed it and discarded the frame, using only
best_epoch_predictions.parquet and result.json. So 3.8 GB shipped to make a
readability probe pass. It is now optional: a run that lacks it stays
reusable, and it is still verified when it is present, because a run carrying
a corrupt one is a run that did not finish writing. learning_curves.parquet,
result.json and training_log.parquet stay required.

nasdaq100_microstructure is 2.59 GB even trimmed, so download_artifacts.py
learns to fetch a split bundle: ARTIFACT_PARTS names how many parts a case
study ships, _fetch_parts() downloads <cs>.tar.gz.part00, .part01, ... and
concatenates them before anything is checked, so the whole-file checksum in
ARTIFACT_SHA256 still decides whether the download is good. A failed part
leaves no partial tarball behind.

RELEASE_TAG and the checksums are not touched here; they change when the
release is published.

Tests: a cached tabm run survives the loss of its epoch dump, with a negative
control asserting the cache is still refused when a file the reuse path reads
goes missing. The positive test fails against the previous code. The split
test asserts byte-identical reassembly and that the parts are cleaned up.
86 passed in tests/test_research_models.py and tests/test_download_artifacts.py.

Insight selectors read the live generation and carry the AUC columns their tables print (#1108)

* Insight selectors read the live generation and carry the AUC columns their tables print

Three defects in the shared readers behind the cross-case-study tables of chapters 11 through 14,
all found while closing errata sweep gaps.

A registry keeps every generation and records supersession one layer up, in official_populations,
so a reader that joins training_runs to prediction_metrics ranks history alongside the present and
cannot tell them apart on the numbers. That is not neutral: a generation is usually refitted
because it was short or narrow, a narrower sample is an easier one, and the stale rows therefore
run toward the top of the ranking. On cme_futures the retired deep-learning generation covers

them: 9 of 9 case studies at 39 to 66 features, 826 retired identities excluded, and the same
nine spine prediction hashes.

Three places that asserted something about history without checking it (#1106)

* Five notebooks took a workspace and registered in the published store anyway

`open_study` answers a canonical run with no workspace through `Study.regenerate`,
which writes through the generated-artifact symlinks to the released case
directory. #1100 fixed the two `research_workflow.open_study` definitions that
ignored a workspace at that tier; five callers in
`sp500_equity_option_analytics` still read `WORKSPACE` on their preview branch
only, so a canonical run given one reported the workspace it was asked for and
registered its rows in `~/ml4t/artifacts/`. No exception, no warning. That is
what left 60 allocation rows and 201 files in the published `sp500_options`
store on 2026-09-15, under a run whose exit status said it had refused.

13_model_analysis is the read-side half of the same defect: it reports on the
released registry while the caller believes it is reading the workspace.

All five now pass `execution_tier=EXECUTION_TIER` and `workspace=WORKSPACE or
None`, which is what the other 108 notebooks in the fleet already do. The local
name changes from `_preview_study` to `_workspace_study`, because at the
canonical tier it now holds a canonical study.

`tests/test_notebook_workspace_routing.py` asks every notebook declaring a
`WORKSPACE` parameter - 113 of them across all nine case studies - for the same
thing, and reds on all five pre-change files. It carries its own negative
control on the defective shape and a selection check, so a checker that matches
nothing cannot pass quietly.

Folded with sync-inert rather than re-executed: each recorded run declared
`parameters {}`, so `WORKSPACE` was the empty string and the new branch is not
taken. The outputs are byte-for-byte the ones those runs produced.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* A returning prediction pool could not find the plan that covers it

Two findings the review gate raised against 524d3b3b, both in what that
commit's plan lookup asserts about history.

**A pool that returns to an earlier generation.** The lookup took the most
recently published plan for a stage of a label. `OfficialPopulation.create` is
idempotent on membership, so a pool moving A -> B -> A is answered with A's
existing population, keeping its original `created_at`. The most recent name is
then B's, whose grid prices a prediction A's pool does not admit, and the sweep
that does cover the pool in force is reported missing. Re-running it cannot
clear that: the re-run reuses A's snapshot and its timestamp again, so the
report survives every remedy it offers.

`_plan_names_in_force` returns every recorded plan for the stage, newest first,
and `_plan_in_force` asks each in turn and takes the first that answers.
Recency now decides only which failure is reported when none does - which keeps
a real gap a gap, rather than turning "no plan covers the pool" into silence.

**A refusal the registry contradicts.** The baseline message said the members it
names "entered the pool after this sweep planned its grid, so the stage has
never been run against them". On the canonical `sp500_equity_option_analytics`
registry that is false for all three it names: `8764e506ec46`, `7037b8a2eaf6`
and `d921d9c4f747` each carry three signal-stage validation backtests from
2026-09-06, registered before the plan was. They left the pool under a coverage
screen and came back under `dd44ff59`. What is true is what the check measured -
this plan does not price them - so that is what it now says.

Two regressions: the A -> B -> A pool finds its own plan, and a pool no recorded
plan covers is still reported against the most recent one. The first reds on the
most-recent-only lookup; the second reds if the loop returns None instead of
re-raising.

**And the cost-curve refusal now carries the reasons it had already collected.**
`06_cost_survival` raises when no curve loads, and printed the per-case-study
exclusions on the line after it - so the all-excluded case, which a clean clone
with no registries reaches, reported only that nothing was found. The lines are
built once above the check by `CarrierCostCurves.exclusion_lines` and go into
the refusal. Folded with sync-inert: the recorded run loaded 67 curves, so that
branch was not taken and the cell prints the same strings in the same order.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* An interrupted sweep could be answered by the plan before it

The plan fallback added in the previous commit caught every failure, so it fell
past an incomplete or unattested plan to an older one. The review gate called
that reachable and it is.

A plan name hashes the whole prediction pool, while coverage is checked per
label. So changing one label's predictions mints a new plan name for every other
label whose predictions did not move. If one of those new sweeps is interrupted -
and a sweep publishes its grid before executing it, which is the whole point of
the plan - its predecessor covers exactly the same predictions and would be
accepted. An interrupted sweep reported as finished is the one thing this module
exists to prevent.

The fallback now catches `_PlanDoesNotCover` alone. That is the only failure
about *which* plan was asked; completeness and attestation are about the sweep
behind it, and both propagate from the first plan that fails them. It subclasses
RuntimeError, so `unfinished_sweep_plans` reports it unchanged.

The regression is the case above - `fwd_ret_5d` untouched, `fwd_ret_21d` gaining
a prediction, `fwd_ret_5d`'s new plan left incomplete - and it reds on the broad
catch.

Three values written down once and then used as rules (#1104)

Three infrastructure defects, two of them the same shape: a value that was
correct when it was written down, used afterwards as if it were a rule.

## 1. A pasted training hash kept NASDAQ-100 out of the cross-study cost chart

`case_studies/utils/analytics.py` resolved eight case studies' carriers through
`resolve_canonical_rank1_lineage` and routed the ninth around it, onto two pasted literals.
The 2026-09-05 registry reset replaced that lineage, so the training hash has matched zero
rows since and NASDAQ-100 quietly left the chart in `20_strategy_synthesis/06_cost_survival`.

The reading behind the literals - that NASDAQ's deployed carrier is a screened 12-gbm
ensemble the resolver cannot name - has lapsed. The `family == "ensemble"` clause left that
case study's rung pin on 2026-09-14 (`paired_metrics.RUNG_PINS`), and the carrier it ships is
the one the resolver already returns: `gbm/default_multiclass` on `fwd_dir_15m`, backtest
`a2d22880e93f`, which is what `nasdaq100_microstructure/20_strategy_analysis` publishes and the
lineage its single holdout was spent on. So the special case goes and every carrier resolves by
the same rule, re-read on every run.

NASDAQ-100 stays absent, now for a stated reason: its 24 cost-sensitivity backtests on the
carrier's lineage all run `equal_weight_top_k` while the carrier is a
`slot_persistent_signal_exit` slot strategy. **The curves do not move** - 67 entries across the
same 6 case studies, before and after.

The four bare `continue` statements that hid this now report:

```
Loaded 67 carrier cost-sweep entries across 6 case studies
  no curve for ETFs: no cost sweep on the carrier's lineage - 0 validation cost_sensitivity backtests on training_hash=ab5300c0cda4, carrier linear/ols on fwd_ret_5d
  no curve for NQ100: cost sweep is on a different strategy - 24 cost_sensitivity backtests on training_hash=7a0c26a08db7, none matching the carrier's strategy signature (slot_persistent_signal_exit)
  no curve for SP500 Options: cost sweep is on a different strategy - 8 cost_sensitivity backtests on training_hash=e698033183d9, none matching the carrier's strategy signature (equal_weight_top_k + score_weighted)
```

Rendered with `jupytext --update` -> papermill -> strip -> sanitize -> stamp; the notebook diff
outside the timing metadata is the loader cell, one markdown cell, the Known Limitations and one
alt-text sentence.

## 2. A sweep plan expired on a screen correction that moved no data

A sweep plan was looked up by a name carrying `members_digest` of the prediction sets in
force - an equality against a quantity `prediction_members_in_force` derives in repo code.
`dd44ff59` narrowed the coverage denominator for persistent-panel models, admitted three
`latent_factors/pca` prediction sets registered 2026-09-06 and unchanged since, and every plan
in `sp500_equity_option_analytics` became unfindable the same day.

`_plan_in_force` now finds a stage's plan by `(case_study, stage, label)` - still complete,
still attested - and asks the covering question of its contents, in both directions:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| `in_force - planned` | predictions with no planned backtest | baseline only; the stage after it prices what its upstream advanced |
| `planned - in_force` | predictions this grid priced that the pool has dropped | every stage; the ranking has moved under it |

The two need different work and the digest reported both as "no plan is recorded", the same
sentence a sweep that never ran gets. `predictions_identity` stays in the name as the record it
always was, so every plan already on disk stays findable and no sweep re-runs to be seen.

Measured on the canonical `sp500_equity_option_analytics` registry, 807 members in force under
`fe0f6ceeb71c` against plans recorded under `f4d4788c6b80`:

- **before** - all 15 plans absent
- **after** - 6 of 15 satisfied outright (both direction labels, every stage); the other 9 are
  three baseline sweeps short exactly one prediction set each, reported by hash

## 3. The session output dir was chosen by whichever test reached the fixture first

`seeded_output_dir` is session-scoped and read `ML4T_OUTPUT_DIR` live. `restore_output_root` is
function-scoped and captures its `before` after every higher-scoped fixture for that test has
set up, so a module- or session-scoped fixture anywhere that writes the variable hands the whole
worker its own `tmp_path` and the restore faithfully puts the leak back. The variable is now
captured while `tests/conftest.py` is imported - before any test module is collected - and the
fixture reads that. CI exports it at the workflow level before pytest starts, so that path is
unchanged.

The probe suite walks into the leak deliberately: two modules under `tests/`, in file order, the
first installing a leak from a module-scoped fixture and the second asserting the seeded
directory is not inside it. Reverting the one line to `os.environ.get` fails it.

Three guard tests come with these: the cost-curve loader fails on a case-study name or a
registry hash appearing in `analytics.py` at all, and removing the plan covering check reds
three of the sweep-plan tests.

fix(mobile): keep relay sessions stable during push lease updates (#7745)

Enabling push notifications could repeatedly reset the relay session:
reserving a lease generation updates community metadata, which rebuilt
the relay configuration even though the connection identity was
unchanged. This made the avatar and inbox flash and prevented the new
lease from publishing.

Select only the community ID, relay URL, and signing identity as
configuration dependencies. Push bookkeeping keeps the session intact;
real community, URL, and identity changes still notify listeners.

### Validation
The production-provider regression test failed before the fix and passes
afterward; 48 focused mobile tests and static analysis pass.

A personal signed profile build on a physical iPhone published a fresh
lease and received a background notification with the actual message
text. The user confirmed the flashing stopped and tapping the
notification opened the correct community/channel and highlighted the
exact message.

Signed-off-by: Tom Brow <tomb@block.xyz>

fix(desktop): keep managed agent avatars usable across communities (#7732)

## Summary

Fix Desktop-managed agents losing avatars after joining another
community. The saved persona/instance stores one desired source URL, but
authenticated media belongs to a community. Republishing community A’s
URL in B does not make that image accessible in B.

- Before comparing or publishing kind-0, reuse or copy
configured-community avatar media into the pinned destination. Keep
exact image bytes, including animation, and leave the saved source
unchanged.
- Keep the previous profile on transfer/publication failure so existing
reconciliation can retry. Reuse destination bytes during source outages;
after source removal, reuse only an already-published signed destination
picture with the same original content hash.
- Refresh source permissions through narrow, serialized IPC without
reconnecting or resetting the active community. Startup waits until the
latest permission update completes before restoring agents.

### Related issue

Refs #2366 (avatar portion only, not runtime availability). Related
#2659 deliberately excludes avatar/media mirroring; this change
addresses that media boundary without introducing runtime fan-out.
Searched existing issues/PRs for `avatar community` before opening.

## Contract and safety

Desktop-managed profiles still follow the saved persona source; this
does not introduce community-specific persona editing. Agent-managed
profiles still opt out of automatic reconciliation.

Authenticated transfer requests use the fixed agent key/NIP-OA tag,
origin-scoped Blossom auth, and the pinned destination, never mutable
active-workspace owner credentials. They refuse redirects, enforce
30-second request timeouts and bounded bodies, verify SHA-256 and
detected image MIME, and validate the returned descriptor’s
origin/hash/MIME/size. Source permission is rechecked after an awaited
destination HEAD miss. The removed-source fallback verifies the
destination profile’s signature, kind, signer, origin, and
original-media hash without contacting the removed source.

Ordinary external images retain passthrough behavior and receive no
community credentials. No public-media policy change, image-reader URL
rewriting, new persistence, background service, or global profile merge.

## Testing

Normal commit and push hooks passed on exact head
`925781eece66d5f6a4b084b3b3abd6309cda357e`; working tree clean before
and after:

- Desktop formatting/lint, typecheck, and **6,508 tests**.
- Full native workspace suite, including **3,204 desktop-library tests**
(19 ignored), integration tests, terminal crates, and doc tests.
- Native Clippy on default and `mesh-llm` workspace/all-target
configurations with warnings denied; repository file-size and
branch-skew gates.

Regression coverage exercises production reconciliation/shared
publication against two local HTTP fixtures: add/edit/restart, upload
and rejected-publication retry, removed-source local-image preservation,
fixed signer/destination, redirect/hash/descriptor/size failures,
revocation during pending HEAD, and opt-out no-I/O. Mounted
initialization tests cover inactive-list changes without workspace
reset, two deferred permission updates, and rejection of either update.

Earlier working-tree validation at base
`4ab4f786085a23fe6126529861840eff6048ceee` also passed the E2E frontend
build and four Chromium mock-bridge community flows (boot, switch,
active removal/fallback, leave-final/setup). Subsequent production
changes only serialize permission writes and wait for a stable latest
update; the complete suites above cover the final commit. Mutations
independently removing serialization or stable waiting failed the new
regression.

## Remaining validation and limitations

- No live production avatar was changed. Native GUI rendering against
two hosted communities remains to be verified with a build containing
this fix; local HTTP fixtures and the browser mock bridge do not
establish that outcome.
- A removed/unreachable source with no existing destination copy cannot
be recovered automatically. Choose a reachable image/source in that
case.
- This is a publication/reconciliation fix, not a visual redesign. No
before/after native GUI screenshots are claimed. Broad repository CI
remains required; it was not duplicated locally.

## Review

Independent security/scope and caller/ordering reviews are clear after
the bounded fixes. Final hook-ordering reread covered the staged tree
that became this commit. Commit authorship/sign-off use the implementing
Carl identity and configured Carl signing key.

chore: update lance dependency to v13.0.0-beta.6 (#4224)

Updates the Rust workspace Lance dependencies, Cargo lockfile, and Java
lance-core from 13.0.0-beta.4 to
[v13.0.0-beta.6](https://github.com/lance-format/lance/releases/tag/v13.0.0-beta.6).
Fixes the redundant visibility qualifier on the internal identifier
delimiter constant reported by Clippy.

Validation: `cargo clippy --quiet --workspace --tests --all-features --
-D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all --quiet`, and `git diff --check`.

feat: define a materialized view by its query, with Functions in FROM position (#4190)

A view definition was a structured record under a `kind` tag, one kind
per query shape, and a Function returning `list<struct>` was about to
add a third. That names shapes instead of describing a relation.

A materialized view is now a relation defined by a query, stored as one
canonical SQL string under a format number:

```sql
SELECT columns FROM [ns.]table [, function(args) AS alias | , UNNEST(column) AS alias]
[WHERE predicate] [LIMIT n]
```

Any other clause is refused at parse time. Older readers report the view
as unrefreshable, the pre-format layouts still read, and a legacy view
is rewritten on its next refresh that commits, rebuilt only where its
raw text meant something else under lance's parser.

A Function in FROM position yields one row per element it returns, as a
table function does in any dialect. The server stages its list output in
a hidden table and records that binding beside the query, which stays as
the user wrote it; refresh scans the staging and unnests the column, the
same operator as UNNEST over a list column the table already holds. Row
ids repeat per element, so eviction and incremental append are
unchanged. A local database refuses a Function in FROM position, since
it has no executor.

fix(python): decode file URIs in OpenCLIP (#4131)

## What

Decode the path component of `file://` image URIs before passing it to
Pillow.

## Why

`Path.as_uri()` percent-encodes characters such as spaces. Passing
`parsed.path` directly to Pillow therefore tries to open a literal `%20`
path and fails.

## Testing

- Added a regression test that opens an image whose local filename
contains a space.
- Verified the focused URI conversion behavior against the changed
method.
- Ruff check, formatting check, and `compileall` on both changed files.

Part-of: <https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/librsvg/-/merge_requests/1212>

Use a temporary EntityData struct to avoid having unsafe code in xml/mod.rs.

From sax_entity_decl_cb() (the callback which lets libxml2 call us
when a new entity is being declared), we need to do this:

- Convert the entity's name into a String, to test if it already
  exists in our hashmap.

- If it doesn't exist, actually create an xmlEntityPtr with
  xmlNewEntity() and store it in the hashmap.

- If it exists, just ignore it.

However, doing the second point directly in xml/mod.rs means that we
need an unsafe call there.  Instead, use a temporary struct EntityData
that will be consumed with its .into_xml_entity() method only if
needed.

The only remaining "ugly" bit in xml/mod.rs is that
XmlState::entity_lookup() returns an Option<xmlEntityPtr>, because
internally it needs a cell::Ref to get at the hashmap.

Part-of: <https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/librsvg/-/merge_requests/1211>

xml2_load.rs: Declare our XmlEntity wrapper here

Let's really make this file about the interface to libxml2; the caller
should have only librsvg-specific logic.

Remove obsolete comment

Part-of: <https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/librsvg/-/merge_requests/1211>

(#1241): Fix use-after-free with duplicate XML entities

When an included XML document declares an entity with a duplicate name
as an existing one, librsvg would deallocate the old xmlEntityPtr in
XmlEntity::drop() when the duplicate entity is inserted in the hash
table.  However, libxml2 still keeps pointers around to the entity
declared in the base document, and makes use of them.

This commit makes librsvg ignore entity declarations when they come in
with the same name as an entity that has already been declared.  This
is probably not 100% correct in terms of XML semantics, but I don't
recall seeing text about that in the Xinclude spec.

Thanks to Rafael B. Dias for reporting this in detail.

feat(web-shell): show a Goal's turn and active-time ceilings on the status strip (#12201)

The strip above the composer showed spend against the token budget but
active time with no ceiling and no turn figure at all, so a Goal armed
with model.goalMaxTurns or model.goalMaxActiveMinutes showed how far it
had run and not how much room was left; only the workspace Goals dialog
did. The strip now reads 12m 3s / 30m 0s and 3 / 20 turns when those
ceilings are set, and is unchanged for a Goal without them. The dialog
takes its active-time label from the same helper.

test(core): await full run exit before resuming in the authoring-hint test (#12196)

The completion callback fires synchronously from fail()/complete() while
the runner's finally block (snapshot write, journal drain, checkpoint
removal) still holds the run's handle. A resume that lands in that
window is refused by reserveStart with "has not exited yet". On loaded
CI runners the cleanup I/O regularly outlasts vi.waitFor's poll, so the
test failed 3/3 attempts on main.

Await the handle's completion promise (resolves after releaseHandle) at
both resume points, matching the idiom already used elsewhere in this
file.

refactor(goal): read the unreadable-state running card through the core reader (#12194)

The trailing cleared card for a Goal whose saved state could not be read
found its running card with a second scanner in the cli, restoreGoal.ts,
next to core's findRunningLegacyGoalCard. Recovery fails that way only
when no goal_state record parses, so the replay showed a card for none of
them and the one running card it can have ended on is a pre-#7895 one:
the core reader over the records with the unreadable goal_state records
set aside is the same answer. restoreGoal.ts and its tests go; the two
rules only they pinned move to the core reader's tests, which now also

feat(core): assemble the system prompt from the resident tool set (#12145)

* docs(design): assemble the system prompt from the resident tool set

Design for step 1 of #12032: resolve the declared tool-name set once per
session start, pass it to the prompt builder as a trailing options
object, and gate the tool-policy bullets and the tool-call examples on
it. Safety, permission and dangerous-action text stays unconditional,
and the prompt cache prefix is rewritten no more often than today —
per-reveal regeneration is named as follow-up work rather than proposed.

Records the constraint that pulls against #12029, the three prompt
references that are not interpolated from ToolNames and so need editing
before they can be gated, and the test surface that moves (17 full-prompt
snapshots plus the example/validator equality assertion).

English and zh-CN versions per docs/design/README.md.

Refs #12032

* feat(core): gate tool-specific prompt text on the declared tool set

Implements step 1 of the design in this PR. `startChat` snapshots the tool
names it declared — after the registry is warm and the budget preload has
settled — onto Config, and the prompt builder receives that set through a
trailing options object, so the seven-parameter public signature of
getCoreSystemPrompt is unchanged and callers without a session keep
today's output.

Gating is a line filter over `## Using Your Tools` plus an `<example>`
block filter over the tool-call examples, and both return their input
untouched when no snapshot is present. A line survives only when every
tool it names is declared, so the prompt can no longer steer the model
toward a tool it was not given. Safety, permission and dangerous-action
text, and the CodeModeOnly guidance (whose tools are reached inside
`exec` rather than declared), are never gated.

Also corrects four points in the design doc that the implementation
settled: multi-tool bullets need every tool declared, not any; the
`GlobTool` mention stays verbatim because ToolDisplayNames.GLOB is
`Glob`; examples that call no tool are never gated and the heading goes
only when no block survives; and prompt-tool-examples.test.ts keeps
passing because the default path stays ungated. Two prose mentions of
read_file outside the gated sections are recorded as known residue.

Nothing was run locally; CI runs the tests.

Refs #12032

* fix(core): gate examples as whole blocks and tolerate a Config without the setter

Both defects came out of CI on the previous commit.

`startChat` called `setPromptToolSnapshot` unconditionally, which threw on
the partial Config stubs that client.test.ts builds and failed every test
in that file. The call is now optional: a Config without the setter simply
leaves the prompt ungated.

The example filter split on blank lines, but an example can contain blank
lines of its own — the refactor example's later paragraphs were separated
from the `<example>` tag that gates them, so its `edit` call survived a
session that never declared `edit`. Blocks are now matched as
`<example>`/`</example>` pairs.

Design doc updated in both languages with the paired-tag rule and why
blank-line splitting was wrong.

Refs #12032

* fix(core): keep the startup profile stable and update the prompt-arg assertions

Two more CI failures from the previous commit, both in client.test.ts.

The snapshot no longer gets its own profiler stage: it is a map over
declarations the registry has already built, and the startup stage list is
asserted, so a stage there is noise the test correctly rejected.

The four exact-argument assertions on getCoreSystemPrompt now carry the
trailing options object the prompt builder receives.

Refs #12032

* docs(verification): hand off the measurement this PR cannot do

Records what still has to be proven and how, because CI green here only
means the unit tests pass: it does not show the prompt got smaller, and it
does not show the other prompt consumers are untouched.

States up front that a default session saves exactly zero — every tool is
declared, so nothing is gated — and that any measurement taken without a
trimmed tools.eager will read 0 and say nothing about the change. Carries
the statically simulated sizes to compare against (the gated sections are
7,209 chars ungated; a file-work allowlist drops ~4,012 of them, ~1k
tokens), the QWEN_WRITE_SYSTEM_MD before/after recipe, the three-way split
that separates this change's saving from tools.eager's, grep checks for the
safety anchors and for tool names that must no longer appear, a
ten-row blast-radius table including the two reverse checks that must show
NO change (code mode, QWEN_SYSTEM_MD override), and the weakened recall
check that is all the repo's missing eval harness allows.

Refs #12032

* test(core): make the prompt saving and its blast radius visible in CI

The validation plan had five items and only one of them was automated;
the rest were handed to another machine, which meant CI green here proved
nothing about the change's effect. Four are now tests:

- the saving itself, asserted in a 3,500-4,500 character band (measured
  4,012, ~1k tokens, for a file-work allowlist) so a lost saving and newly
  added ungated tool text both fail here rather than silently
- nothing outside `## Using Your Tools` and `# Examples` moves
- a mechanical sweep of every ToolNames value against the gated text,
  replacing three hand-picked not.toContain assertions
- the two reverse checks: code mode renders identically with and without a
  snapshot, and getMainSessionBaseSystemPrompt really reads
  Config.getPromptToolSnapshot() — the property that keeps /context and the
  request on one source

Design doc §7 now says which items CI covers and which still need a real
session, and the verification brief no longer asks for the four that are
automated; what is left there is the provider-side token measurement and
the recall check.

Refs #12032

* fix(core): gate every example notation, and correct the saving I mis-measured

Two things static inspection caught that CI never would have.

The example filter only understood `[tool_call: …]`, which is the general
and code-mode notation. `getToolCallExamples` hands qwen-coder an XML
form, qwen-vl a JSON form and Gemma 4 a native form, so for every Qwen
model with its own example set the examples were not gated at all. All
four notations are now recognised — the JSON alternative keys on the
`"arguments"` field that follows it so a `"name"` in unrelated JSON is not
read as a call.

And the saving I reported was wrong. The script that produced "4,012
characters / ~1k tokens" parsed tool-names.ts into one map, so
ToolDisplayNames overwrote the tool names and every example looked like it
called an undeclared tool. Re-measured: a file-work allowlist saves 1,104
characters (~276 tokens) of policy bullets and keeps all seven examples,
because those examples only call file tools and the shell. Reaching ~1k
tokens needs an allowlist narrow enough to exclude edit, write_file and
glob (4,327-5,069 characters depending on the model's example set).

Tests now bracket both cases and cover the model-specific notations. The
brief and both design docs carry the corrected figures, and say plainly
that this change is worth having for correctness — it stops the prompt
recommending tools the model was not given — rather than for the tokens.

Refs #12032

* test(core): withhold every tool in turn, and pin the kept guidance

Two gaps the earlier tests left.

The invariant only ran against the sets it happened to name. It now
withholds one tool at a time across all 66 names and all four model
example sets — the config-independent version, and the check that would
have caught the example notations going ungated in the first place.
`ask_user_question` is the single documented exception: it is exempt from
tools.eager and the bullet naming it also carries the do-not-ask policy
for headless runs, so gating that bullet would drop real guidance.

Nothing asserted the other half of the invariant either, so a new test
pins the guidance that must survive for the tools a session does declare.

perf(core): manifest-only refresh for the extension catalog route (#12153)

* perf(core): manifest-only refresh for the extension catalog route

GET /extensions only reads seven identity fields per extension, but it
paid for a full cold load: per-extension skills scans, commands globs,
agents scans, and MCP config loads whose results the response discards.

Factor the manifest head out of loadExtension (install metadata, parsed
manifest, extension id, base Extension object) and add
refreshCatalogSnapshot, which walks the extensions dir through the head
only. The agent-plugins-v1 MCP merge is gated behind loadMcpServers so
the catalog path never runs its createDataDir write side effect. The
route now uses the catalog refresh; full-load fail semantics (corrupt
manifest skipped, broken entry stat fails the whole load) and the
fingerprint baseline rules (full commits, name-filtered does not) are
preserved and pinned by tests.

Bench (100 extensions x 40 skills / 10 commands / 5 agents, 12 runs):
full-load median 452-522 ms; catalog refresh median 18-20 ms.

* fix(core): share the extension traversal with the catalog refresh

Address review: fix the invalid installMetadata literal in the catalog
test (missing source, unknown originSource) that broke tsc --build and
every CI job behind it; route the manifest-only load through
loadExtensionsFromExtensionsDir instead of duplicating its traversal
and fail semantics; keep the names filter with its no-baseline rule
pinned by a test; add a baseline test for the unfiltered refresh.

* fix(core): make the catalog load stateless and inclusion-exact

Address review: the manifest-only load now runs inside loadExtension
via a manifestOnly option, reusing its catch and skip warning instead
of a second traversal; the head's MCP load runs on both paths (data-dir
creation still gated) so the catalog's inclusion set cannot diverge
from the full load; refreshCatalogSnapshot returns the result directly
without touching extensionCache or the fingerprint baseline, which
removes the shared-manager poisoning hazard and the per-request
fingerprint walk; the bench resolves the repo root one level deeper and
the route reads the returned extensions instead of the manager cache.

fix(cli): keep full-turn tool cancellation out of the error path (#11154)

* fix(cli): keep full-turn tool cancellation out of the error path

The full-turn branch of useReactToolScheduler awaited resolveForModel() and
then treated every scheduler.schedule() rejection as a genuine failure. When
the shared scheduler is busy, an aborted queued request rejects with "Tool
call cancelled while in queue.", which is a cancellation, so the catch
synthesized status: 'error' / UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION calls, appended them to the
active tool list, and ran the completion handler. use-llm-stream commits that
group to history and records the tool result before its cancellation checks,
and allToolsCancelled only matches status === 'cancelled', so pressing Esc was
persisted to the chat recording and submitted to the model as a real
scheduling failure.

Complete an aborted rejection as 'cancelled' instead, mirroring the normal
branch's signal.aborted guard and core's pre-validation cancellation. Routing
it through the existing completion handler rather than returning early is what
releases toolBatchIdByCallIdRef, interactionOwnersByToolCallIdRef and
continuationOwnersByToolCallIdRef for the cancelled callIds, and what makes
allToolsCancelled fire so nothing is submitted as a tool error. Genuine
runtime-resolution and scheduling failures still fail closed with
UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION.

fix(core): stop session recovery from flagging unanswered notifications (#12007)

* fix(core): stop session recovery from flagging unanswered notifications

A background notification is persisted before its automatic turn runs, so a
notification whose turn never ran leaves a `role: 'user'` tail that nothing
will ever answer. The record's `subtype: 'notification'` and
`provenance: 'system'` do not survive the projection into `Content`, so
`detectTurnInterruption` saw an ordinary unanswered user entry and classified
it as `interrupted_prompt` with `canContinue: true` — pinning the Web Shell
recovery banner on a session whose last real turn had ended with `end_turn`.
Trailing system-injected notification envelopes are now skipped before
classifying, which also stops them from masking a dangling tool call underneath.

Separately, `getRecoveryStatus` gated `canContinue` on `pendingPrompt` alone.
Notification and cron turns run their own streaming loop and never install it,
so a healthy automatic turn in flight still reported `canContinue: true` — and
an accepted continuation is driven through normal prompt admission, which
aborts `notificationAbortController` / `cronAbortController`. The gate now uses
the existing `#hasActiveTurn()`.

Patrol-Run: qwen-issue-patrol/jmu3ra3yk84

* fix(core): gate the notification trim on user role

`isSystemNotificationContent` decided provenance from the part text alone, so
a MODEL entry whose whole text is a `<task-notification>` envelope got trimmed
too. That exposed the prompt the model *did* answer as the tail and returned
`interrupted_prompt` with `canContinue: true` for a session that ended cleanly
— the false recovery banner this change exists to remove, re-introduced.

Model output is never defanged (`sanitizeMonitorLine` covers monitor lines
only), so the envelope shape cannot carry provenance on its own. The role can:
`createNotificationRecord` builds every real notification from
`createBaseRecord('user')`, so requiring `role === 'user'` cannot drop one.

Also export the trim as `effectiveHistoryEnd` so the reconcile-side guard in
`prompt-terminal-ledger.ts` can read the same tail the classifier reads, and

* fix(core): decide the recovery notification trim by provenance, not shape

Session recovery trimmed any trailing user entry whose whole text is a bare
`<task-notification>` envelope. A real user prompt shaped exactly like that
(pasted, or requested as a verbatim echo) satisfies every clause of the shape
predicate, so `effectiveHistoryEnd` ate it, `detectTurnInterruption` then read
the PREVIOUS model turn as the tail and returned `none`, and the recovery plan
mapped that to `{ kind: 'clean', canContinue: false }`. The orphaned prompt got
no banner and no Retry, and the next send popped it out of live history through
`stripOrphanedUserEntriesFromHistory`.

The record's own stamp can tell the two apart, and `Content` (from
`@google/genai`) cannot carry it. So the projection reports it on the side
channel it already returns next to `apiHistory`:
`buildSessionHistoryFromConversation` now also yields
`trailingSystemNotifications`, the count of trailing entries whose source
record `createNotificationRecord` stamped `provenance: 'system'` plus
`subtype: 'notification'`. The accumulator keeps a parallel flag array so the
count stays aligned across the slash-command pop, the mid-turn merge, the
compression reset and thought stripping.

`effectiveHistoryEnd` and `detectTurnInterruption` take it as an OPTIONAL
extra argument that can only NARROW the trim: an entry is trimmed when its
shape matches AND it falls inside the authoritative run. One-argument callers
get byte-identical behaviour, so the cross-package consumer
`tailHoldsAnyFunctionCall` in packages/cli needs no change.

Zero is emitted rather than omitted, because here zero is information: the
recorder affirmatively saying the tail is NOT a notification is exactly what
saves the envelope-shaped prompt.

The second documented residual is NOT closed and the docblock now says why: a
delivered-then-failed notification turn and a cold persisted record both funnel
through the same `createNotificationRecord`, so they carry an identical stamp.
`backgroundTurn` is the only differing field and the `channelTask` admission
branch runs it with the context exited, so it is not a reliable discriminator.
That still needs a distinguishing record field or a daemon-side re-drive.

Tests pin both directions: the envelope-shaped real prompt now recovers as
`interrupted_prompt` end to end through the plan, while a genuine cold
notification is still trimmed to `clean` (the bug this PR originally fixed).
Each new assertion was verified to fail under a targeted mutation of the fix.

fix(web-shell): keep the mermaid canvas fixed while zooming out (#12177)

Zoom was a transform on the box that also carried the canvas background and
the diagram's own horizontal scrollbar. A transform moves paint, not layout,
so zooming out scaled the scroll viewport along with the diagram and left the
pan range computed from the unscaled width: at half size a 3223px diagram
painted 1612px inside a 489px sliding strip in the middle of a 978px row,
while the scrollable range stayed 2277px and matched nothing on screen.
Panning was a second translate on the same box on top of that — unbounded
horizontally, so dragging past the content origin pushed the leading edge of
the diagram out of the scrollable region, where no scroll brought it back.

Give the three roles their own boxes: the wrapper is the canvas and the only
scroller, the inner box carries nothing but the diagram, scaling uses `zoom`
so layout moves with the paint and the reachable range tracks the diagram
rather than its full-size box, and dragging drives the scroll position instead
of a transform. The canvas takes the diagram's own size, read from its svg:
mermaid marks everything outside flowchart `width="100%"`, so those diagrams
keep shrinking to the canvas width while the rest sit at their design size — a
`fit-content` box cannot resolve that percentage and would fall back to the
300x150 default object size. The canvas holds the diagram's unscaled height so
zooming never reflows the transcript, and it offers the grab cursor only while
part of the diagram is out of view: a diagram that already fits cannot be
moved by dragging, and the cursor should not promise otherwise.

refactor(goal): retire recovery of Goals recorded before Goal state was journaled (#12155)

* refactor(goal): retire recovery of Goals recorded before Goal state was journaled

Builds before #7895 (2026-07-29) journaled /goal as goal_status cards in
slash_command records, and recovery migrated the newest running card into
a paused Goal v2 record on resume. Nothing has written those cards for
seven weeks. Recovery now reads goal_state records only: a transcript
whose Goal records are all legacy cards restores with no Goal, nothing is
migrated, and restore never writes to the journal.

The cards stay in the replay as history. A client that derives the live
Goal from the newest card would then show a legacy set card as running,
so the ACP session keeps its trailing cleared card and emits it whenever
the runtime recovered no Goal and the replay ends on a running legacy
card, now worded to say the Goal was recorded by an earlier version and
can be set again. The session list keeps reading the legacy card for its
label, which is display, not recovery.

Removes recoverLegacyGoal, createMigratedGoalState, the legacy GoalRecovery
kind and the runtime's migration branch, narrows the recovery candidate
and normalisation helpers to goal_state, and drops acpAgent's legacy
bootstrap. The migrated cause stays as a legacy enum value so records a
migration once wrote still parse.

* refactor(goal): restore the hooks files this branch had rolled back

The first commit was squashed from a tree that predated #12138 and
#12139, so it carried their reverse: hook-event-display, hook-timeout,
the hooks listing's disabledReason, the locale strings, the hooks dialog
and acpAgent's agentScope filter. None of that is Goal work. Every one of
those files is back at what main has.

* refactor(goal): guard the legacy supersession card and share its reader

Review round on #12155. The trailing cleared card for a running card a
build before #7895 wrote now needs the runtime to drive no Goal and the
card to be the transcript's newest Goal record: a Goal set after the
resume, or any goal_state record after the card, means a journaling build
has had the last word. The live-restore path appends the same card after
the replayed page, which it did not before; a cold load did. The card's
reader moves to core as findRunningLegacyGoalCard and the session list's
label reads through it, so the two agree on what a running card is.

Also: prepareRestore loses a check and a try/catch nothing could reach
once a restore stopped writing, with a test that disposal while the
preparation is still queued is what the remaining check is for; the
comments that still explained the session-writer wait and the migrated
cause by the deleted journal write say what is true now; the user doc
scopes the trailing card to daemon clients.

* refactor(goal): keep the legacy supersession card from failing a live load

The card a live load appends after the replayed page is presentation.
It is skipped on a partial replay, since the page did not end where the
transcript does; rendering or sending it is caught and logged; and on a
bulk page already at the update or byte limit it is dropped rather than
tipping the envelope over the limit the page was cut to. A runtime test
pins that a goal_state record with a malformed blockedAudit is the
unreadable case: the parser rejects the whole record, so prepareRestore
never sees a partially parsed one and later writes stay blocked.

* refactor(goal): give cold and live loads the same rules for the trailing Goal updates

One helper appends a load's Goal updates to a bulk replay page only when
the page still fits its limits, so a transcript that loads on a live
session does not fail with transcript_page_too_large on a cold load. A
cold bulk load tells the renderer when the page is partial, and the
legacy supersession is then not rendered, as the live path already did;
recovered state still publishes, since it is the runtime's, not the
page's. The live streamed path renders the card after the page is
delivered, so it reads the Goal as it stands then. The legacy card
reader stops its setAt walk at a goal_state record: the run the card
belongs to started after it. The new core value import in the cli goes
to its defining module.

* refactor(goal): deliver the recovered Goal state a full cold bulk page cannot carry

appendGoalUpdatesWithinLimits reports whether it appended. On a cold
bulk load a full page's Goal updates are the recovered state itself,
which the client must still get; they are sent as live updates once the
session is up, the way a streamed load sends them, with the publication
key primed as before so the subscription does not publish the same
state twice. Before this the state was dropped and the primed key kept
any later publication from filling the gap. On a live load the dropped
update is the presentation card, which goes without.

feat(web-shell): draw the commit history as a lane graph, across all branches, with search (#12152)

* feat(web-shell): draw the commit history as a lane graph, across all branches, with search

The history tab listed HEAD's commits as a flat list: branch structure was invisible, other branches were unreachable without a checkout, and there was no way to find a commit by message, author, or hash.

The daemon log route now takes `all=1` to walk HEAD plus every local branch, remote branch, and tag, and `search=<text>` to keep only commits whose message, author, or hash prefix matches (case-insensitive fixed strings; git ANDs `--grep` with `--author`, so the two walks are unioned and paged by commit date). Every walk is `--date-order`, so a parent never precedes a child and the client can lay out lanes from `parents` alone.

The history tab gains a search field, an "All branches" toggle, and a lane graph column: one lane per concurrent line of development, S-curves at forks and merges, hollow nodes for merge commits, and lanes drawn straight through an expanded commit's detail block. The branch chip offers a "History" action next to "View Changes".

feat(web-shell): render the compression outcome from structured meta (#12141)

* feat(web-shell): render the compression outcome from structured meta

The compression commands stream their outcome as English sentences over ACP,
which a host that owns its own UI language cannot render. They now carry the
outcome as machine-readable `_meta` next to the sentence, the transcript record
and replay pass it through, and the web shell renders it in the user's language
with the token counts formatted for that language.

A compression that finds nothing to strip reports a terminal no-op phase rather
than reusing the pending one: the payload-driven row has to state the outcome,
and a pending row is dropped once the turn ends.

The invocation note rides its own `_meta` key rather than sharing the result's.
The daemon UI reducer folds a turn's text frames into one block and spreads
`_meta` key by key, so a shared key would be overwritten by the frame that
follows. Nothing else reads the new keys and no frame gains the
discrete-message marker, so a host that renders text as-is sees the same
sentences it saw before.

Opening a session whose last action was a compression also reconciles the
composer's context counters once. They are seeded from the last usage frame in
the replay, and a compression emits none, so they described the context it
replaced; a read is only written back while the session is live and its model
and context window have settled, which is what the reconcile waits for.

* docs(design): describe the structured compression outcome

The design records why the outcome travels as metadata beside the sentence, why
the invocation note needs its own key, why the no-op is a terminal phase, and
how the composer counters reconcile on an attach that ends on a compression. It
also keeps the compatibility analysis for other clients, which is a constraint
of this change rather than a follow-up.

feat(workflows): record a checkpoint for every run and surface runs a restart interrupted (#12159)

A run's snapshot is written when it settles, and the registry that knows
about a live run dies with the process. A run whose process was killed,
crashed or closed mid-run left only its journal: it was missing from
/workflows and from an ACP client's task list, and nothing told the user it
could be resumed.

Every registered run now writes <runId>/checkpoint.json beside its journal
and removes it when it settles. The write is not awaited at start; the
settlement waits for it before removing it. A later process claims a
checkpoint whose writer is gone (same host, pid no longer running, or this
process's pid with no session here holding the run or its lock): it writes
a failed snapshot with an "interrupted" error, agent counts from the
journal and the script, meta and args the run started with, then removes
the checkpoint. A checkpoint rewritten since it was read, or one a snapshot
of the same attempt already covers, is not claimed.

ACP claims before a new session reads workflow history. The interactive
CLI claims at startup and shows a notice listing each interrupted run with
the call that resumes it. Headless runs do not claim.

Snapshots now keep the run's args (up to 256 KiB, else argsOmitted), which
retrying from history will need.

* fix(browser-use): deliver bridge messages in arrival order and keep dev info flags fast

Three fixes from the round-3/4 verification and review round 7–8:

- Transport: a response only settles a promise, so its consumer ran on the
  microtask queue while events from the same socket chunk were emitted
  synchronously and overtook it. Playwright installs a page's renderer and
  lifecycle listeners inside `Page.getFrameTree().then(...)`, so an
  overtaking `Runtime.executionContextCreated` found no listener and a
  claimed tab lost its main world for good (B1). Inbound messages now go
  through one per-socket queue whose drain yields a macrotask after
  settling a response, so every continuation runs before the next message;
  chunks arriving meanwhile join the same queue. Regression:
  `delivers a response ahead of the events that share its socket chunk`.
- Relay: `requireControllableTab` judged a popup by `tab.url`, which is
  empty until the navigation commits, while the claim keyed on
  `pendingUrl`; the runtime's immediate `tabs.get` therefore rejected the
  tab the relay had just reported (R8-2). It now judges by
  `pendingUrl || url`, like the claim. Regression:
  `a popup known only by its pending URL stays controllable`.
- dev launcher: the dev-mode runtime staging skips `--version`/`--help`
  (and `-v`/`-h`), restoring the fast path the existing tests pin (R7-1).

fix(workflows): refuse a resume that has no journal, and keep a run's sourceRef across restarts (#12097)

* fix(workflows): refuse a resume that has no journal, and keep a run's sourceRef across restarts

A resume replays a run's journal. With the journal missing, the runner
loaded an empty replay and dispatched every agent again under the old run
id, so a run that read as a continuation was a full re-run, and the tool
description promised exactly that.

- WorkflowJournal.load() reports a missing file and an unreadable one apart
  from an empty replay. A resume whose journal is missing or unreadable is
  refused before any agent is dispatched or anything is written. A journal
  that exists and holds nothing still resumes, so run ids from before this
  change stay usable.
- A fresh run queues a 'launched' record first, never a resumed one, so the
  journal of a run that launched is not empty.
- The guard that keeps a run's sourceRef read the in-process registry, which
  does not outlive the process. After a restart it now reads the run's
  snapshot, so a resume whose journal lost the source record is refused
  instead of settling unattributed and overwriting the snapshot that held
  the reference.
- reserveStart says what to do about a run id that is still running, paused,
  or not yet exited, instead of only that it is active.
- The trailer, the recovery advice, the background diagnostics, the
  resumeFromRunId description and the authoring skill no longer promise a
  live re-run without a journal; a run that wrote no journal is offered no
  resume call.

* test(core): give the name-only registry test the journal a resume call needs

The test registers a run with a script path and no journal path, and
expects the recovery block to offer a resume call outside a name-only
session. A resume is now offered only beside a journal to replay, so the
run it registers carries one.

* fix(workflows): wait for queued journal writes before removing a failed start's journal

A fresh run queues its 'launched' record without awaiting it. When a
cancel lands while the journal is being created, the next synchronous
check fails the start and the cleanup removes the journal while that
append is still in flight. The append then lands after the delete and
recreates the file (writeLine creates the directory too), so a run id
that never registered is left with a non-empty journal, which a later
resume accepts and runs every agent for.

WorkflowJournal.remove() now drains the queued appends before deleting,
so no write queued before the cleanup can outrun it. The comment at the
launch record said every journal write on the start path is unawaited,
which was wrong: the source record is awaited. It now says why this one
is not, and what keeps it safe.

The new test lets the real writeLine run, a beat late, and cancels the
start while the journal is being created.

* docs(core): keep buildResumeCall's comment on the function it describes

* fix(workflows): restore a resumed inline script from its snapshot after a restart

A resume that fails to start puts back the inline script copy it
overwrote, but only from the registry entry, which does not outlive the
process. After a restart the original run's copy stayed overwritten by
the script of the attempt that never ran. The runner now reads the run's
snapshot once, for the sourceRef guard and for this restore.

A run that is still pausing cannot be resumed yet (resume() wants
paused), so its refusal now says to wait for it to pause first.

refactor(goal): cut what the Goal tools cost every model request by two fifths (#12123)

* refactor(goal): halve what the Goal tools cost every model request

get_goal and update_goal are registered in every session, Goal or not, so
their descriptions and schemas ride along with every request: 5 860
characters for the three tools. Say each thing once and where it applies:
the blocker rules move onto the blockerKind parameter, the objective
format onto the objective parameter, and what the tool result already
tells the model (one proposal per turn, how a terminal result is
reported) leaves the description. 3 421 characters now, and a test holds
the figure.

view and evidenceRefs, deprecated and ignored since the verifier started
reading the transcript tail, leave the advertised schemas. A call that
still sends one is served: the key is dropped before the schema check,
while any other unknown key is refused as before.

* fix(goal): keep the plan-mode hint and the infeasible guardrails, and guard the param filter

Review of #12123: propose_goal is declared in an interactive plan-mode
session and refuses at confirmation time there, so its description keeps
the one static hint. blockerKind gets back "or wanting to ask" and "why
no in-scope work could satisfy the objective", both aimed at a model
reaching for infeasible too early. withoutDeprecatedParams leaves a
non-object for the schema check to describe instead of throwing on the
in operator.

* fix(goal): strip deprecated params before build, and keep the rules where code mode can read them

Review of #12123. The strip of view and evidenceRefs ran in
validateToolParams on a copy, so the schema validator's in-place repairs
(a number sent for a string) landed on the copy and the invocation
executed with the original: a proposal carrying both a deprecated key and
reason: 42 validated and then threw. The strip now happens in build, on
the one object that flows through validation into the invocation.

Code mode carries a tool's description but not its parameter
descriptions, so the blocker rules and the objective format go back into
the descriptions, once, and the parameters point at them. Pinned on the
descriptions and on the code-mode declaration; the request budget moves
to 4 100 for the three tools.

* test(goal): set the Goal tool request budget to 3 800 characters

* fix(goal): say what the verifier does with an immediate blocker, not that the Goal stops

"Those three stop the Goal at once" was wrong: authority, external and
infeasible are sent to the verifier on the first turn they are proposed,
the verifier judges them under the blocked policy and can reject, and a
rejected proposal leaves the Goal running. The sentence contradicted the
one before it, and the contract test pinned the wrong promise.

fix(core): purge a deleted session's prompts from the log history (#11769)

* fix(core): purge a deleted session's prompts from the log history

`/delete` removed a session's transcript but left its rows in the
project-shared `<tmp>/<project-hash>/logs.json`, so the prompts kept
resurfacing in cross-session ↑-history and stayed on disk indefinitely.

Add `Logger.removeSessionMessages(sessionId)`, mirroring
`removeLastUserMessage`: optimistic in-memory removal so the ↑-history
list re-rendered by the "Session deleted" history item is already
correct, then a serialized read/filter/write on the shared write queue
so a concurrent `logMessage` is not clobbered, with rollback when the
disk read or write throws. `useDeleteCommand` calls it for every session
a delete actually removed, single and batch.

The fix drops the deleted session's rows rather than filtering
`getPreviousUserMessages` by session id: cross-session ↑-history is
intentional, so sessions that still exist must keep their prompts.

Fixes #11762

* fix(core): batch the log purge and keep queued removals out of the cache

Review of #11769, R1-1 and R1-3.

A batch delete called the purge once per removed session, and each call was its
own read → filter → write of the whole project-shared `logs.json`, with the next
`logMessage` queued behind all of them. `Logger.removeSessionsMessages(ids)` now
does one optimistic removal, one queued op and one file rewrite for the whole
batch; `removeSessionMessages(id)` delegates to it, so the single-delete path is
unchanged.

The same site had a correctness shape: every op assigned the cache from its own
disk snapshot, and that snapshot still held the rows of any purge queued behind
it — so an earlier op re-adopted rows a later optimistic removal had already
dropped, and a read landing in that window returned a prompt from a session the
user had just been told was deleted. A pending-purge set, added synchronously
and released in a `finally`, is filtered out of both snapshot assignments, so
the documented contract holds for two in-flight purges as well as one.

`AppContainer.tsx`'s `logger,` wiring is the only thing that makes the purge
live, and nothing observed it: the option is optional, every use inside the hook
is `logger?.`, and deleting that line left all three suites green. A test now
records what the component hands the hook. The suite's shared logger mock also
gains `removeSessionsMessages`, without which the first test to drive a
successful delete would report it as a failure.

Also from the review: the batch assertion now pins the call COUNT, since
`.flat()` cannot tell `[['a'],['b']]` from `[['a','b']]`; a core test purges rows
this logger never had in its cache (the multi-instance shape, where the purge is
the only thing that can clean the shared file); and one test drives two
un-awaited purges and reads after only the first resolves.

* style: format the log purge with prettier

* docs(core): attach the batch purge JSDoc to its method

* perf(core): roll back a failed log purge without per-row cache copies

* test(core): pin that a failed purge stops hiding its session

* test(core): pin the pending-purge filter on the no-match purge branch

* fix(core): route every log cache adoption through the pending-purge filter

Only the purge's own two adoptions filtered queued purges, so a logMessage
or removeLastUserMessage queued ahead of a purge still put the purged rows
back into the cache until the purge's write landed. All four of their
adoptions now go through one helper that filters the cache (never the
array written to disk) and keeps the row the adopting op just wrote.

* docs(core): count the session purge among the log write-queue users

* test(cli): assert a failed log purge is reported on the console

* docs(core): say the batch purge only saves rewrites

Per-id purges no longer re-adopt rows another purge dropped: every cache adoption goes through adoptDiskSnapshot, and the per-id test shows it. What batching still saves is the extra full rewrites of the shared log file.

fix(serve): read channel settings from user scope when workspace is home (#11083)

* fix(serve): read channel settings from user scope when workspace is home

loadSettings disables the workspace scope when the workspace directory
resolves to the home directory, so WorkspaceChannelSettingsStore read
an empty scope there: saves returned 200 but subsequent snapshots and
the Web Shell channel list saw nothing. Fall back to the user settings
scope when the workspace scope is inactive; in that layout both point
at the same file, so reads now agree with writes. Adds a regression
test that mocks os.homedir() to the workspace and re-reads via a fresh
store instance.

* fix(serve): write channel settings to the scope they are read from

The home-directory read fallback resolved the owning settings scope for
reads only: upsert, remove and setStartupNames kept writing through
loadSettings(...).workspace, whose path is unconditionally
<workspace>/.qwen/settings.json. When the workspace is $HOME and QWEN_HOME
is redirected the two disagree, so a mutation answered 200 while writing a
file no scope reads, and the snapshot it returned re-read the other one.

Route all three write paths through the same channelSettingsScope() helper
the read path already uses.

Tests:
- pin the write scope with a QWEN_HOME-redirected home workspace
- mock the node:os default export so default-import consumers resolve the
  mocked home instead of the real one
- assert sibling channels survive an upsert in the home layout

* fix(serve): keep stored env references when writing channel settings

`workspaceValues` composed the write set from the env-resolved settings
object, so a save rewrote every untouched sibling channel with its
resolved literal, materializing `$VAR`-indirected secrets in plaintext in
the user-global settings file. Rotating the variable afterwards silently
stopped applying to those channels.

Derive the write set from `SettingsFile.originalSettings` instead, which
`loadSettings` clones before resolution and which `saveSettings` already
uses as its own default write basis. Validation still runs against the
resolved value, and a preserved secret is persisted in its stored form,
so `assertManagedConfig` and the optimistic-concurrency revision keep
behaving as before.

Also pin the home-layout branch for `remove()` and `setStartupNames()`,
which were re-routed onto the resolved scope without coverage, and assert
the `workspaceSettingsActive` precondition so the tests cannot pass while
the fallback branch never executes.

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>
Patrol-Run: qwen-pr-closeout/jmtow5pgslz

* fix(serve): skip reserved channel keys when reading the stored form

A settings file keeps `__proto__` as an own key through JSON.parse, so
`channelRecordMap` assigning onto a plain object literal turned a planted
`channels.__proto__` entry into that map's prototype. The read view is spread,
so `list()` and the revision never showed the plant, but `assertRevision`
returns `storedChannels` unspread and `storedChannels[name]` then resolved it:
an upsert of the planted channel name persisted a secret the caller never
supplied and validation never saw, also escaping the env-reference rejection.
Skip `UNSAFE_OBJECT_KEYS` where the map is built, mirroring the write path
(`assertSafeChannelName`, `assertValidChannelSecretUpdates`).

Also pin three assertions the review found non-discriminating:

- `preserves an existing secret when its operation is omitted` now sets
  BOT_TOKEN, so it fails when the write set is derived from the resolved form.
- `keeps a sibling channel's stored environment reference on save` now asserts
  the write reached the redirected user file and not the workspace file, so it
  fails when `channelSettingsScope` always returns the workspace scope.
- `writes channel configs to the scope it reads them from` uses the
  `useRedirectedUserScope` / `readUserSettings` helpers instead of a second

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>
Patrol-Run: qwen-pr-closeout/jmtp6vibomd

* fix(serve): take the channel type-match gate from the resolved config

The stored-form lookup that keeps a preserved secret as its on-disk `$VAR`
reference was gated on the raw stored `type`, while the value it shadows is
gated on the env-resolved one. A stored `type` that is itself an environment
reference never equals the resolved type the client sends back, so the two
guards disagreed, the restore was skipped, and the save persisted the
resolved secret in plaintext. Decide the match once, from the resolved
config, and keep taking only the values from disk.

Also pin two guards this file added that no test witnessed:

- a remove whose surviving sibling holds a resolvable secret, so the write
  set has to keep coming from the stored form rather than the env-resolved
  snapshot (reverting it to `current.channels` previously stayed green);
- the reserved-key read filter for all three keys it covers, asserted on the

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>
Patrol-Run: qwen-pr-closeout/jmtpfg5ewmp

* fix(serve): keep stored env references when saving a channel

Two gaps in the stored-form restore, both reachable through the channel
editor:

- A secret field that does not declare `envResolvable` had its
  hand-written `$VAR` written back after `assertManagedConfig` had
  already run, so the daemon persisted a value its own validator
  rejects. Once that variable is unset the reference resolves to itself,

- Non-secret `envResolvable` fields of the edited channel were persisted

Both now share one predicate: restore the stored form only for a
descriptor that permits a reference, and only when the client returned
the resolved value unchanged, so a deliberate edit still persists what
was submitted.

The reserved-key read guard's stated justification claimed a planted key

`upsert` asserted workspace ownership only on the client-supplied config,
