fix(core): treat only space/tab/newline as word separators in isAsyncOperator (#11865)

* fix(core): treat only space/tab/newline as word separators in isAsyncOperator

JavaScript's \s also matches \r, \v, \f and  , none of which bash
treats as word separators (its default IFS is space, tab and newline).
When one of those characters sat between a redirection operator and a
bare &, the backward scan in isAsyncOperator skipped past it, concluded
the & belonged to a redirection, and kept both halves of something like
'echo x >\r& rm -rf ~/important' in one segment — letting the first
command's allow rule cover the second (fail-open).

Skip only [' ', '\t', '\n'] (BASH_WORD_SEPARATORS) instead, and pin all
four characters, the spaced variant, and the 2>&1 exclusion with
regression tests.

Fixes #11851

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>

* fix(core): keep bash word characters when trimming shell segments

`String.prototype.trim` also strips `\r`, `\v`, `\f` and `\u00a0`, which bash's
lexer keeps as ordinary word characters, so a redirect target made only of
those characters was deleted before op extraction. With a `Write(//project/**)`
deny and an allow rule matching the first command, `echo x >\u00a0& echo y`
fell from `deny` to `allow`.

Trim only the characters bash skips, at both layers that touch the segment: the
compound splitter's segment trim and `stripShellWrapper`'s edge trim, which
`walkCompoundCommand` applies to the same segment before extracting ops. A CRLF
pair still loses its `\r`; a lone `\r` stays, since bash treats it as a word
character.

* fix(core): preserve carriage-return redirect targets

* fix(core): keep line-terminator paths and CR targets matchable

Four review findings on #11865, all consequences of now keeping the
characters bash treats as ordinary word characters:

- matchesPathPattern handed the raw strings to picomatch, whose `**` body
  is `.`-based and so excludes \r, \n, \u2028 and \u2029. A redirect target
  ending in one (`echo x >out\r& echo y`) missed every `**` deny rule, so
  evaluate returned allow for a write inside a denied tree. Substitute all
  four with a length-preserving placeholder on the pattern and the
  candidate alike: the matcher stays symmetric for the deny, ask and allow
  callers of matchesRule, and `*` still cannot cross `/`.

- The `\n` terminator's CR strip was unconditional, so when the CR *was*
  the whole redirect target (`cat >\r\necho hi`) the write vanished and
  the bare operator became a spurious `read_file '<cwd>/>'` — matchable,
  so a Read(//project/**) deny fired on a file nobody reads. Skip the
  strip for that shape only; CRLF normalization is unchanged.

- stripShellWrapper's `$`-anchored `g` regex was quadratic on an interior
  whitespace run (~1.4 s at 40 k characters; the 64 k test payload took
  12.6 s here), synchronously, on model-controlled input inside the
  permission gate. Replaced with a linear two-pointer trim.

- The NBSP verdict-level test was already a deny at the merge base, so it
  pinned nothing. Added the \u00a0 row to the compound it.each that does
  discriminate (allow at base, deny here).

[Server] Keep the metrics event loop free while the federation routes work (#10812)

* [Server] Keep the metrics event loop free while the federation routes work

/metrics, /gpu-metrics and /endpoints-metrics are served by one uvicorn
worker on one event loop, and the two federation routes open with a
synchronous prologue: reload the server config (a database read on
Postgres-backed deployments), drop the request-level caches, re-read the
kubeconfig. While that runs the loop is blocked, so /metrics is not even
read off the socket -- and the deployment scrapes it with a 20s timeout,
so a prologue slowed by a database outage marks the target down and hides
exactly the incident the metrics are needed for. An earlier change moved
the collectors' own queries off the scrape path; the route sitting next to
them on the same loop still read that database inline.

- Resolve the federation targets in a worker thread instead. Awaiting a
  thread leaves the loop free to answer /metrics. At most one prologue
  runs at a time and both routes share its result, so a prologue hung on
  an unreachable database cannot add a stuck thread per scrape and
  starve the executor the port-forwards run in. The in-flight flag is
  released by the worker rather than by the awaiting coroutine: a scrape
  that Prometheus gives up on cancels the handler, never the thread.

- Report the freshness of that resolution as
  sky_apiserver_federation_targets_last_success_timestamp_seconds. A
  prologue that never returns leaves both routes federating a frozen
  cluster list while the loop, /metrics and the scrape all look healthy,
  so without this the degradation would be invisible.

- Tear port forwards down on a thread as well. The teardown cannot be
  awaited -- it runs in a finally that asyncio.wait_for() may already be
  cancelling, where an await would re-raise CancelledError and leak the
  kubectl child -- but running it inline charged a terminate-and-wait to
  the loop once per context. Also bound the wait after SIGKILL, which
  cannot be caught: anything unreaped past it is stuck in the kernel and
  waiting forever would pin the thread for the life of the process.

- Measure the metrics server loop's own scheduling lag as
  sky_apiserver_metrics_loop_lag_seconds. Deliberately its own metric
  rather than a label on sky_apiserver_event_loop_lag_seconds: that
  series belongs to the request-serving loops, carries no label to tell
  one loop from another, and an alert is keyed on it. Nothing else runs
  on this loop, so a non-zero value here is a route blocking the scrape.
  The lag timer itself now has one implementation, shared by both loops,
  which also collapses the duplicated tick cadence into one constant.

Tested:
- 11 new unit tests. The endpoint test is parametrized with a control arm
  that restores the inline shape and asserts /metrics really does stall
  behind it, so the fixed arm's assertion cannot pass vacuously; both
  arms pass. Full run of the three changed files: 159 passed. Broader
  regression scope (tests/unit_tests/test_sky/server/, the burn-rate and
  time_me metrics tests): 1081 passed.
- Live check against a real metrics server, which the unit tests cannot
  cover because they patch the prologue: /metrics, /gpu-metrics,
  /endpoints-metrics and /debug-gpu-metrics all answer 200, the real
  prologue runs (208-347ms with an empty kubeconfig and no Postgres, the
  work now off the loop), /endpoints-metrics reuses the snapshot, the
  single-flight guard is released afterwards, and the new loop-lag series
  ticks.
- Standalone reproduction of the failure mode on the same app shape: an
  8s block in the async route made a concurrent /metrics take 7.49s
  before, and 0.0013s after.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [Server] Serve the federation target list from the last refresh, not this scrape

Follow-up to the previous commit, from review. Resolving the targets in a
thread the handler awaits keeps the event loop free, but every scrape
still waited out the full resolve -- and both federation routes are
scraped every 60s with a 45s timeout. A resolve landing in that band is
therefore cancelled by Prometheus on every single scrape, each one
starting a fresh attempt that finishes just in time to be discarded, so
the routes federate nothing for as long as it lasts. The cached snapshot
never helps, because two scrapes never overlap for it to be reached. That
is where a reachable-but-wedged config database lands, and it was worse
than not caching at all: the refresh succeeds every time, so the
freshness timestamp stays fresh while the series are simply gone.

So a scrape no longer waits for the resolve either. resolve() returns the
last snapshot immediately and asks for a background refresh, which is the
shape the collectors already use. Staleness is bounded by one refresh
instead, the first refresh is primed when the metrics server starts so
the first scrape is not the one paying for it, and a failed refresh keeps
the previous list rather than publishing an empty one -- every cluster's
series vanishing at once is worse than a slightly stale list, and the
freshness timestamp reports the staleness either way.

Also from review:

- Use multiprocess_mode='max' for the freshness gauge, not 'livemax'.
  livemax needs prometheus_client >= 0.15.0 while dependencies.py allows
  >= 0.8.0, where it is rejected at import -- the server would not start
  at all. 'max' is equivalent for a timestamp that only moves forward,
  since a dead writer's value is older and can never win, and it keeps
  the series present after the writer exits, so an alert on time() minus
  it does not need an absent() clause.

- Cite the reason concurrent readers of the reloaded config are safe:
  _reload_config_as_server() builds the new config fully and swaps it in
  with a single assignment, and says so.

Tested:
- The new case is covered directly: a refresh slower than the scrape
  interval must still leave the routes federating the previous list, and
  a scrape must not wait on it. 160 passed in the three changed files.
- Added the guard the suite was missing: every other test patches the
  prologue, so nothing exercised the real config reload. The new test
  runs it for real on the refresh thread and asserts from the calling
  thread that _get_prometheus_target() sees the config the refresh
  loaded -- the assumption the whole off-thread design rests on. Without
  it, a future change that ran the refresh under a cloned context would
  leave every test green while the prometheus target and the Slurm URLs
  silently reverted to the start-up snapshot.
- Live check: the first /gpu-metrics now answers in 3ms rather than
  347ms, served from the primed snapshot, and the freshness timestamp is
  populated at start-up.
- Fault injection against a real metrics server, both arms: with the
  refresh off the loop the worst /metrics scrape during a 50s refresh is
  0.04s; with it inline, 48.02s. The control arm stalling is what makes
  the fixed arm's measurement mean anything.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [Server] Make the federation target read pure, and never leak its refresh guard

Three review follow-ups, no behaviour change to the healthy path.

The single-flight guard was set in one method and cleared in another with
nothing pairing them, so three paths left it set for the life of the
process: a thread that fails to start, a BaseException out of the refresh,
and a logging call that raises while handling one. Any of them leaves
every later scrape serving a frozen cluster list and starting nothing --
the exact state this class exists to avoid, recoverable only by restart.
The guard is now released in a finally, which covers all three, and a
thread that cannot be started gives it back explicitly.

resolve() both read the snapshot and asked for a refresh, which meant
every caller that only wanted to read had to know it would also start
one. That caught the tests twice, and both call sites had grown a comment
warning the next reader off -- when a method needs that, the name is
doing the wrong job. It is now snapshot(), a pure read, and the two
routes pair it with an explicit start_refresh_if_idle().

The freshness timestamp is now stamped inside the same lock that
publishes the snapshot, so a reader cannot observe a new list with the
old timestamp or the reverse.

Tested:
- 160 passed. The refresh-failure test now asserts the guard is released
  as its first assertion, which is what would catch a regression here.
- The endpoint test's control arm was blocking for its release timeout
  (~30s) rather than the 3s it asserts against, because the release can
  only fire after the /metrics fetch it is blocking returns. The block is
  now sized from the same constant: that arm is 3.05s and the three
  changed test files run in 28s rather than 55s.
- Live check unchanged: the first /gpu-metrics is 2ms, the freshness
  timestamp is populated at start-up, and all four routes answer 200.

feat(cua-driver): observe agent cursor moves/presses and report the system cursor shape (#3883)

* feat(cua-driver): cursor hook to observe agent cursor moves and presses

Add `cua_driver_core::cursor_hook`, a per-process observer fired from the macOS
cursor write path on every commanded move (pressed=false) and on click/drag
press edges (pressed=true), carrying the cursor id and screen point. It mirrors
the existing `pip_hook` idiom: a single registered closure, a no-op until an
embedder registers one, so there is no cost on the daemon or CLI path.

This lets a host that renders cursors as overlays track every agent cursor
without polling or driving the overlay itself.

Restores work that was written on 2026-09-10 and reviewed as part of the
remote-desktop host effort, but was lost: the branch carrying it was deleted
before it merged and the commit became unreachable, so the only copy left was a
downstream checkout. rcdp consumes cua-driver by path from a submodule and
fails to build without this module:

  error[E0433]: cannot find `cursor_hook` in `cua_driver_core`

Rebased onto current main, which had moved 838 commits since. Verified with
`cargo check -p cua-driver-core -p platform-macos` and `cargo fmt --all
--check`, and by building the full downstream workspace against it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(cua-driver): report the system cursor shape

A remote viewer needs two things to draw a pointer: where it is, and what it
looks like. The driver had only the first (`cursor_hook` reports position and
press). Nothing anywhere sampled `NSCursor`/`GetCursorInfo`/`XFixesGetCursorImage`,
so a streamed desktop showed an arrow over a text field, a link and a window
edge alike, which is why the stream felt dead.

Per the cross-platform contract the vocabulary and dispatch go in the common
crate and the adapter stays thin:

- `cua-driver-core::cursor_shape` defines `SystemCursorShape` (a small closed
  vocabulary plus a `Custom` bitmap escape), the probe registration, and the
  behaviour when nobody answers.
- `platform-macos::cursor::shape` implements the probe from AppKit and
  installs it during tool registration, gated on graphic access rather than on
  the agent-overlay flag: a viewer wants the I-beam even when Cua draws no
  cursor of its own.

`Unknown` is deliberately distinct from `Default`. It means "this host cannot
tell you", not "the pointer is an arrow", so a consumer can publish the
limitation instead of rendering a confidently wrong arrow. Windows, X11 and
Wayland install no probe yet and therefore report `Unknown` rather than
pretending; `cursor_shape_supported()` lets a host state that explicitly.

Two traps found by testing rather than by reading, both of which produce code
that looks correct and is not:

1. `+[NSCursor currentSystemCursor]` returns a FRESH object, while the standard
   cursors are cached singletons, so `currentSystemCursor == IBeamCursor` is
   always false. A pointer-equality classifier reports `Default` for every
   shape. Classification is by hot spot plus a hash of the cursor image
   instead, built from AppKit's own accessors so it tracks whatever the running
   OS version draws.
2. `+[NSCursor arrowCursor]` and friends return NULL until an `NSApplication`
   exists, and objc2's generated accessors `expect()` non-NULL -- so the first
   implementation aborted the process in any host without AppKit. Note this is
   NOT the same condition as `currentSystemCursor` returning None: that one
   answers from Window Server state and succeeds earlier, so gating the
   singletons on it still aborts. Every standard accessor is now a raw
   `msg_send!` with its own null check.

`probe_degrades_to_unknown_without_appkit` covers (2) and is meaningful
precisely because the test harness has no AppKit: it observed the abort before
the fix. An unmatched cursor ships its own PNG as `Custom` rather than
degrading to an arrow.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* style(cua-driver): rustfmt the cursor shape classifier table

The Rustfmt gate failed on all three runners. The classifier's
(cursor, shape) table in platform-macos/src/cursor/shape.rs was written
with one entry per line; rustfmt wraps the entries whose expression
exceeds the width limit onto separate lines.

Formatting only -- no behaviour change. `cargo fmt --all --check` is
now clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cua-driver): route cursor press events through the resurrection guard

`CursorRegistry` refuses to touch a cursor whose id is empty or whose
session has ended -- the write-boundary resurrection guard repeated at
every mutator in cursor/state.rs. `update_position` applied that guard
before firing the cursor hook, but the press edge was pushed straight to
`push_cursor_event` from four call sites in tools/click.rs, bypassing it.

The cursor hook is itself a write boundary: it publishes cursor activity
to an embedder that draws pointers on a remote viewer. Escaping the guard
meant a click landing after `session_end` still reached the embedder, so
the viewer re-drew a cursor the driver had already cleared -- a ghost
pointer with no subsequent event to remove it. It also meant the empty
cursor id, which `update_position` treats as "no cursor at all", reached
the hook as a real cursor, giving the same sentinel opposite meanings on
the two paths.

Presses now go through `CursorRegistry::note_press`, and both paths share
one private `emit_cursor_event` choke point so the suppression rule cannot
drift between them again. `note_press` deliberately records no position:
a press is an event, not a new resting place, and the move that precedes
it has already stored the coordinates.

`cursor_hook_registry.rs` covers this. Demonstrated before/after by
reverting `note_press` to the pre-fix unguarded push: the empty-sentinel
assertion fails, and with an empty-id-only guard the session_end assertion
fails. Both pass against this commit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(cua-driver): publish the cursor hook's platform limitation

Only the macOS adapter drives `push_cursor_event`; the Windows and Linux
adapters have no cursor write path wired to the hook. But
`set_cursor_hook_fn` succeeds on every platform, so an embedder that
trusted `cursor_hook_enabled()` would conclude on Windows or Linux that
cursor tracking was live and then wait forever for a first event. The
viewer shows a pointer frozen at the origin, indistinguishable from a
hung stream.

AGENTS.md is explicit: where a platform cannot support the contract it
must publish that limitation rather than substitute misleading behaviour.
`cursor_shape` already does this via `cursor_shape_supported()`; the hook
had no equivalent.

Adds `cursor_hook_supported()` and `declare_cursor_hook_emitter()`,
mirroring that idiom. macOS declares itself during tool registration;
Windows and Linux declare nothing and therefore report unsupported, so a
host can say "cursor tracking unavailable on this platform" at startup
instead of inferring it from silence. The two questions stay separately
observable: `cursor_hook_enabled()` is "does anybody want these events",
`cursor_hook_supported()` is "will any arrive".

Public surface added (additive only, no existing signature changed):
  cua_driver_core::cursor_hook::cursor_hook_supported() -> bool
  cua_driver_core::cursor_hook::declare_cursor_hook_emitter()

Tests, each in its own binary because the hook and the emitter flag are
process-global one-shots that cannot be un-set:
- cursor_hook_inert: the hook is silent and panic-free with nothing
  registered, single- and multi-threaded. This is the path taken by
  almost every cua-driver consumer, and it must stay free.
- cursor_hook_registered: fields survive verbatim; distinct sources keep
  distinct cursor ids, so N participants cannot collapse onto one pointer;
  a second registration is ignored rather than hijacking the stream; 8
  threads x 100 events all arrive exactly once.
- cursor_hook_platform_support: registering an observer must not be
  mistaken for the platform being able to produce events.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(cua-driver): lock cursor-hook emission to a single choke point

The guard added in the previous commit is only worth something if it
cannot be walked around, and the original bug was not a wrong guard --
it was four tool call sites that never reached one. The natural way to
wire the hook into the next tool is to copy an existing
`push_cursor_event(...)` block, which is exactly how the bypass would
come back.

After the fix `push_cursor_event` is called from exactly one place in
this adapter: `CursorRegistry::emit_cursor_event`. Every tool reaches it
through `update_position` or `note_press` and is guarded automatically.

There is no runtime signal for "a tool pushed an event directly" -- such
a call simply works and silently skips the guard -- so this asserts the
invariant over the adapter's sources. Demonstrated by adding a direct
`push_cursor_event` call to tools/scroll.rs: the test fails and names the
offending file. Restored, it passes.

Also drops a stale reference to a test name that never existed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cua-driver): stop the cursor-shape probe aborting on a nil AppKit result

`custom_shape` is the path taken for every application-specific cursor --
the common case for any app that ships its own pointer. Three objc calls
in it bound their result to a non-Option `Retained`, which panics when
AppKit returns nil:

- `-[NSCursor image]` via objc2's generated accessor, which `expect()`s a
  non-NULL result. A cursor built from a Window Server description can
  carry no image.
- `-[NSImage TIFFRepresentation]`, nil for an image with no bitmap
  representation.
- `+[NSBitmapImageRep imageRepWithData:]`, nil for bytes AppKit declines
  to decode.

`custom_shape` already returns `Option` and already uses `png?`, so the
graceful-degradation intent was explicit -- these three lines defeated it.
The same file got it right 94 lines earlier: `tiff_bytes` took
`TIFFRepresentation` as an `Option`. The `standard_cursor!` macro exists
precisely to avoid this hazard but was only applied to the class-method
singletons, not the instance accessors.

This matters because the probe's only caller is the downstream embedder:
a panic here aborts the host process rather than degrading to `Unknown`,
which is exactly the outcome the module's `Unknown`-is-not-`Default`
design is built to avoid.

Every nil-able call is now `Option` + `?`. `cursor_image` and `tiff_data`
centralise the two image reads so both call sites share one nil-safe
path. An unclassifiable cursor now reports `Unknown`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf(cua-driver): check hook registration before building the event

The module documents "no-op until an embedder registers a hook, so there
is zero cost in the common (daemon / CLI) case", and `cursor_hook_enabled`
exists to deliver that -- but nothing called it. `CursorHookEvent` owns its
id, so every commanded move heap-allocated a `String`, built the event, and
handed it to `push_cursor_event`, which dropped it on the floor when no
hook was registered.

That is the path taken by almost every cua-driver consumer. The registration
check now comes first, ahead of both the allocation and the session lookup,
matching the `pip_hook` idiom this module says it mirrors (which does call
`pip_enabled()` to skip the work).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(cua-driver): stop the AppKit cursor test reporting coverage it has not got

`fingerprint_distinguishes_arrow_from_ibeam` opened with
`if !appkit_cursors_available() { return; }`. The Rust test harness has no
`NSApplication`, so in CI it returned before its first assertion and still
printed "ok" -- a green tick standing in for coverage that never ran.

Marked `#[ignore]` with a reason instead, so CI reports it as *ignored*,
and turned the silent early return into an assertion so running it
explicitly on an AppKit host fails loudly rather than vacuously passing.
Run with `cargo test -p platform-macos -- --ignored`.

Mutation-checked the sibling test that does run,
`probe_degrades_to_unknown_without_appkit`. Making `current_shape` return
`Default` where it returns `Unknown` for an unbuildable fingerprint table
turns it red, so it is real. Worth recording that the *other* Unknown
branch -- the `currentSystemCursor()` early return -- is NOT exercised
here: mutating it to `Default` leaves the suite green, because
`currentSystemCursor` answers from Window Server state and succeeds even
with no AppKit. That branch is only reachable with no Window Server
session at all.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(cua-driver): report whether cursor hook registration took effect

`set_cursor_hook_fn` did `let _ = ONCE.set(...)`, discarding the error.
Registration is one-shot and there is no deregistration, so a second
caller silently got nothing: its closure was dropped, the first observer
kept the stream, and the second host rendered no pointers with no way to
discover why. A silent no-op is the worst available outcome for a
registration API.

It now returns `true` when it installed the observer and `false` when one
was already registered, so an embedder can detect the conflict at startup.
Two consumers in one process need a fan-out observer registered once, not
two calls here -- the doc comment says so.

Safe to change now: the API is new in this PR and unreleased, and the one
downstream caller (rcdp-cua-provider) invokes it in statement position,
where discarding a `bool` is source-compatible. Not `#[must_use]`, to
avoid warning that existing call site.

The test asserts both directions and is mutation-checked: making the
function always return `true` turns it red.

Deliberately NOT addressed here: there is still no deregistration, so a
hook capturing a session handle keeps firing after that session is
dropped. That needs a handle-based registration API and is a larger
design change than this PR should carry.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

---------

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

test(release): assert the release-title contract, not which file restates it (#3955)

`test_agent_and_human_guidance_explain_the_release_title_contract` required
both AGENTS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md to contain "fix(cua-driver):",
"feat(lume):", "no-release" and "squash".

#3927 ("docs: deduplicate repository agent guidance") deliberately removed
that restatement from AGENTS.md and replaced it with a link to
CONTRIBUTING.md, which is now the canonical copy and still carries all four
strings. The test then failed on `main` itself -- and because CI tests the
merge result, on EVERY open pull request, regardless of content. Two of the
three red checks on #3883 were this, not that PR.

Restoring the literals to AGENTS.md would undo the deduplication and bring
back the two-copies-that-drift problem #3927 was written to fix. The
contract did not change; its home did. So assert what actually matters: the
contract is documented in the canonical file, and an agent reading AGENTS.md
is pointed at it.

Verified three ways rather than assumed:
  - the original test fails on main (the bug, reproduced);
  - the new test passes on main;
  - the new test still FAILS when CONTRIBUTING.md is mutated to drop
    "fix(cua-driver):", so it is not weakened into a tautology.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

zephyr-cp: stop recompiling every file on every build

An unchanged rebuild recompiled all ~400 CircuitPython objects, and so did each of the 16 extra language builds in CI, at about 90 s each. Two generated files were rewritten on every build with a new modification time, and everything that depends on them followed:

- `zephyr2cp.py` walked the device tree with a `set` of node objects, whose order depends on memory addresses, so the generated `board.c` came out in a different order every run. Walk with a list, write `board.c` only when it changes, and use a `range` instead of a `set` for GPIO pin numbers.
- `collect_defs()` wrote each `.collected` file with several `cat` commands, so the later appends made the file look newer than the first command's record. Concatenate in Python and write only when the content changes.
- Pass `check_hash` for `makeqstrdata.py`, `makemoduledefs.py` and `make_root_pointers.py`, so an unchanged header keeps its modification time.

An unchanged rebuild now compiles nothing, and a language switch compiles `translate.c` and the two per-language files. A clean build round-tripped through de_DE and back to en_US is byte-identical.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

zephyr-cp: compile in parallel when make's jobserver is not a fifo

`cpbuild._create_semaphore()` only recognized the `fifo:` jobserver of GNU make 4.4+ and otherwise compiled one file at a time. The ubuntu-24.04 CI runners have make 4.3, which passes the jobserver as file descriptors that are closed for the `west build` recipe, so every CI zephyr-cp build compiled its ~400 CircuitPython objects serially, for each of the 17 languages.

Fall back to one compile per available CPU instead of one. A 395-file rebuild with no jobserver went from 44 s to 8 s on a 20-core machine.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
Refuse to build a fork's branch

An issue_comment workflow runs in the base repo's context, so this job holds
the subscription token and a write-capable App token — and it now installs,
builds and runs the checked-out branch. On a fork's PR that hands both to
code we don't control, through lifecycle scripts before a test ever runs.

A maintainer commenting @claude is the trigger, but the branch is what
executes, so the actor check is not the control that matters here. The job
now refuses outright when the PR is cross-repository.

Also drops Bash(node:*): running the suite already implies running repo code,
so the extra grant bought nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Give the agent a workspace it can actually build in

The implement run on #1707 wrote the change and then reported it could not
run a single test: no --allowedTools, so Bash refused yarn, and a bare
checkout has no node_modules. Test-first is the rule the skill is built on,
and the environment made it impossible to follow.

So the job now installs, builds, and starts a virtual display before handing
over — mirroring ci.yml, cache key included — and allows the tools the work
needs. The display means `yarn test` is the same command here as it is on a
contributor's machine, so the skills don't need to special-case CI.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Consolidate before review, and review the docs

Implement gains a pass over its own diff before anyone else reads it: drop
scaffolding, match surrounding naming, confirm each criterion has a test and
each user-visible change has its docs and changeset. It is explicitly a
tidiness pass — the author of a change is the worst placed to find its logic
errors, which is why the reviewer is a different model that never sees the
plan.

The reviewer now also treats a feature shipped without user documentation, or
with documentation that explains the implementation instead of the use, as a
finding.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Review the PR when it leaves draft

Drafts carry specs and plans; leaving draft is the statement that the
implementation is done, so that is the trigger. The implement skill marks the
PR ready as its last step, and events from the Claude app do start workflows —
only the default GITHUB_TOKEN is special-cased — so the chain closes without
anyone watching it.

The reviewer runs on Fable and is denied specs/**/plan.md: a reviewer who
knows the intended approach checks whether the code matches the plan, when the
job is to check whether the code is right. It comments and nothing more —
merging stays a human decision.

Only PRs from this flow are reviewed automatically. Someone else's PR gets a
review by asking for one in a comment.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Drive stages from PR comments instead of labels

A label is the right trigger while there is nothing to comment on: it opens
the PR from an issue. Once that PR exists it is already the queue entry and
the state, so a second label per stage adds a workflow and a taxonomy to say
what the branch says anyway — and a comment can carry qualifiers a label
cannot ("implement, but leave the CLI wiring for a follow-up").

So `agent:spec` stays, the later stages become `@claude plan` and `@claude
implement`, and the write-spec PR body now prints those two phrasings
verbatim so invocations stay comparable. The skills they reach for exist here
rather than being improvised per run.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add the @claude workflow for steering

Labels move work between stages; an @claude mention is how you talk to the
agent within one. Without this workflow the mentions go nowhere, which is
what happened on #1707.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Pin the spec workflow to Opus

Left unset, the action picks its own default (Sonnet on the first run) and
that default can move without us noticing. Spec writing is judgment-dense and
infrequent, so it is worth the stronger model.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Added wikilink embed tests

Added more always excluded patterns

Foam now always excludes `.git`, `.hg`, `.svn`, `.DS_Store` and `Thumbs.db` from
the workspace, regardless of configuration. `foam.files.exclude` is an array
setting, so a user value replaces the default rather than extending it — adding
a single pattern of your own previously dropped every built-in exclude with it.
These paths are never knowledge base content, so they are no longer left to
configuration.

Document the spec flow for agents and contributors

AGENTS.md gains a Specs section and points at the write-spec skill, which is
a document any agent can read rather than a Claude Code feature. CLAUDE.md
adds only the invocation and the workflow that runs it unattended, and
CONTRIBUTING.md points humans at specs/README.md.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add the spec stage: label an issue, get a spec PR

Feature work now starts from a committed spec rather than notes that only
exist on one machine. `specs/<slug>/spec.md` says what and why and is
reviewer-visible; `plan.md` says how and is deliberately kept from the
reviewer. One branch and one PR carry a feature from spec to merge, with
`agent:<stage>` labels starting each stage.

Only the spec stage is automated: labelling an issue `agent:spec` runs the
write-spec skill in Actions, which opens a draft PR with the spec. The later
stages are documented but driven by hand until a handoff earns its workflow.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
updated agent instructions

fix(#171): answer a sealed group's members from the row the seal wrote

A preparation wave takes its membership snapshot once, from
`lookup::locations`, before any of the wave's own writes. A group is framed and
placed as a whole, so a seal publishes rows for every member it holds --
including members that arrived in earlier waves and are still waiting. Every
other member of that group, later in the same wave, then misses the stale
snapshot and is no longer a pending member either, so it fell through to
`owner.offer` and was inserted a second time. `objects.object_id` is the primary
key, so SQLite refused the row:

    UNIQUE constraint failed: objects.object_id

This is the documented behaviour failing, not a new capability. `cas/save.rs`
already states the invariant it was breaking: "an identity whose group is still
open has no row yet, so it is sealed on demand and resolved through the ordinary
verified path instead of being inserted a second time. Inserting a second row is
a hard constraint failure, and a store that fails on repeated content fails on
exactly the workload it exists for."

The fix records the identities each seal writes, in `MutationOwner::sealed_rows`,
and `flush_batch` consults that set beside the wave snapshot and the pending
members. `seal_group` is the only place object rows are written, so recording
there covers every seal path -- the on-demand seal from the `pending_member`
branch and the group-target seal inside `offer` -- not just the one that was
diagnosed. The set is cleared at the start of each wave and is bounded by the
members one wave can seal, never by the size of the operation; a row written in
an earlier wave is already answered by that wave's own lookup.

A previous attempt recorded the decided identities in the wave-local `prepared`
map and did nothing: that map is keyed to indices into the current wave's object
vector, and the members a seal writes are not all in the current wave.

Measured on the eight admission rows that carried the constraint failure
(`dedup-cross-file-identical-{10,100,500}`, `dedup-cdc-insert-{10,100,500}`,
`dedup-cdc-delete-{10,100}`): seven now `PASS`; `dedup-cdc-insert-500` moves off
the constraint failure and is now refused only by the complete-command budget
(29.926 s), the WP-D cause the handoff already records for its siblings.

Regression test `a_group_sealed_mid_wave_answers_its_other_members_from_that_wave`
reproduces the exact `UNIQUE constraint failed: objects.object_id` against the
previous source and passes with the fix.

fix(#171): invalidate the delta reader's pack cache when a pack is appended to

First product fix of Stage 6, under the owner's ruling that product bug fixes are
permitted while new features are not. This is a bug fix: the product's own
contract already requires what was failing.

**The defect.** `MutationOwner::pack_cache` maps `pack_id -> whole pack bytes` and

ordinal")` to **PASS**. The three `dedup-cross-file-identical-{10,100,500}` rows

The previous commit's comment claimed that "the same inputs replay successfully
into a retaining `TreeStore`". That was not true as written, and the row returned
early on the measured failure so the claim was never executed. This corrects the
claim by measuring it.

`replay_update` was passing the caller's *base* store as the overlay's first
side, so the reader never saw the objects the operation emitted during its own
run. It failed with `MissingObject` for exactly the same reason the measured
phase did — which made the two failures look like one cause when they were two
different wiring mistakes.

test helper uses: the in-flight objects first, then the base. With it:

reads back objects it emits inside its own operation, and a purely discarding
measured phase cannot serve it. A build does not — a 200-binding build completes
against an empty provider and a discarding consumer — which is why only the
update-shaped rows are affected.

overlay in `measure_update`); it is not made here because it would put a

  small-file, read waves and footprint. The other eight report `NOT_RUN` with

  a resident file before it claims to de-warm one), space (no `COALESCE`; a
  missing `object_packs` is INCOMPLETE, never a zero), trace (flatness, sequence
  and worst-gate aggregation, re-derived), receipt (append-only, 15/25/60 s
  budgets, the measurement lock), copyladder (R0-R3; R1 refused where `st_blocks`
  gates; the 1.05x ENOSPC preflight), analyze (the band table re-implemented so a
  published figure is re-derived where it is read), experiments (E1-E4).
- `runner.py` — list | prepare | perf | verify | report | self-check | calibrate.

The one measurement rule every driver obeys: a timed phase runs with a
non-retaining consumer, so no harness allocation inside the heap window can be
charged to the product, and every oracle is a **second, unmeasured, byte-identical
operation**. The two roots must agree, which is itself a gate — a replay that did
not reproduce the measured operation is caught rather than verified.

E1-E4 ran for the first time, and one of them refuted its own premise.
E2 (SATISFIED): after the master is read fully, a fresh clone is 0-resident, and
`msync(MS_INVALIDATE)` on the clone de-warms it to 0 while the master keeps all
4096 pages. E3 (SATISFIED): cloning a quiescent Store preserves page count and
`quick_check`, and the master digest is unchanged after mutating the clone.
E4 (SATISFIED): mode, mtime, symlink target, xattr and file link count all match
across a directory clone. **E1 (REFUTED)**, and the refutation is the useful part:
the clone's `st_blocks * 512` equals its apparent size on this volume (67,108,864
for a 64 MiB clone), so the figure is a full-size number rather than a
sharing-aware one. The contract's stated reason for forbidding R1 on `c2.footprint`
("a COW clone's st_blocks double-counts blocks shared with the master") is not what
this host measures; the measured fact is that `st_blocks` cannot distinguish
sharing at all. The rule survives, on better evidence than the assumption it
rested on. E1's isolation and inode checks both passed (distinct inode, master
digest unchanged after writing the clone).

Two over-broad checks were corrected during E1-E4 and are recorded rather than
quietly fixed: `st_nlink == 1` is asserted for **files** only, because a
directory's link count is structural and asserting 1 for it would refute every
faithful clone; and extended attributes are compared through libc `setxattr`,
because this build's `os` module has neither, and an experiment that silently
skipped the attribute comparison would be reporting a fidelity it never checked.

docs(#171): the single-worker rule, and the init_namespace exception that does not reach Stage 6

AGENTS.md section 3.8 and benchmark/AGENTS.md carve out init_namespace as the one
case allowed multiple workers. c1.fs.build-scale derives from init_namespace's C1

no std::thread, no thread::spawn, no rayon, no available_parallelism. The only
Arc/Mutex use is Store's pool_index, which spawns nothing. Telemetry's TimingScope

place. Single-threaded product execution is structural here, not enforced by
convention.

10 ms RSS sampler is its own thread. The handoff now states the distinction -- one
worker on the product's work, not one thread in the process.

perf(core): P2-2 — one INSERT per bound chunk of a group's rows

#178 Phase 2 item (#177 F8). `seal_group` inserted one object row per statement -
8,191 statements for an 8,191-row save - where the engine takes a bounded set of
rows per statement.

- `write::insert_objects` inserts a group's rows with one multi-row `INSERT` per
  chunk, and reports the statements it issued; the owner charges that report, so
  `statements` cannot drift from the engine's work.
- `insert_chunk_rows` derives the chunk from the connection's **own** limits:
  `k = min(SQLITE_LIMIT_VARIABLE_NUMBER / 7 columns, SQLITE_LIMIT_SQL_LENGTH /
  16 bytes of placeholder text, 128)`, read back through rusqlite's `limit`, never
  copied as a constant. The 128 cap bounds the prepared-statement cache (one entry
  per distinct chunk size) rather than the engine.
- SQLite applies each multi-row `INSERT` atomically, so a chunk's rows all land or
  none do, and a failure is the same engine/integrity error the single-row form
  produced - the attribution the per-row loop had was the statement, and that is
  what is preserved. `insert_object` is deleted with its loop.

Gate measured on the frozen set:

  c2.ceiling   statements 8,191 -> 72    inserted 8,191 unchanged    commits 31 unchanged
  c2.small     statements 1,023 -> 9     inserted 1,023 unchanged

72 rather than the ideal `ceil(8191 / 128) = 64` because rows are inserted one
**sealed group** at a time, so the total is `sum_g ceil(rows_g / k)`; collapsing
that would defer a group's rows past the group that sealed them, which is a
transaction-accounting change and not this item. `sqlite_master` is untouched: the
pinned schema identity is verified at every open and the arms' stores are
byte-identical.

`tests/statement_batching.rs` (V5's file, which the plan assigns to both items)
moves to the post-batching reading - every row present in the engine, `statements`
strictly below `inserted` and at least `ceil(inserted / 128)`, the controls kept -
and gains a case pinning the derivation itself: the chunk is read from the
connection's limits, at least one row and never above the cap. Both moved cases
fail on the parent tree.

perf(core): P2-5 — one presence query per wave, one pooled reader per save

#178 Phase 2 item (#176 Tier 0-10), measured against V8's counter.

**Batched presence.** `Availability::validate` issued one paged presence lookup per
offered object whose references were not already known. The wave knows every
reference its offered objects carry before it offers any of them, so `flush_batch`
now seeds availability with one lookup for the whole wave (`Availability::seed`,
counted through the same counter). Availability semantics are unchanged: the seed
records what the engine answered and nothing else, and `validate` still refuses an
object whose reference the query did not find.

On the nominated rows (`phase0client c2-references <rows>`: a first save of `rows`
leaves, then a second save of `rows` different leaves each naming one of them),
`dependents presence_queries` reads:

  rows 64   -> 1     rows 512  -> 1
  rows 1024 -> 2     rows 4096 -> 8     (before: 64, 512, 1024, 4096)

which is one query per preparation wave: the wave bound is 512 objects. On the
frozen set the counter is unchanged (the pipeline rows read 1 before and after,
because each carries one such object), and the receipt says so rather than implying
a movement the frozen set cannot show.

**One pooled reader per save.** `pool_base` built a fresh `PoolReader` per trial, so
each trial re-materialised the base packs and re-paid the decode work. It now uses
the owner's own reader, which `select_pooled` already uses. That sharing has one
hazard and it is handled here rather than assumed away: a pack body is **not**
immutable while a save runs - placing a group rewrites the pack's blob, because the
directory grows and every body moves with it - so `write_pack` now releases the
reader's pack cache (`PoolReader::release_packs`). Its decoded-value cache survives:
an ordinal's value is written once and never moves.

The new case `a_pooled_reader_releases_pack_bodies_when_the_store_writes` pins that:
three groups in one pack, the first read retains the pack, the next two groups'
extents are replaced, a reader without a cache refuses the damage from the start,
the warmed reader still answers from the retained body - and after
`release_packs` the same read is refused.

perf(core): P2-4 — one decompression per distinct group

#178 Phase 2 item (#176 Tier 0-9). The ordinary resolver decompressed a group's
whole body once per record served out of it, so `k` records sharing one group cost
`k` full decompressions; `packs_read` charges one per pack per wave and `objects`
one per returned object, so neither counter could see it. V6 measured it (2 decodes
for 1 group on the pipeline readbacks); this is the cache that removes it.

  `(pack, group)`, ported from `PoolReader`'s discipline: owner the read
  operation, bound `DECODED_GROUP_CACHE_BYTES` (512 KiB, a new declared policy
  constant with the pooled cache's ownership/lifetime/release documentation),
  released wholesale when the next body would cross the bound, dropped with its
  owner. A hit charges no `group_decodes`.
- The cache is carried by the pooled `ReadSession`, not by a wave or a resolver:
  a wave-scoped cache removes nothing (the frozen readbacks reach one group from
  two waves), and the operation is the scope whose group reuse is real.
- `Resolver` takes the wave's cache and consults it in `decode_canonical`'s
  ordinary arm, where the decompression happens.

**Visibility before cache, pinned in `tests/visibility.rs`:** the ceiling is
re-read per wave while the cache outlives a wave, so `Resolver::decode_at` checks

decodes a group under an unbounded ceiling, then resolves the same location with
the same cache under a ceiling below its pack, and requires a `VisibilityCeiling`
refusal rather than a cached body.

perf(core): P2-7 — consolidation adopts its newest run instead of copying it

#178 Phase 2 item (#176 Tier 0-12). `consolidate()` copied the newest live run into
a fresh handle before merging the older tiers under it, and the copy's own comment
gave the reason: "Copies one run into a fresh handle so a merge never aliases its
own input." Two research reports flagged that reason UNKNOWN, so the copy is
dropped here only after the property is *proved*:

- `merge_runs` appends exclusively to a run it created, so the handle that
  survives consolidation is never written into;
- `consolidate()` therefore adopts the newest source instead of rewriting it;
- `copy_run` and its call are deleted.

The proof is a test, not an argument. `tests/filesystem_ordering_consolidate.rs`
(new binary) spills twelve batches, seals every run that exists before the
consolidation - an append into a sealed run is an error - and then requires the
consolidation to succeed and the row stream to be unchanged. A control in the same
case takes a handle before the seal and shows an append after it fails, so the
detector is live. A scratch-tree control confirms the case does what it claims:
with one `append` aimed at a pre-existing run inside `consolidate`, the case
fails.

It now lives in its own test binary rather than in `filesystem_ordering_scan.rs`
as the plan sketched: that binary carries an allocation-budget probe over a
*global* allocator, and a second case allocating in parallel disturbed it (15

perf(core): P2-6 — one hash per resolved record

#178 Phase 2 item (#176 Tier 0-11, the safe half). The requested object of every
read wave was hashed twice: `encoding/delta/read.rs` computed
`ObjectId::for_bytes` over each decoded record to authenticate it against its
locator, and `cas/read.rs` then hashed the returned bytes again to check the same
identity. The resolver's hash is the one that authenticates; the second pass added
nothing.

- `Resolver::resolve`, `resolve_dependency` and `resolve_at` return
  `(Vec<u8>, ObjectId)`: the canonical bytes and the identity the resolution
  computed and checked;
- `cas/read.rs` compares that identity with the requested one instead of hashing
  the bytes again (same error class, one fewer pass over the object);
- the chain path keeps exactly one hash per record, now named `verified`;
- `cas/owner.rs::resolve_location` and the selector take the bytes: membership
  keeps its own re-hash by policy (that invariant is parked, T2-21, not this
  item's to change).

Two external cases in `tests/cas_reuse.rs`:

- `the_read_wave_does_not_hash_what_the_resolver_authenticated` is the
  fail-closed guard for the property itself - a hash is not charged by any
  counter, so the case reads the wave's own source and rejects a second
  `ObjectId::for_bytes` there. **It fails on the parent tree** (the call is
  present) and passes here;
- `a_locator_whose_identity_does_not_match_its_bytes_is_refused` rewrites a
  locator row to claim an identity whose bytes differ and requires the read to be
  refused - the tamper detection this change must not weaken, with its own control
  (the same object read successfully before the rewrite). That case passes on both
  trees by design: it pins unchanged behaviour.

body of the open pack for every candidate group (`assembled_length` over the
tail), so placing `g` groups into one pack cost O(g²) body measurements, g bounded

docs(#171): c2 family spec - clone allocation hazard, footprint SQL, store custody

Closes the gap left by f5fb7567d, which applied the five design reviews to the c1,
resource, cache and gates specs but not to c2.

- The reflink copy rung is forbidden for c2.footprint and every row gating allocated
  bytes: a COW clone's st_blocks double-counts blocks shared with the master, so
  store_allocated_bytes stops being occupancy. Rows on the byte-copy rung carry
  allocation_attribution: exclusive.
- The footprint SQL can silently become a fabricated zero after a table rename, and
  0 <= database passes the O6 gate. space.py must assert the table exists and must
  not use COALESCE.
- Store custody: journal_mode = MEMORY is per-connection and not persisted in the
  file header, so a copy carries no sidecar risk - but the sidecar refusal cannot
  detect a Store that is currently open, and with synchronous = OFF a mid-transaction
  copy captures a torn page. Quiescence is enforced structurally: staging, close,
  fsync, atomic rename, chmod, and never releasing the master path to a sample.
- prepare has no producer: nothing in the design builds objects/ or store.sqlite, and
  construction is a product operation. The child needs --emit-objects and a
  fresh-store mode, or the prepare verb is unimplementable.

#178 Phase 2 instrument, authorised by ruling 2. `P2-2`'s claim ("8,191 single-row
statements become 64") is unobservable today: `OutcomeCounters` and `SaveOutcome`

  statements issued for object rows. Statements, not rows: a multi-row INSERT of
  `k` rows is one statement, while `inserted` counts rows.

  reports the statements it executed (`Ok(1)` today), and the owner adds that
  report. A batched insert reports its chunk count the same way, so the counter
  cannot drift from the engine's work.

  transaction statements are already visible as `packs_created`/`pack_appends`,
  `pool.groups`, `transactions` and `commits`.

#178 P1-12. `Engine::push` re-summed every key's encoded width after every append

   split drain subtracts each drained row's width as it moves to the right page
   (whose own total `append_entry` accrues). `nearest_half`'s one-off widths vec
   stays: it runs once per split, not once per append.

   width, and the two must not be conflated. A re-grep for other direct
   `page.entries` mutations found only the `push` drain and `append_entry`'s own
   push.

feat(core): P1-4 — batch validation's record demands behind one memo

#178 P1-4. Validation demanded base inode records one at a time — `lookup_many`
over a single serial — so an update binding k stored children paid k root
descents, and the three walks (the decision loop, the alias walk and the
effective-cycle walk) re-demanded the same serials. On D2 that was 21 demands,
42 read waves and 42 inode pages for a three-name rename.

1. `ValidationState` memoizes the base records validation reads. The memo answers
   a repeated demand **without a read while still charging the demand**, so
   `inode_demands` (the work-limit charge) is bit-identical and only the I/O
   moves. Absence is deliberately not memoized: a serial with no stored record
   keeps today's lookup and today's charge.
2. `check` prefetches every serial its decision loop will demand — the parents it
   must classify and every child it binds, both known from the input — in **one**
   grouped demand before the loop runs. The loop then reads the memo, so the
   verdicts and their order are unchanged and one descent replaces one per
   binding. The batch pays the pages and waves it reads; the demand charge is
   paid where the demand is made, which is what keeps `inode_demands` equal to
   the number of logical demands rather than to the batch size.
3. The memo is threaded through `check_parent_aliases` and
   `check_effective_cycles`, which demand the same serials again.

Measured on the frozen set (`filesystem_timing_c1`, the V1 print):
  D2 c1.directory-update  validation: waves 42 -> **2**, inode_pages 42 -> **2**,
                          inode_demands **21 (identical)**, objects **21 (identical)**,
                          entries_examined 0 (identical)
  D4 c1.hardlink-move     validation: waves 6 -> **1**, inode_pages 6 -> **1**,
                          inode_demands **6 (identical)**
  D1/D3/D5/D6             every field identical (they demand no base record)
  D25/D26/D7/D8/D9 and the edits/c2 rows: identical (no frozen row outside D2/D4
  demands a stored inode record)
Roots and emitted bytes are identical everywhere.

Tests: `binding_lookups_are_batched_per_phase` — renaming every file of a
500-entry and a 1,500-entry directory demands 1,001 and 3,001 records with the
**same** wave count (≤ 4) and pages an order of magnitude below the demand count;
it fails on the parent tree, where the wave count follows the demands.
`a_wide_branch_page_reads_its_children_in_one_wave` (P1-1's) had pinned

feat(core): P1-2 — pool the read connection and decode arena per operation

#178 P1-2. A read wave paid two fixed costs before it read anything: a connection
with the declared pragma profile, and a decode arena. Both were per **wave**;
both belong to the operation. Measured before this commit (V3's baseline,
`edits.pipeline.*`, `readback connection opens`): **3 opens for one readback**,
one per wave.

1. `cas/read.rs` gains `ReadSession`: the connection and the
   `DecompressionWorkspace`, opened once, reused by every wave of one operation.
   The visibility ceiling is deliberately **not** pooled — `ReadSession::read`
   re-reads `schema::retained_pack_ceiling` per wave, because it is the
   publication watermark and a save that completed between two waves must be
   visible to the second one. Pooling it would turn an operation's later waves
   into a snapshot of its first.
2. `cas/provider.rs`: `StoreProvider` holds `RefCell<Option<ReadSession>>` plus
   the `opens` cell. Its first wave opens the session; later waves reuse it and
   report `opens: 0`. The session lives in the provider and **not** in `Store`,
   which stays shared and `Sync`; the provider is `!Sync`, which is its honest
   shape — one operation's adapter.
3. The wave's declared demand bound survives the pooling. `read_objects` never
   enforced `READ_OBJECT_LIMIT` itself: the check lived at `Store::read_batch`'s
   entry point, and the pooled path bypassed it. `check_read_demand` moves into
   `cas/read.rs`, runs inside `ReadSession::read` as well, and the provider calls
   it **before** the session exists — so a demand over the ceiling is refused
   without opening anything, exactly as before. Found while writing the item's
   error-path test; it is the same variable (the session must not lose a bound the
   wave had), not a drive-by fix.

  edits.c2.small/chunked  opens 1
This is P1-2's gate: the same operation must report 1 after pooling, while the
wave count itself does not move.

New test `cas_roundtrip::a_read_wave_reports_the_connection_it_opened` pins the
per-wave counter (one call, one connection; a grouped demand of 8 ids is still
one call and one connection) and the provider's sum as a **bound** — `0` before
any wave, `1..=2` after two — deliberately not an equality, because P1-2 is
authorized to lower it and an equality would have to be re-pinned by that item.
The counter did not exist on the parent tree, so the pre-item failure is that the
observable is absent.

Architecture doc `core/docs/architecture/10-counters.md` updated in the same
commit: the inventory row gains `opens`, §15.6 gains the misreading it invites
(per wave, not per operation), and the document's pin line names V3.

commits.message:
Merge pull request #1967 from doronz88/bugfix/rsd-handshake-stable-uuid

remotexpc: Share one host-wide UUID across RSD handshakes (iOS 27.2)

remotexpc: Share one host-wide UUID across RSD handshakes (iOS 27.2)

Since iOS 27.2 the device remembers the handshake UUID of the last RSD peer
on a tunnel -- even after that peer disconnected -- and re-attaches when the
next peer presents a different one ("Peer UUID changed across reconnect;
reattaching so clients re-discover it"), closing every service listener it
advertised, to the newcomer and to earlier peers alike. Every RSD connection
sent a fresh random UUID, so anything joining an existing tunnel failed right
after the handshake:

    $ pymobiledevice3 remote rsd-info --rsd fd88:51e2:a06c::1 60658
    ConnectionRefusedError: [Errno 61] Connect call failed (...)

cdba41b3 covered only the native tunnel's own RSD connection; `--rsd`,
tunneld clients and get_rsds still sent random UUIDs.

Default the handshake UUID to one host-wide identity instead: the host
remoted's UUID on macOS (remoted shares RSD endpoints with us and keeps
reconnecting with its own UUID, so no other identity survives there), and
the deterministic pairing host id elsewhere. The remotectl helpers move from
native_tunnel to remotexpc, which native_tunnel already depends on.

Fixes #1966

Restored to formatter output (matches `main`). `black 26.5.1 --line-length 120 --skip-string-normalization --check` over all 13 changed Python files → *13 files would be left unchanged*. - Migration-lock correctness fix: the first eviction implementation popped the lock entry whenever `asyncio.Lock.locked()` was false. `Lock.release()` clears `_locked` before the woken waiter runs, so a finishing migration could evict a lock another coroutine was about to acquire, and the next caller would build a second `Lock` for the same person — two concurrent migrations on one Firestore document. fix(omi-linear-app): resolve team targets, sanitize identifiers, survive null fields (#14501)

Chat-tool inputs arrived loosely typed and human shaped, and GraphQL
responses were trusted to be non-null. Four failure modes shipped
together (issue #14344):

- tool_create_issue silently created issues in teams[0] when the user
  belonged to several teams, and a team key (ENG) or name failed the
  GraphQL mutation because only UUIDs worked
- dirty issue identifiers ('#ENG-123', 'issue: #ENG-123', pasted web
  URLs, untyped values) failed or crashed the exact issue lookup
- null optional fields (team/state/project/labels, nodes: null) crashed
  tool_get_issue / tool_update_issue_status with AttributeError,
  KeyError, or TypeError
- whitespace-only or untyped status values leaked into
  find_state_by_name partial matching

Changes:
- resolve_team(): tiered resolution (UUID -> key/name exact ->
  substring); ambiguous or unknown targets return candidate lists and
  refuse silent mutation; create_issue honors the default team, then a
  single-team workspace, then prompts - never teams[0]
- sanitize_issue_identifier(): one shared helper returning the canonical
  uppercase identifier or None; wired into get/update-status/comment
- null-safe extraction across get/update-status/add-comment/create and
  the teams/states node lists
- find_state_by_name rejects non-string and whitespace-only targets
- create_issue maps numeric priority strings ('1' -> 1, out-of-range ->
  omitted), supports an optional initial workflow state, and the
  omi-tools manifest + models now declare team and status

Verification:

  (hermetic: fastapi/db/models/requests stubbed; drives the real
  handlers through dirty inputs and null-laden responses)
- same suite against unpatched main.py -> FAILED (failures=14,
  errors=26)
- full plugin suite (test_team_disambiguation + test_issue_lookup +
  test_graphql_errors + test_list_issues_params) -> 48 tests OK
- declared FC-chat-tool-input-assumed-typed-and-complete with this
  change as first evidence (evidence_prs: [])

fix(google-calendar-app): escape reflected error and encode uid in setup pages (#14581) Two unauthenticated routes render client-controlled input into HTML with no encoding. GET /auth/google/callback takes `error` straight off the query string and interpolates it into the page body:

{error}

so /auth/google/callback?error= executes on the plugin's origin. No code, state or prior session is needed — the `if error:` branch is the first thing the handler does. GET / reflects `uid` into two href attributes and a hidden input value; a uid of "> breaks out of the attribute, and a bare & or # corrupts the query instead. Follows the encoding pattern of #13658 (six sibling apps) and #14579 (omi-dropbox-app): quote(uid, safe="") for URL contexts, html.escape() for text and attribute contexts. * harden(app): retire the five satisfied C1 lifetime pending markers

#14327 landed c1_lifetime_review_test.dart and c1_lifetime_terminal_test.dart
on main with pendingContract('C1') still set. The behaviour they pin was
already implemented on this branch by f04ec71709 and acdc197180, so after the
merge-forward all five executed green and the contract harness failed them as
XPASS ("remove the pending marker") rather than as unmet contracts. No
implementation change is required, and none is made here; only the five stale
markers are removed, which is the one edit the spine protection allows.

What each contract pins, and the capture_lifetime.dart behaviour that
satisfies it:

- concurrent close joins outstanding cancellation: a second close() used to
  hand back a fresh completed future and report teardown finished while the
  first drain was still awaiting an own() cancel. close() now short-circuits
  only on _closeFinished and otherwise returns the memoised _closing future,
  so every caller joins the same drain.
- asFuture preserves completion untracking: _inner.asFuture replaces the
  subscription's done handler, so the listen-time drop() never ran and the
  registration outlived its future. _LifetimeSubscription.asFuture now chains
  whenComplete(_drop).
- C1 asFuture error completion releases its registration: the same path on the
  error completion - whenComplete(_drop) untracks on throw as well as on done.
- replaced callbacks and errors stay closed while cancellation drains: a
  handler installed through onData/onError after listen bypassed the closed
  guard and could still fire while close() was blocked on an earlier release.
  Those wrappers now consult _isClosed() before forwarding.
- C1 original and replacement done callbacks respect closing: both the
  listen-time onDone wrapper and an onDone replacement now drop() the
  registration but return without calling the owner once _closed is set.

* harden(app): retire the five satisfied C1 lifetime pending markers

#14327 landed c1_lifetime_review_test.dart and c1_lifetime_terminal_test.dart
on main with pendingContract('C1') still set. The behaviour they pin was
already implemented on this branch by f04ec71709 and acdc197180, so after the

implementation change is required, and none is made here; only the five stale

What each contract pins, and the capture_lifetime.dart behaviour that
satisfies it:

- concurrent close joins outstanding cancellation: a second close() used to
  hand back a fresh completed future and report teardown finished while the
  first drain was still awaiting an own() cancel. close() now short-circuits
  only on _closeFinished and otherwise returns the memoised _closing future,
  so every caller joins the same drain.
- asFuture preserves completion untracking: _inner.asFuture replaces the
  subscription's done handler, so the listen-time drop() never ran and the
  registration outlived its future. _LifetimeSubscription.asFuture now chains
  whenComplete(_drop).
- C1 asFuture error completion releases its registration: the same path on the
  error completion - whenComplete(_drop) untracks on throw as well as on done.
- replaced callbacks and errors stay closed while cancellation drains: a
  handler installed through onData/onError after listen bypassed the closed
  guard and could still fire while close() was blocked on an earlier release.
  Those wrappers now consult _isClosed() before forwarding.
- C1 original and replacement done callbacks respect closing: both the
  listen-time onDone wrapper and an onDone replacement now drop() the
  registration but return without calling the owner once _closed is set.

on main with pendingContract('C1') still set. The behaviour they pin was

What each contract pins, and the capture_lifetime.dart behaviour that
satisfies it:

- concurrent close joins outstanding cancellation: a second close() used to
  hand back a fresh completed future and report teardown finished while the
  first drain was still awaiting an own() cancel. close() now short-circuits
  only on _closeFinished and otherwise returns the memoised _closing future,
  so every caller joins the same drain.
- asFuture preserves completion untracking: _inner.asFuture replaces the
  subscription's done handler, so the listen-time drop() never ran and the
  registration outlived its future. _LifetimeSubscription.asFuture now chains
  whenComplete(_drop).
- C1 asFuture error completion releases its registration: the same path on the
  error completion - whenComplete(_drop) untracks on throw as well as on done.
- replaced callbacks and errors stay closed while cancellation drains: a
  handler installed through onData/onError after listen bypassed the closed
  guard and could still fire while close() was blocked on an earlier release.
  Those wrappers now consult _isClosed() before forwarding.
- C1 original and replacement done callbacks respect closing: both the
  listen-time onDone wrapper and an onDone replacement now drop() the
  registration but return without calling the owner once _closed is set.

The flag alone lights nobody: `utils.free_tier_cohort` makes a lit flag mean

empty, or malformed. So the cohort is set too. `pct:100` is safe precisely here
— the harness runs against the Firebase emulator (project `demo-omi-local`) with
one local account per instance, so "100%" is every account that can exist on it,
and none of them belongs to a real user.

* desktop: render the on-device summary the client already uploads

The free tier replaces cloud summarization with an on-device projection. The
produce side was complete: summarize locally, store, upload to
`client_processing`. Nothing rendered it, so a free-tier user saw the
deterministic minimum forever and the whole feature was invisible.

The backend is deliberate about this. The bind endpoint "updates only
`client_processing`. Never touches `structured`", and
`ConversationProcessingState`'s docstring makes rendering a client contract:
clients check `client_processing` first and render the projection regardless of
`processing_state`. `ServerConversation.init` decoded the field and dropped it.

Every display consumer - the list, the automation bridge, the reconciliation
policy, the GRDB mirror - reads `ServerConversation.structured`, so selection
happens once at the decode seam and every surface is correct without touching
any view.

What the seam had to get right, beyond the mapping:

- Staleness. A projection names the transcript it summarized. When the response
  includes segments, the digest is recomputed and a mismatch is refused. List
  responses omit segments, so they rely on the server's binding and record
  `transcriptVerified: false` rather than pretending it was checked.
- Unknown schema versions, in two layers. A future envelope is stripped before
  decoding so it cannot make the conversation unreadable, and `resolve` renders
  v1 only.
- Precedence. `processing_state` cannot establish it - it is absent for both
  enriched and projected rows. The projection is selected only when the
  canonical structure is the deterministic minimum, which
  `build_deterministic_minimum_structured` defines as empty overview, category
  `other`, no sections, action items, or events. Cloud enrichment outranks a
  retained projection. Known limit: a title-only cloud result with otherwise
  default fields is indistinguishable from the minimum here.
- Action items merge on exact description with canonical winning, including when
  `completed` is false, because OR-ing completion would resurrect a task the
  user had reopened.
- Display attribution persists in its own `localSummaryJson` column.
  `clientProcessingJson` stays the producer-owned immutable retry blob; mixing
  them would corrupt retries.

Drafted with codex gpt-6-astra, then reviewed, verified, and finished here. The
precedence guard was checked field by field against the backend builder rather
than taken on report.

That function answers False whenever it is given no uid, on purpose:
`utils.free_tier_cohort` makes a lit flag mean "lit for the configured cohort",
and a caller that cannot name the account is never admitted, so a boolean alone
lights nobody. Called bare, it always returned False.

genuinely lit on a real bundle. The backend said so plainly once it was:

  free-tier cohort: FREE_TIER_LOCAL_PROCESSING consulted without a uid;
  admitting nobody at that call site until it passes one

* desktop: the free-tier client gate defaults on in Beta

The flag read env-or-UserDefaults and defaulted off, and nothing in the app ever
wrote it. A shipped Beta build therefore had the client half dark with no way to
light it short of a rebuild.

That is not a missing convenience, it is the takeaway-before-replacement case.
Beta serves through the development plane while keeping production identity. Lighting
FREE_TIER_LOCAL_PROCESSING there with the client dark means an identified-basic
user's conversation arrives carrying no projection; the policy resolves
`store_projection if has_projection else deterministic_minimum`, the minimum is
terminal, and the cloud summary is gone with nothing in its place. The two halves
have to be lit together, so Beta is where the client default belongs.

Only the absence of both an environment value and a stored default falls through
to the channel default, so this stays a kill switch in both directions:

- `object(forKey:)` rather than `bool(forKey:)`, because the latter cannot tell a
  stored `false` from a key that was never set - without the distinction Beta
  could not be turned off without a rebuild.
- A blank environment value is "unset", not "off", so an exported-but-empty
  variable cannot silently dark the channel.

Stable and every other bundle are unchanged and still default off.

Coordinator turn-4 review authorizes the V1 fixture correction. Exact before/after digests pin the revised oracle; immutable revision records do not permit builder assertion edits. Active tests reject missing/tampered records and prove the fake machine response. Verification: full harness 289 passed, 7 skipped, 40 strict xfailed; UTC app 2020 passed; spine 24 pending/7 protected; make preflight 16 passed. No live device acceptance claimed.

* harden(dev-harness): preserve marker retirement across spine revisions

Track retained marker occurrences rather than counts so retiring a second test cannot restore the first test's retired marker. The active regression covers this swap and legitimate continued retirement. Verification: full harness 290 passed, 7 skipped, 40 strict xfailed; spine 24 pending/7 protected; make preflight 16 passed. Dart sources unchanged after the earlier UTC app 2020-pass run.

* harden(dev-harness): retain corrected spine oracles through squash merges

A squash can introduce a corrected contract and its review records in the same commit. Absorb only the revision prefix ending at that introducing file's exact digest, preserving immutable records and later marker-only edits. Active temp-repo regression covers multiple corrections in one squash and rejects restoring old or altered assertions. Verification: harness 291 passed, 7 skipped, 40 strict xfailed; B1 make preflight 20 passed; final B1 journeys 20/20. Dart unchanged after UTC app 41 opt-in and 2051 ordinary passed.

Verification: UTC app 2064 passed; full harness 303 passed, 7 skipped, 55 strict xfailed; spine 37 pending/9 protected; preflight 16 checks passed. Isolated reviewed-broker probes failed 9/9 as documented in the conformance report. No real app/device launch.
