`sessions.e2e.test.ts` built its git fixture in `beforeEach`: six `git`
processes per test, seven tests. On the loaded packages lane that exceeded the
30s hook budget (run 35322311770, PR #7381). Bun runs the test body anyway, and
the cwd was still where the worker started — `apps/cli`, which resolves to this
checkout with remote git@github.com:kortix-ai/suna.git. So `sessions new`
pushed the session branch at the REAL repository:

    ✗  Could not create the remote session branch with local git credentials.
    error: src refspec refs/heads/main does not match any
    error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/kortix-ai/suna'

It failed only because actions/checkout leaves a detached HEAD with no
refs/heads/main.

Two changes. `beforeAll` parks the process in a temp directory outside every
git repository for the whole file, so a fixture that never got built can only
produce an immediate local git error — proven: the old spot resolves to this
repo with the real remote, the new one to nothing. And the fixture repository
plus its bare origin are built ONCE and copied per test, leaving one `git
remote add`: 1150ms -> 548ms for the file, full suite 1279 pass / 0 fail.

Also pins the isolation contract in tests/unit/test-runner-contract.test.ts,
whose existing assertion literally required the `--parallel=2` that killed the

that adds --isolate/--parallel must be allowlisted with a reason.

fix(db): stop the packages lane dying on a Bun isolate stdio leak

`bun test --parallel=2` implies `--isolate`. Under isolation on Linux, Bun
1.3.14 (0d9b296a) re-creates process.stdout/stderr for every test file,
duplicating the stdio fd and registering it with epoll, and never ends the
outgoing sinks at the isolate swap (oven-sh/bun#37968; fix PR oven-sh/bun#38008
is still open). A reused fd number then fails EPOLL_CTL_ADD with EEXIST, which
Bun reports as "Unhandled error between tests" and counts as a failure that
names no test:

    error: EEXIST: file already exists, epoll_ctl
      at new WriteStream (internal:fs/streams:244:58)
    error: Cannot call describe.skip() after the test run has completed
    259 pass, 17 skip, 1 fail, 2 errors  ("1 tests failed:" list EMPTY)

Reproduced on run 35331083850 attempts 1 and 2 at the same SHA. Drop
`--parallel`; 28 files do not need worker processes. Measured cost, Linux
container, real disposable-PostgreSQL containers: 11s parallel -> 34s serial.

The same "failure that names no test" class had a second, local-only source:
nine copies of a module-scope `Bun.spawnSync(['docker', 'version'])` probe,
which THROWS ENOENT when Docker is absent. That turned a Docker-less machine
red with nine unnamed failures. One `docker-available` module, probed once,
never throwing.

fix(models): the model picker spun forever for every project member

A member on dev opened the composer model picker and got a spinner that
never resolved, while the UI's own /model-picker calls had already
returned 200 with a populated catalog. The models were in the browser.
Nothing drew them.

model-selector.tsx renders the spinner on `modelsLoading ||
entitlementsPending`. `modelsLoading` is useRuntimeProviders().isLoading,
which settles, so entitlementsPending was permanently true.

It was permanently true because a DISABLED react-query never leaves
`status: 'pending'` — with no fetch to settle it, isPending stays true
for the lifetime of the component. useModelConnectionGate compensated by
restating each query's `enabled` condition inline, by hand:

    (!!projectId && projectDetailQuery.isPending) ||
    (!!projectId && llmGatewayEnabled && secretsQuery.isPending) ||
    accountStatePending

secretsQuery is `enabled: !!projectId && llmGatewayEnabled &&
canReadSecrets`. The restatement is missing canReadSecrets.
project.secret.read is manager-tier, so for a member the query never
ran, the middle clause was true && true && true forever, and the picker
spun for everyone below manager. 1c8b5434b8 added canReadSecrets to the
query and not to its copy.

The third clause never had a guard at all, and useAccountState disables
itself whenever the billing-account context is unresolved. Same failure,
one render away.

Stop restating `enabled`; ask what the query is DOING. resolveEntitlementsPending
holds the gate only while a query is genuinely fetching a first answer —
isPending && fetchStatus === 'fetching'. A disabled query reads idle and
releases it, an offline-paused one releases it rather than spinning over
a catalog already in the browser, and a background refetch cannot re-open
it. Adding a fourth input now costs one array entry and no condition to
keep in sync.

Swept the rest of apps/web and packages/sdk for the same shape: four
queries with a conditional `enabled` whose isPending is read, and this
was the only live one. project-access-boundary and
use-account-section-redirect mirror their conditions correctly,
connector-tools returns early for !canWrite before its skeleton, and
useModelAccess's mislabelled isLoading has no consumer that renders off
it.

test(kortixd): budget the first-ready waits for a real respawn on a loaded runner

`OpenCode lifecycle first ready response > reports the first successful
readiness response once` failed twice in a row on `main` (run 35305122951,
both the original and the --failed rerun) at 5,340 ms.

Cause is the deadline, not the daemon. Every step `waitFor` gates here is a
real process transition — spawn, SIGKILL, respawn, then an HTTP readiness
probe — and it had 5,000 ms. The packages lane runs this suite with
`--parallel=4 --isolate` alongside the other package suites, and the CI log
shows `{"msg":"[opencode] ready"}` at 04:09:50.974 with the failure thrown at
04:09:50.993: readiness arrived 19 ms AFTER the deadline expired. A correct
respawn, reported as a failure.

The invariant these waits sequence is `reports === 1` — the first ready
response is reported exactly once — which is timing-independent. The deadline
only decides how long a slow machine is tolerated. Per the learnings
register's 5x-margin rule, budget 25 s per wait against the observed ~5 s, and
raise the test's own cap from 15 s to 90 s so three of them fit.

No assertion changed.

Verified: 3 pass / 0 fail on three consecutive runs, and again under 8-way CPU
load. NOT claimed: a local reproduction of the CI failure — it passes here at
~1 s, so the case is the 5,340 ms measurement plus the 19 ms overshoot in the
CI log, not a reproduced red test.

docs(tui): three OpenTUI traps wave 2 hit, each re-measured

All three cost a wave time and none of them is in the type definitions.
Re-verified in the headless renderer before writing them down:

1. `<code conceal>` defaults to TRUE, so a markdown file renders as a RENDERING
   of itself: `# Heading` -> `Heading`, `**bold**` -> `bold`. A source viewer
   must pass `conceal={false}` (features/files/file-viewer.tsx already does).
2. An explicit `width`/`height` on `<scrollbox>` or `<diff>` paints outside the
   viewport. In a 46x10 bordered box, `<scrollbox width={46} height={10}>` wrote
   `row 8` into the bottom border (`└row 8──────┘`). No explicit size +
   `flexGrow={1}` + `overflow="hidden"` on the container draws a clean border —
   the shape transcript.tsx already uses.
3. A fixed one-row `<text>` beside a `flexGrow` child in a fixed-height column
   collapses to zero: a 6-row column rendered its header as `bodyE0-ROW`, the
   body's first line painted through the collapsed header. `flexShrink={0}` on
   the chrome rows fixes it.

Reported: a live transcript frame with `1` … `17` on rows of their own, filed
as `<markdown>` rendering an ordered list's numbers without their items.

1124e1b1-9e3d-481f-a028-7713a42bdfb7 the turn above it is the user prompt

renderer and three rows in 0.5.11. That is why bare numbers looked like a list,
and it is what a transcript wants — but a height calculation that assumes
paragraph folding will be wrong. Both written into docs/opentui-notes.md.

feat(sdk): add variant (reasoning effort) to SessionPicks

sendParts already accepted `variant` as a per-send override, but SessionPicks
carried only model + agent — so every host kept the effort in a store of its
own (useModelStore in apps/web) and re-passed it on every call. It now falls
back to picks.variant exactly as model and agent already did, persisted under
the same kortix:picks:<sessionId> key.

No wire change for an existing caller. Nothing could set picks.variant before
this commit, and the SDK is the only writer of that storage key, so a stored
entry cannot already contain one. resolveSendOptions pins the property that
matters: with no variant from either source the key is ABSENT, not undefined.

Two things the extraction found, both now covered:
 - a legacy {model,agent} entry parsed `variant` as undefined, not null;
 - a stored ModelKey is an OBJECT ({providerID,modelID}), so it is validated

feat(sdk): add useAccounts and useProjects to @kortix/sdk/react

(qk.accounts.list / qk.projects.list) but no hook, so every host rewrote the
useQuery wiring. apps/tui/src/features/sidebar/sidebar.tsx invented a key of
its own — ['tui','accounts',host,url] — that shares nothing with the rest of
the cache. staleTime is per-OBSERVER in React Query, so a copied fetcher/key/
gate drifts silently: 'N readers, one request' becomes N requests.

Identity is an argument, not an assumption: qk.accounts.list(userId) exists
because ['accounts'] is one entry for every user, and /new resolves its create
target out of that list. The framework-free core cannot see a host's auth
context, so a multi-user host passes userId; a single-identity CLI/TUI process
may omit it.

The key, the gate and the freshness contract are split into pure option
builders (accountsQueryOptions / projectsQueryOptions) because this package
has no React test renderer and a source-text assertion cannot tell a working
gate from a deleted one.

literal with a wrong value type is still rejected.

sessionParentId also rejects a non-string (metadata is jsonb, a malformed row
must not escape as a session id) and a self-referential link (a session that

feat(tui): composer, command palette, and the model/effort/agent pickers

<Composer> takes the whole useSession result and owns no session state. Every
write goes back through the SDK.

- Enter sends. An idle session with an empty inbox calls session.send; a busy
  one, or one with rows already waiting, enqueues through useSessionPrompts —
  the durable server-side inbox. useSession.send does not queue, and
  @kortix/sdk/message-queue is deprecated, so this is the one ordering-safe
  path. The footer reads `queued N` off the inbox; there is no local queue.
- Ctrl+J is the portable newline (it arrives as the linefeed byte, which the
  textarea's own default binding already inserts). Alt+Enter is handled
  explicitly. Shift+Enter works only under the kitty keyboard protocol: raw
  mode sends a bare \r for both, verified with mockInput.
- Alt arrives as KeyEvent.meta, not .option, in a raw terminal. The composer's
  matcher accepts either flag; src/keymap.ts tests .option only.
- Esc clears the draft; empty and busy, it arms and a second press within 1.5s
  calls session.cancel().
- / at column 0 opens the palette: the project's runtime commands plus the
  built-ins. Ids are prefixed, so a project command named 'new' cannot collide
  with the built-in.
- Model picks persist through session.picks.setModel (the store sendParts
  reads), agent through session.picks.setAgent, effort through
  useModelStore().setVariant keyed by model.
- Models group by their REAL provider (FlatModel.provider, falling back to the
  namespaced wire id) — the gateway serves everything as 'Kortix'. Models the
  project turned off stay listed, dimmed and tagged 'off'.

ui/Picker is not usable here: it wraps ui/Modal, which is absolutely positioned
at the full terminal size and is therefore clipped by the session panel when
mounted from inside the composer (verified: zero rows rendered). pickers/

fix(web): stop a sent message coming back as the project-home draft

Type "Hi" on project home, press Enter, land on the new session, then return
to project home: "Hi" was still in the composer.

Root cause: TipTap's `setEditable` emits the editor's `update` event by
default, and this editor's `onUpdate` is `createUpdateHandler` — a DOCUMENT
change reporter feeding the draft saver. Every flip of `disabled` therefore
reported the live document as a change the user had made.

The project-home composer flips `disabled` on send and deliberately keeps the
sent text in the box (`clearOnSend={false}`). In a production build that
phantom change lands AFTER the send's own `clearSavedDraft()`, so its 400 ms
debounce re-saves the just-sent message as the project's unsent draft, and the
next visit restores it.

Measured on dev.kortix.com before the fix:

    SET    kortix_draft:project:<id> "Hi"   @309014   (typing debounce)
    REMOVE kortix_draft:project:<id>        @309416   (clearSavedDraft on send)
    SET    kortix_draft:project:<id> "Hi"   @309822   (phantom, +406 ms)
    composer after returning to project home: "Hi"

Fix: pass `emitUpdate: false`. Editability is not content. The view still
refreshes — `setOptions` calls `view.updateState` either way.

Local dev servers cannot show this bug: React StrictMode's double-invoked
effects commit the disabled render before the send's await resolves, so the
clear lands last and the draft stays clean. Verified against a local
production build (`next build` + `next start`), where the only writes are now
the typing debounce and the send's clear.

support/testing: test_squid: new runtime test

Signed-off-by: Julien Olivain <ju.o@free.fr>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Petazzoni <thomas.petazzoni@bootlin.com>

support/testing: add tests for openscap

Add basic tests for openscap, ensuring that it builds and runs a minimal
command with different cryptographic backends:
- libgcrypt
- libnss
- no crypto backend

Signed-off-by: Alexis Lothoré <alexis.lothore@bootlin.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Petazzoni <thomas.petazzoni@bootlin.com>

package/openscap: allow building when crypto backend is not gcrypt

When enabling the openscap package and the libnss library _but not_
libgcrypt, the build can fail on the following error:

  ../src/libopenscap.so.33.1.3: undefined reference to `crapi_init'

The issue is due to the fact that the corresponding Makefile
systematically forces -DWITH_CRYPTO=gcrypt: openscap CMake
instrumentation then searches only this backend, fails to find it,
assumes that no crypto backend is available, and so does not include the
crapi_object in the final link step.

Commit 7c85f3adf4a8 ("package/openscap: new package") took into account
the fact that openscap isn't currently able to build if no crypto backend
is provided (see [0]), and so made sure to force libgcrypt inclusion if
libnss is not included. Since then, two fixes ([1] and [2]) have been
integrated upstream to allow building openscap with any backend.

linux/linux.mk: forcibly (re)enable Make jobserver for linux-rebuild-with-initramfs target

Commit 0b9efc991f8a ("linux: use BR2_MAKE", 2023-04-10) replaced $(MAKE)
with $(BR2_MAKE) in a number of recipes. As a consequence, the child
make is unable to discover the job server, in some cases. In those
cases, we get a warning such as:

> warning: jobserver unavailable: using -j1. Add `+' to parent make rule.

See [1] and [2].

Falling back to single job can make build considerably longer.
This longer build time issue can be reproduced in specific
conditions. This situation happens when:

1. The top GNU Make is using a "pipe" jobserver.
   This is the default when GNU Make <= 4.3 is used (and v4.3 is the
   version inside the current Buildroot Docker reference image).
   Make > 4.3 changed the default jobserver style to "fifo".
   See [3][4]. With Make > 4.3, the issue can be reproduced by
   calling "make --jobserver-style=pipe ...".
2. The root filesystem is an initramfs linked into the Kernel
  (i.e. using the config BR2_TARGET_ROOTFS_INITRAMFS=y)
3. Buildroot per-package directories is used
  (i.e. using the config BR2_PER_PACKAGE_DIRECTORIES=y)
4. The build is made in parallel, with 2 or more jobs. For example:
   make -j$(nproc)

Overall, the issue can be reproduced with the commands:

utils/docker-run
cat >.config <<EOF
BR2_aarch64=y
BR2_TOOLCHAIN_EXTERNAL=y
BR2_PER_PACKAGE_DIRECTORIES=y
BR2_LINUX_KERNEL=y
BR2_LINUX_KERNEL_USE_ARCH_DEFAULT_CONFIG=y
BR2_TARGET_ROOTFS_INITRAMFS=y
EOF
make olddefconfig
make -j$(nproc)

The Linux Kernel is built once (with a fake empty initramfs cpio
image), when build log is showing ">>> linux 7.2.6 Building". Then,
at the end of the Buildroot build, once the CPIO filesystem is
complete, it is integrated inside the Kernel with an extra "make"
invocation when the build log shows
">>>   Rebuilding kernel with initramfs".

This second kernel "make" is not expected to rebuild the whole
kernel, since compiled objects from the first compilation are still
here. However, in the described conditions, the second kernel is
fully rebuilt. This is an undesired behaviour. The Make jobserver
issue adds up to that: this second full kernel is rebuilt with only
one job, which can significantly increase the build time.

Running the previous example on a host with 128 CPUs:
without this change, build takes 1h5m,
with this change, build takes 7m.

Note: using GNU Make >= 4.4 (with a fifo jobserver style by default)
or removing per-package directories no longer produces the issue.
For reference, running the example, without this change and without
per-package directories on the same host, the build takes 10 mins.

This commit improves the situation by prefixing the recipe with "+",
to inform the parent Make that $(BR2_MAKE) can deal with the job
server. This will give a chance to do jobs in parallel, in general.

Note: the pkg-generic.mk infra already has '+' for _BUILD_CMDS, which is
why other $(BR2_MAKE) invocations in linux.mk does not need this '+'.
See [5].

[1] https://www.gnu.org/software/make/manual/html_node/Error-Messages.html
[2] https://www.gnu.org/software/make/manual/html_node/MAKE-Variable.html
[3] https://www.gnu.org/software/make/manual/html_node/Options-Summary.html#index-_002d_002djobserver_002dstyle
[4] https://cgit.git.savannah.gnu.org/cgit/make.git/commit/?id=7ad2593b2d2bb5b9332f4444d8bf93ac6f958bc6
[5] https://gitlab.com/buildroot.org/buildroot/-/commit/069b33a30e6d71454ba8cf3b41d1ee2db14549e7

package/python-grpcio: disable for the MIPS n32 ABI

python-grpcio builds its own bundled copy of abseil-cpp, which only
implements DirectMmap() with mmap2 for the o32 ABI on MIPS:

    #if ... (defined(__mips__) && _MIPS_SIM == _MIPS_SIM_ABI32) || ...

With the n32 ABI, the "remaining 64-bit architectures" fallback is
selected instead, which fails to build because long is 32-bit there:

    third_party/abseil-cpp/absl/base/internal/direct_mmap.h:130:39:
        error: static assertion failed: Platform is not 64-bit
      130 |   static_assert(sizeof(unsigned long) == 8, "Platform is not 64-bit");
          |                 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~
    third_party/abseil-cpp/absl/base/internal/direct_mmap.h:130:39:
        note: the comparison reduces to '(4 == 8)'

This is the same defect fixed for libabseil-cpp in the previous patch,
but the dependency added there does not help here: python-grpcio does
not use the Buildroot abseil, it compiles the copy bundled in the
tarball.

Using the Buildroot-provided abseil instead is not an option today.
setup.py does have a GRPC_PYTHON_BUILD_SYSTEM_ABSL knob, but it is
hardcoded to the build machine paths:

    if BUILD_WITH_SYSTEM_ABSL:
        CORE_C_FILES = filter(
            lambda x: "third_party/abseil-cpp" not in x, CORE_C_FILES
        )
        ABSL_INCLUDE = (os.path.join("/usr", "include"),)
    [...]
    if BUILD_WITH_SYSTEM_ABSL:
        EXTENSION_LIBRARIES += tuple(
            lib.stem[3:]
            for lib in sorted(pathlib.Path("/usr").glob("lib*/libabsl_*.so"))
        )

i.e. it would pick up the host headers and host libraries, so it cannot
be used when cross-compiling without patching setup.py. And even with
such a patch it would not fix this build failure, since Buildroot's
abseil has the very same limitation.

So just disable the package for the n32 ABI. The o32 and n64 ABIs are
unaffected. Note that n32 is the default ABI for BR2_mips64/BR2_mips64el,
so this affects every mips64 build that does not explicitly select n64.

For the LTS maintainers: python-grpcio gained MIPS support in commit
2bfad952c374, released in 2024.02, and the autobuilders have been hitting
this ever since, already with grpcio 1.60.0, the version shipped in
2024.02:

    https://autobuild.buildroot.net/results/e6cb7f473a28af8b53e7cbb8d8a582adffdeb66e/

It is still reproduced on 2025.02.x:

    https://autobuild.buildroot.net/results/9cf98bff7ce05262d6ff4221953901ae5543880e/

so a backport is needed there.

Fixes: 2bfad952c374258e37ffdf46a2c450d860640e11 ("package/python-grpcio: add BR2_PACKAGE_PYTHON_GRPCIO_ARCH_SUPPORTS")
Fixes:
https://autobuild.buildroot.net/results/90405c0a3d0b2e929d5074305906e6fe3679298c/

package/libabseil-cpp: disable for the MIPS n32 ABI

absl::base_internal::DirectMmap() only implements mmap() via mmap2 for
the o32 ABI on MIPS:

    #if ... (defined(__mips__) && _MIPS_SIM == _MIPS_SIM_ABI32) || ...

With the n32 ABI, the "remaining 64-bit architectures" fallback is
selected instead, which fails to build because long is 32-bit there:

    absl/base/internal/direct_mmap.h: In function 'void* absl::lts_20260107::base_internal::DirectMmap(void*, size_t, int, int, int, off_t)':
    absl/base/internal/direct_mmap.h:130:39: error: static assertion failed: Platform is not 64-bit
      130 |   static_assert(sizeof(unsigned long) == 8, "Platform is not 64-bit");
          |                 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~
    absl/base/internal/direct_mmap.h:130:39: note: the comparison reduces to '(4 == 8)'

direct_mmap.h is included by absl/base/internal/low_level_alloc.cc and
absl/base/internal/poison.cc, which are always built, so the failure is
unconditional. Upstream abseil has no support for the n32 ABI, so
disable the package for that ABI.

Since n32 is the default ABI for BR2_mips64/BR2_mips64el, this affects
every mips64 build that does not explicitly select n64. The o32
(BR2_MIPS_OABI32) and n64 (BR2_MIPS_NABI64) ABIs are unaffected, and all
in-tree mips64 defconfigs use n64.

For the LTS maintainers: the ABI list in direct_mmap.h is identical in
abseil 20200225 (the version in tree when the arch dependencies were
introduced) and in the current 20260817.0, so the failure has existed
ever since mips64 was allowed. It is still reproduced on all maintained
branches, e.g.:

2.1.2 fixes CVE-2026-37539 (CVSS 3.1 score 9.8, CWE-121): a stack based

and decodeFrame() in decoder.cpp, allowing remote attackers to cause a
denial of service (crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via
crafted CAN FD frames.

The advisory names v2.0.0 explicitly, so the version used so far is
affected. The CVE is not reported by
https://security.buildroot.org/master/component/cannelloni because its
NVD entry has no CPE data (vendor and product are both "n/a") and can
therefore not be matched against the package version.

Apart from the security fix, 2.0.0..2.1.2 contains only a handful of
changes: undeliverable frames are dropped after a timeout on a broken
CAN bus, variable length arrays are gone, the default remote address is
fixed, and pthreads are looked up with the CMake module instead of by
hand. 2.1.1 is a maintenance release only, as the 2.1.0 tag pointed to
a commit that was not the final one.

commits.message:
DEVELOPMENT: queueing an OTA tells the tag to sleep for an hour

contentmode 5 sets nextupdate = 3216153600 on the AP, so the nextCheckIn it
hands out is enormous and the tag sleeps its 3600 s cap. A tag that was
mid-cycle when the OTA was queued therefore goes quiet for a full hour, which
is indistinguishable from a dead tag -- Weather6 did exactly this today,
13:33 to 14:35, and was fine.

Both tags are now on v0.26 (reported version 38): bench tag displaying a
pushed test card, Weather6 displaying weather again after a clean apply
(OTA-APPLIED sectors=6 retries=0 unverified=0).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EgYBSh93LDt8zjKAArdzTz

Cap the reported version at 38: 39+ makes the AP send zlib images

Images stopped displaying on both tags today, and the cause was the version
number, not the image path. The AP decides whether to compress from the tag's
reported version: tagtypes/35.json carries "zlib_compression": "27", read as
hex (39), and contentmanager.cpp compresses when tagSoftwareVersion >= that.
A tag reporting 39 or more is served DATATYPE_IMG_ZLIB (0x30); this firmware
reads it as raw, runs past the end of the data and fails the next block's
checksum on every retry, so nothing ever displays again. The capabilities
field the tag sends has no say in it.

I walked into this by bumping the version for each OTA test until it crossed
39. Reported version is now 0x26 (38), with the ceiling documented where the
constant is defined and in DEVELOPMENT.md; builds are identified by commit.

Decoding zlib properly is now the top entry in PLAN.md: the same weather image
is 5.8 KB compressed against 33.6 KB raw, and the raw download is 77% of the
daily battery budget.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EgYBSh93LDt8zjKAArdzTz

Battery budget on v0.26, and the compressed-image gap

Re-measured on the bench at 3.0 V with the debugger detached: sleep floor
38.8 uA, a check-in with nothing pending ~0.2-0.5 uAh, a panel refresh
0.032 mAh (37.9 s, three refreshes within 8% of each other). With the weather
tag's cadence -- update every 2 h, check-in every 15 min -- that is 4.17 mAh a
day, so ~450 days on 4x CR2450, up from ~410 before the sleep fix.

The interesting part is what dominates: the image download is 77% of the daily
budget, because the images are raw (33.6 KB BW, 67.2 KB BWR). The AP already
offers compressed images -- dataType 0x30, ~2.3 KB for the same content -- and
this firmware does not decode them: it reads them as raw, runs past the end of
the data and fails block 1's checksum on every retry, so those images never
display. Pre-existing, not a regression: firmware from before this week fails
identically on the same push. Recorded in PLAN.md as the next thing worth
doing, for battery life as much as for function.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EgYBSh93LDt8zjKAArdzTz

Pull the panel's control lines up during sleep: 59.8 uA -> 39.3 uA

A third of the tag's sleep current was the panel's control lines sitting at an
undefined level. Pulled up, the floor drops by 20 uA; driving them high does no
better than the weak pull, so the pull is enough and is the safer of the two
into an unpowered panel.

Measured at 3.0 V from a PPK2 with the debugger detached, production firmware,
median of the quiet seconds between check-ins:

  floating (all nine panel lines)           59.8 uA
  + pull-ups on BUSY/RST/DC/BS/CS           39.3 uA
  + pull-ups on the SPI bus as well        >500 uA, never settles

The SPI bus is shared with the external flash and has to stay
high-impedance. On a tag whose panel has never been powered (DIAG_SLEEP_ONLY)
pulling every panel line up reaches 29.9 uA, so there is ~10 uA more to be had
once the bus side is understood.

The panel still comes back: EXTRA_DEFINES=-DBENCH_SPLASH_LOOP refreshes,
sleeps 20 s and refreshes again, three times, all clean (OTP load, PON, ~37 s
DRF, POFF). uc8159_init() re-drives BS and DIR before powering the panel, so a
pulled-up BS during sleep cannot leave it in the wrong bus mode.

The pin sweep that found this is in the DIAG_SLEEP_ONLY build:
DIAG_PIN_MODE (1 = pull down, 2 = pull up, 3/4 = driven low/high) applied to
DIAG_PIN_MASK. Every other pin group made things worse, so the panel interface
was the whole of the controllable part.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EgYBSh93LDt8zjKAArdzTz

Back off failed transfers without silencing the tag

A tag that fails the same transfer repeatedly used to apply the retry back-off
to its sleep interval, so it stopped checking in for up to 15 minutes. At the
AP that is indistinguishable from a dead tag, and it delays everything else the
AP wants to tell it. Found while bench-testing rejected OTA images: offer a tag
an image it refuses (bad vector table) and it disappears.

The back-off now gates only the transfer. The tag keeps the AP's check-in
cadence and declines to *start* a download until the hold expires, which also
stops a rejected image from costing a 21 KB download every minute. A different
dataVer — the AP offering a replacement — cuts the hold to one check-in rather
than clearing it outright: an AP with several transfers queued offers a
different dataVer at every check-in, and clearing turned that into a continuous
download loop (seen on the bench before this bound was added).

Bench A/B with a bad-vector image queued: before, silence for 15+ minutes at a
time; after, 14 consecutive check-ins over 10 minutes with no re-download
(no block requests in the AP log).

Also makes OTA_APPLY_MIN_MV overridable so the battery gate can be tested by
raising the threshold above the bench supply.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EgYBSh93LDt8zjKAArdzTz

OTA: verify every flash write, mark "applied" only after a verified copy

The staging→active copy was the one irreversible step in the firmware and the
least checked one: it threw away the status of every erase and program, never
read a sector back, ran with the RF core still powered from the XferComplete,
and wrote the "this dataVer is installed" record *before* the copy started. A
failed erase or a reset in that window left a brick or a tag that skipped the
update forever. External review findings H8, M14, M15, L19–L22.

The apply now:

- checks both ROM flash statuses and reads each sector back, retrying the
  whole erase/program/verify up to 5 times (the RAM buffer still holds the
  data, so a retry is free);
- reads back with the VIMS cache off. The cache does not snoop flash writes,
  so the old readback could have compared against cached bytes of the image
  being replaced. Staging verifies invalidate the cache the same way;
- writes the dataVer record from the RAM function after the copy verifies, so
  an interrupted apply is retried instead of skipped;
- shuts the RF core down and requires ≥ 2400 mV before the first erase — and
  before the download even starts, which is where the charge actually goes;
- requires the staged reset vector to have the Thumb bit set and to point
  inside the image. A vector with bit 0 clear passed the old bounds and would
  have HardFaulted before the new image ran an instruction.

Staging writes mask interrupts around the ROM flash calls (no code may execute
from flash while the bank is in an erase/program cycle — sector non-overlap is
not the rule) and clear FLASH:CFG.DIS_STANDBY afterwards, which driverlib's
wrappers do and the raw ROM entry does not.

How an apply went now leaves the bench: the dataVer record carries sectors,
retries and unverified count, and the installed image reports them once — over
RTT and to the AP in its first check-in (tools/ap.py shows "OTA-APPLIED
sectors=6 retries=0 unverified=0"). The record lives in flash, not .noinit,
because it has to be read by a *different* image and .noinit moves between
builds.

Bench (00124B00181880B0, PPK2 at 3.0 V, no debugger): six OTA cycles, all
applied and rebooted, fastest 92 s from queue to the new version checking in.
A Thumb-bit-cleared image is rejected before any erase and the tag keeps
running. With BENCH_OTA_FLAKY_APPLY sabotaging sector 0's first program the
tag still came up on the new image — without the readback and retry that
sector would have stayed erased, i.e. a brick.

Also documented two bench traps that cost time today: a running
JLinkGDBServer halts the tag on any reset the firmware performs itself, and a
power gap shorter than ~15 s does not reset the tag (its capacitors carry it
through in standby). bench_sleep.sh now waits long enough and kills the
ppk.py child that actually holds VOUT.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EgYBSh93LDt8zjKAArdzTz

PLAN/DEVELOPMENT: 16 h run on v0.23 clean, next steps

0 radio hangs in 16 h (v0.20: 6 in 14 h), 32/32 pushed images displayed,
1133 check-ins. Records the channel-27 trap for future readers and lists
what's next: OTA robustness, the remaining ~59 uA, a fresh power budget.

fix: skip codex config.toml rewrite when there's nothing to merge (#4564)

* fix: skip codex config.toml rewrite when there's nothing to merge

_merge_toml_fragment() always rewrote .codex/config.toml, even when the
event fragment was empty and there were no Specify-owned hook blocks to
remove. That unconditional rewrite appended stray blank lines and, via
Python's text-mode newline translation on read/write, silently changed
the file's line-ending convention (LF -> CRLF on Windows) — turning a
no-op install into a spurious, unmanifested diff on a pre-existing
tracked file.

Now the merge is skipped (and the file left untouched) when there is no
fragment to add and no owned blocks to remove, matching the existing S5
tracking convention used by the other native-format mergers in this file.

* fix: skip unconditional rewrite in _remove_toml_entries for real no-op path

Review found the prior fix patched the wrong function: the real
"specify integration install codex" repro (no Codex event hooks
configured) resolves to events={}, which routes through
install_integration_events's empty-map branch into
_remove_native_event_hooks -> _remove_toml_entries, never touching
_merge_toml_fragment. _remove_toml_entries still rewrote the file
unconditionally even when the regex strip was a no-op, which (via
text-mode newline translation) mangles line endings on Windows.

Adds the same cleaned == existing guard to _remove_toml_entries, and
replaces the regression test with one that drives the real
install_integration_events(..., events={}) path instead of a synthetic
events map no caller can produce.

* fix: check unchanged content before empty/comments-only deletion in _remove_toml_entries

The no-op guard ran after the "only whitespace/comments remain" deletion
branch, so a pre-existing comments-only or blank config.toml with no
Specify-owned blocks was unlinked before cleaned == existing was ever
checked. Move the unchanged-content check first; the delete-if-empty
branch now only fires once stripping has actually removed a
Specify-owned block.

Remove a dead case pattern in common.sh (SC2221/SC2222) (#4605)

resolve_template_content() rejects unsafe manifest paths with
`/*|*../*|../*)`. The third alternative can never match: `*../*`
already matches every string `../*` does, so shellcheck reports SC2221
(this pattern always overrides a later one) and SC2222 (this pattern
never matches). Removing it changes nothing: checked against
/etc/passwd, ../x, a/../b, ../, x/../../y, .., a/.., ..a, a..b, ./x and

commits.message:
Detect a crashed dtuhidd instead of discarding HID events

Summary:
On a macOS 26 host with an iOS 27 runtime, `dtuhidd` aborts during boot and every HID event sent afterwards is discarded without an error.

The daemon's own start-up races the guest's. CoreSimulator demand-launches `dtuhidd` early in boot; it asks CoreAnimation for the display list and `query_displays()` calls `abort()` when no display is up yet. A crash report from an affected boot:

```
dtuhidd  EXC_CRASH (SIGABRT)
  abort()
  QuartzCore  query_displays() + 1752
  QuartzCore  ensure_displays()
  QuartzCore  +[CADisplay displays]
  CoreDeviceUtilities ...
```

Whether it loses is a function of how slow the boot is, so it is intermittent on an idle host and reliable on a loaded one. On one captured boot the daemon launched 0.4s in, aborted at 14:00:08.9 while the device was still `WaitingOnBackboard`, and the transport connected at 14:00:09.6 -- 0.6s after its peer had died.

Nothing on the client side could observe that. `SimDevice.lookup:error:` vends a port for a demand-launched job whether or not it can run, the connection builds against a daemon launchd has crashed and throttled, `xpc_connection_set_event_handler` discarded every event including the errors, and the barrier timeout in `performColdDrain` was swallowed into a fixed sleep.

`SimulatorDTUHIDTransport.dtuhid(for:)` now round-trips a barrier before handing the transport out, and retries with backoff when nothing answers. The crash window closes once the boot settles, so a retry recovers the full transport rather than losing the keyboard: D117706226 established that Indigo keeps buttons but not keyboard on Xcode 27+, which makes falling back a partial mitigation and worth exhausting the retries first. `livenessAttempts` is sized from a measured recovery of roughly 19s after boot completion, which is launchd's exponential respawn throttle rather than the daemon's own start-up.

The lookup is inside the retried attempt rather than ahead of it. It fails while the job is being torn down to respawn, which is the state the retry exists to ride out, so hoisting it turns the most recoverable moment into a terminal one. `isTransientDTUHIDFailure` keeps that distinct from absent `_4sim` symbols, which no amount of waiting changes.

This is a probe of the connection, not of process residency: D115593130 removed residency as a signal because `dtuhidd` is demand-launched and pressured-exit, so a daemon that is merely not resident is healthy. It also holds here that an explicitly requested `.dtuhid` never silently degrades -- only the auto-negotiated path falls back, and only through the existing `isDTUHIDUnreachable` seam.

A successful probe also means the peer activated, which is what `performColdDrain` otherwise waits for on the first gesture, so its tail is paid at connect and kept out of the user's first touch.

The underlying abort is an Apple defect; this makes the transport survive it rather than removing it.

## Scope, and a separate finding

Investigating "simulator input is dead" turned up two independent causes, and this diff addresses only the first. The second is a caller-side bug, fixed separately in the consuming project: `lifecycle.connectToHID()` vends the simulator's *cached* HID, and `SimulatorNotificationUpdateStrategy` closes that cache via `terminateConnections()` on any CoreSimulator device state-change notification. Those arrive asynchronously, so the notification for a boot that has just finished can land a second or two after a caller has already connected, and the holder of the returned `SimulatorHID` gets no signal at all. `dtuhidd` then cancels all six of its virtual HID services in response to the peer leaving, so the only trace is `No active service, dropping event` in the guest log. That caller now owns its connection instead.

That is worth raising here rather than only in the caller: any consumer holding a `connectToHID()` result across a device state change has the same silent failure, and the API gives it nothing to detect it with.

## Follow-ups

Left to a refactor diff on top of this one, per review: `DTUHIDDrainClock` has grown into a bundle of injected closures and should become a protocol with a live implementation and a test implementation. That also removes the no-op default on `awaitLivenessReply`, which today lets a call site that omits the argument get a probe that always succeeds, and it is the natural place to stop `DispatchTimeInterval` rendering as `seconds(4)` inside the liveness diagnostic.

Reviewed By: lawrencelomax

fbshipit-source-id: 91cc70a729ed33535108309f67aa5c187795b769

Play a demo's terminal in the page

Summary:
A demo's terminal is now played in the page by `asciinema-player` rather than offered as a file to download and play somewhere else. It is a real terminal: the output arrives as it did during the run, and the scrubber carries a marker per step, so the steps are on the timeline and can be jumped between from it.

The terminal and the clip are synchronised in both directions. Scrub, pause or play either one and the other follows, and clicking a step's marker moves the clip to that step just as pressing a step's button in the transcript moves both. The clip is the timeline of record: the terminal follows it, and a gesture made on the terminal is turned into the same gesture on the clip, which then propagates back. Only one of the two is ever written to as a result of the other having moved, so they cannot drive each other in a loop. The terminal reports no event for being scrubbed, so its clock is read on an interval, and a jump larger than playing alone would explain is read as a scrub.

This replaces the hand-rolled step timeline the page carried before, along with the play, restart and clock controls that stood in for a transport. A demo whose clip could not be cut used to run that clock itself; it now has the terminal as its timeline, with the terminal's own transport.

The transcript below the terminal is unchanged and is still the whole of the demo in text: every step, what it showed, and what it printed. The player is built in an effect and so never renders on the server, and it is loaded on demand rather than in the page's main bundle. A reader without JavaScript, or one for whom the player fails to load, gets the transcript and a link to the asciicast; nothing readable depends on the player running.

Adds `asciinema-player` 3.17 to the website, Apache-2.0.

fbshipit-source-id: 23ca9f52d2cc2ee067d1aa61b7a8a9dfccd10bb0

Cut an exact clip out of a recording

Summary:
`sim-video clip --start S --end E input.mp4 output.mp4` cuts an independently playable file out of a recording, and writes the same JSON report beside it that `record` writes: encoding, pixel dimensions and the clip's own duration. The clip's timeline is rebased so its first frame is time zero, so a player reports the clip's duration rather than the recording's and a caller seeks with offsets relative to the clip.

The range is decoded and re-encoded rather than copied through. A recording carries a keyframe at its first frame and then at most every `--key-frame-rate` seconds — four by default — so a passthrough copy cannot open on a keyframe at an arbitrary boundary: it would have to begin seconds early or start on a partial frame. Re-encoding is what buys a clip that begins exactly where it was asked to. The clip inherits the recording's frame size and estimated data rate, rounded to the even dimensions H.264 accepts, and is encoded with a one-second keyframe interval so seeking inside it lands near the offset asked for. It also inherits the recording's display orientation: samples are copied at the size they are stored at, so the transform the track declares is carried onto the encoder rather than dropped, and a rotated recording is not published on its side.

Cutting a clip publishes both files or neither. They are written into a directory this invocation owns and moved into place only once the clip is complete and has been read back and described, so a failure anywhere — decoding, encoding, reading the clip back, or writing its report — publishes nothing. An output that exists is refused before any work starts, and refused again at the end by moving rather than replacing.

The two moves are not one step, and what happens in the window between them is stated rather than assumed: if the report cannot be placed, the clip is taken back only when the file at that path is still the one this invocation put there, so a publisher that replaced it in between keeps what it wrote. This is the ordinary case of two writers asked for the same output; it is not atomic publication against an adversary who can replace files at will.

Cancellation is cooperative, and finalising a file is not a cancellation point, so a cancelled command can still reach the end with a complete clip in hand. It is checked after the clip is finalised and read back, and again immediately before anything is published.

Encoding waits out backpressure rather than spinning on it, and re-reads the writer on every wait. An encoder input that has stopped asking for data because the writer failed or was cancelled never becomes ready again, so the wait ends in that failure instead of hanging. A clip is only reported as written when the writer says it completed.

`--start` past the end of the recording, a range no frame falls inside, and an input with no video track are each rejected with a message naming the range and the recording.

Differential Revision: D120158653

fbshipit-source-id: 7a4ead42b7d0404cecf5a4bc5876f4e17a903b59

Pin the socket server's lifecycle and accept callback

Summary:
Covers `FBSocketServer` directly for the first time. Until now it was only exercised through the device debug server in another framework, which never observes the port or the lifecycle failures. Pinned here: the ephemeral port read back from the kernel after binding port zero, the failure a second `startListening` reports, the failure `stopListening` reports with no active socket, and the delegate callback an accepted client produces.

No behavioural change.

Restarting a stopped server is deliberately not covered. The listening socket is closed by the accept source's cancel handler rather than by `stopListening` itself, so whether an immediate rebind of the port it read back succeeds is a race — and nothing restarts a server.

___

Differential Revision: D120565272

fbshipit-source-id: 42e1ba864352cb85270defb95a264d7267691971

Raise the execution time allowance for every provided-simulator smoke test

Summary:
The smoke suites take a booted simulator from their environment, and every case in them drives a real guest — an application launch, a service spawn, a walk of a live accessibility tree — which regularly runs past a minute. `ProvidedSimulatorTestCase` now raises the per-test execution time allowance to 600 seconds for every case in those suites, so a slow-but-correct test is reported as the pass it is rather than killed at the 60-second default the build script sets.

`AXBridgeSmokeTests` raised its own allowance and `SimulatorGuestServicesSmokeTests` did not, so the latter is the one that failed. On a hosted runner `testGuestServesLaunchCtlBridgeSettingsAndApplications` completed in 112 seconds and the run still reported `** TEST FAILED **` with exit code 65.

The allowance is set on the base class before the simulator is acquired, so it covers the acquisition too: that waits up to 300 seconds for the provided simulator to finish booting, and under the default allowance a harness slow to hand one over was reported as a test that timed out rather than as the boot wait it is.

No new test accompanies this. The defect is the test harness timing out a passing test, which nothing inside the bundle can observe; the reproduction is a hosted run of the smoke scheme against a simulator that takes more than a minute to serve the request.

Differential Revision: D120670075

fbshipit-source-id: 0bb2b0505f8ac92b19c6ca16348619a4fb07e37b

Type profile identifiers as strings

Summary:
No behavioural change. `ManagedConfigError.profileNotInstalled` carried its profile identifiers as `[Any]`, which kept the whole `Sendable`-conforming error non-`Sendable`.

The payload exists only to be rendered into the error's description, so each identifier is converted to its `String` at construction and the case carries `[String]`. The error is then `Sendable` because its contents genuinely are, rather than because the requirement was suppressed. Converting elementwise rather than casting the array keeps a malformed entry visible in the message instead of discarding every identifier alongside it.

Differential Revision: D120560279

fbshipit-source-id: ad9df3fda4a873fd53b880e03958f61a8b72deeb

Make companion address and info sendable

Summary:
No behavioural change. `CompanionAddress` and `CompanionInfo` are immutable value types holding only `String`, `Bool`, `Int32`, and each other, so they are safe to share across concurrency domains — but a public type gets no implicit `Sendable` conformance, so every `Sendable`-conforming error that carries one warned.

Stating the conformance removes those warnings at the source rather than at each use site: it also clears the `ResolvedCompanion` warnings in `ReplConnectionError`, which were only non-`Sendable` because they hold a `CompanionAddress`.

Differential Revision: D120560277

fbshipit-source-id: d65dc50772371dd7f32f4805b7fbaa6bc4446780

Report when a recording's first frame was captured

Summary:
`sim-video record` now reports `startedAt` in the JSON report it writes beside the recording: the Unix timestamp of the recording's own media time zero. A caller that timestamps its own events on the wall clock can now place them on the recording's timeline exactly, instead of measuring from the moment it noticed the recorder come up — which trails media zero by however long readiness took to reach and to detect.

Media zero is the presentation timestamp `AVAssetWriter.startSession(atSourceTime:)` anchored the movie at, and the encoder stamps every presentation timestamp as an offset from `systemUptime` at the first pushed frame. `SimulatorVideo.startedAt()` therefore reads uptime and wall clock as one adjacent pair and differences them, so the answer does not drift with how long the recording ran or how long finalising the file took.

Recording is otherwise unchanged. The field is absent when no frame was ever muxed.

___

Differential Revision: D120661843

fbshipit-source-id: c9bc342ce96d56994d8a7602cc191eab54a64294

Drop the companion tool's unimported dependencies

Summary:
No behavioural change; the same binary links the same archives.

`:idb-companion` compiles one file, `main.swift`, which imports six things. Its dependency list named twelve: `IDBGRPCSwift`, `ReplProtocol` and the four gRPC and NIO packages were left over from when the target was the whole companion rather than its entry point. They are all still linked, reaching the binary through `:CompanionLib`'s `exported_deps` as they do for every other consumer of the library, so the closure the build sees is unchanged.

The list is now exactly `main.swift`'s imports, which is the only thing a one-file target's dependencies can usefully be.

The companion Xcode spec keeps naming `IDBGRPCSwift` and `ReplProtocol` on the tool, and that asymmetry is deliberate rather than drift: every framework in that project is a `staticlib`, so the tool is the build's one link step and has to name each archive that goes into it, including the ones it only reaches through `CompanionLib`. XcodeGen has no equivalent of `exported_deps`. A comment on the target now says so, since the next reader to compare the two definitions will otherwise take it for the drift this stack has been removing.

Reviewed By: bryanyantx

Differential Revision: D120523170

fbshipit-source-id: 73af8bbf58f87962bc10ad20f6d34113b98de9d8

Move the private framework loader to Swift

Summary:
`FBControlCoreFrameworkLoader` is now Swift. Its three subclasses and its only construction sites have been Swift since the simulator loader moved, so nothing needs an Objective-C-visible base class any more: the loader keeps its name, its `frameworkName`/`frameworks`/`hasLoadedFrameworks` surface and its load-at-most-once behaviour, and the header leaves the umbrella.

No behavioural change. Two API details go with the port:

- `loaderWithName:frameworks:` is dropped. It duplicated the initializer, which is how every caller builds one.
- `DeviceControlFrameworkLoader.init()` stops declaring `override`. A Swift base class does not inherit `NSObject.init()` into its subclasses the way the Objective-C one did, so there is nothing to override — the initializer itself is unchanged.

___

Differential Revision: D120565271

fbshipit-source-id: 16db18752feeede57e4f4eebdeed432ccc02f41a

Describe H.264 and HEVC output as sRGB over BT.709 so players stop guessing

Summary:
The compression session was told nothing about colour, so the H.264/HEVC bitstream carried no colour description and each player picked its own — usually BT.709 for these frame sizes, but not reliably, and never the sRGB transfer the pixels actually have. The BGRA→NV12 conversion ahead of the encoder likewise ran on VideoToolbox's default matrix for the frame size, so what the encoder was fed and what a player would assume were two independent guesses.

`VideoColorDescription.sRGB` names what the simulator renders — BT.709 primaries (sRGB's), the sRGB transfer function, the BT.709 matrix — and the same three values now go to both ends of the pipeline: the pixel-transfer session as its destination, so the conversion is done with that matrix, and the compression session, so the bitstream's VUI says so. A decoder now colour-manages instead of guessing, and the two ends agree by construction.

Only H.264/HEVC: JFIF has nowhere to carry a description and its YCbCr is BT.601 by convention, so the JPEG formats are left exactly as they were, converter included.

Reviewed By: williamtwilson

Differential Revision: D120503381

fbshipit-source-id: 9f3573d9c19470f3384c298f518fbf4ca6665066

Pin the compressed-video pipeline carrying no colour description

Summary:
No production code change. Two facts about how H.264/HEVC frames are described are pinned as they stand, each marked `BUG` and flipped by the following commit:

- the compression session is given no `ColorPrimaries`, `TransferFunction` or `YCbCrMatrix`, so the bitstream carries no colour description and every player guesses
- the BGRA→NV12 pixel-transfer session is given no destination colour description, so the matrix it converts with is VideoToolbox's default for the frame size

JPEG sessions are pinned as carrying no tags too; that stays true after the flip, since JFIF has nowhere to put them.

`PixelBufferConverter` gains `destinationColorProperties`, which reads the three destination keys back off the transfer session — a seam for the pin and for the flip. A further test covers the converter producing the requested size and format, which had no direct coverage.

Reviewed By: williamtwilson

Differential Revision: D120503380

fbshipit-source-id: 9d91a83a6bf45e241dbefcd1263769f000df05fd

Refuse a sample whose AVCC length prefixes do not fit its bytes

Summary:
`AnnexB.replaceLengthPrefixes` walked a sample's AVCC prefixes trusting each length: a prefix shorter than its NAL unit made the walk read payload bytes as the next prefix and overwrite them with a start code, so the frame reached the consumer with its payload silently corrupted; a prefix longer than the remaining bytes ended the walk and the truncated sample went out as though well-formed; one to three stray bytes after the last unit rode out with it. The walk now checks each prefix against the bytes that follow — non-zero, no longer than what remains, and the units summing exactly to the buffer — and throws `EncodedFrameWriterError.malformedNALUnitLength` with the offending offset, length and remainder, so a malformed sample is refused rather than emitted. The Annex-B writer and the MPEG-TS writer share the walk and both refuse.

VideoToolbox's output is well-formed, so this changes nothing for a healthy encoder; it turns a corrupt sample from silent corruption downstream into a logged, dropped frame.

Reviewed By: williamtwilson

Differential Revision: D120503379

fbshipit-source-id: 50bccd57719448cdb05d20a73cc1abecda725386

Pin how the Annex-B walk treats a malformed AVCC length prefix

Summary:
No production code change. Two behaviours of `AnnexB.replaceLengthPrefixes` are pinned as they stand, each marked `BUG` and flipped by the following commit:

- a length prefix shorter than its NAL unit makes the walk read payload bytes as the next prefix and overwrite them with a start code, so the frame goes out with its payload silently corrupted
- a length prefix longer than the remaining buffer ends the walk and the truncated sample is emitted as though well-formed
- one to three stray bytes after the last NAL unit, where a prefix should be, ride out with the frame

A further test pins the well-formed two-NAL case so the flip can be seen to leave it alone. The H.264 sample-buffer helper takes the AVCC bytes as a parameter so a test can hand it a malformed payload.

The FBSimulatorControl test doubles' sample buffers wrapped a local array's storage with `kCFAllocatorNull`, a pointer that dangled once the helper returned; the walk read garbage lengths from it and no test looked at the bytes. They now own their bytes, which the following commit's guard requires.

Reviewed By: williamtwilson

Merge pull request #3899 from alvations/robust-dos-timing-bounds

Make DoS/ReDoS timing regression tests load-invariant (fix CI flakiness)

_assert_subquadratic: assert on an explicit ratio for clearer diagnostics

Per review, state the scaling property directly as
    ratio = t_big / max(t_small, noise_floor)
    assert ratio < factor
Mathematically identical to t_big < factor * max(...) (the floor already rules
out division by zero), but the measured scaling factor now appears in the
failure output.

Fix the read_sexpr timing test flake (macOS 3.11 CI)

test_unclosed_sexpr_is_subquadratic used a single-shot t4 < 10*t1 + 0.5; under
macOS contention the 800k big parse inflated disproportionately (and can graze
the redos cap, capping t_big non-proportionally), tripping the ratio. Route it
through _assert_subquadratic (min-of-3, multiplicative floor) at 50k/200k, small
enough that the big parse stays well under the cap even at 10x CI slowdown.

Cover the rest of #3898 Finding 2: SyllableTokenizer and timeout tests

Extend the flaky-timing fixes beyond Snowball to the other tests ekaf named,
each verified against the injected exploit and none loosened:

- SyllableTokenizer test_direction1: replace t4 < 8*t1 + 0.5 with the
  _assert_subquadratic ratio. Its multiplicative floor is a tighter bound than
  the old additive slack; injecting the real O(n**2) list-rebuild fails it 14.7x.
- test_every_match_method_is_bounded and hostile_pattern: replace the
  load-sensitive wall-clock < 2.0 with deterministic pytest.raises(TimeoutError).
  Asserting the cap ENGAGES is stronger, not weaker: a silently-broken timeout
  that still returned fast would pass < 2.0 but fail pytest.raises.

Paice, ConfusionMatrix and gale-church already use deterministic operation
counts; reviews_reader already uses a 60s subprocess kill. Those need no change.
Shorten _assert_subquadratic docstring

Snowball DoS test: assert a scaling ratio, not an absolute ceiling

The absolute < 4.0 ceiling was load-sensitive (could fail a correct linear
stem on a contended runner) and no longer verified scaling. Replace it with
_assert_subquadratic: time the stem at 50k and 200k and assert
t(200k) < 8 * max(t(50k), noise_floor).

For the slower languages 50k is a real measurement, so this is a genuine
machine-independent scaling check (linear ~4x, the pre-patch O(n**2) ~16x).
For the fastest, whose 50k run is near timer noise, the floor caps the bound
(a plain absolute check), which still bites because a reintroduced quadratic
is dramatic (seconds vs milliseconds). Note that on a regressed build the
50k run is quadratic too, so even a floored language reveals the ~16x ratio.
Verified by injecting the real O(n**2) into every stemmer: each language
parameter fails; the clean tree passes.

Give the Snowball O(n**2) DoS test real teeth via an absolute ceiling

test_upcase_loop_is_linear asserted t4 < 8*t1 + 0.5 over sizes 8000/32000.
At those sizes a genuine reintroduced O(n**2) (the pre-patch per-match
string rebuild) runs in ~0.56s, which slips under the additive 0.5s floor,
so the test had no teeth. A wall-clock ratio is also the wrong shape here:
of two very different-length ops the longer one is preempted more under CI
contention, inflating the ratio into a false failure.

Assert a generous absolute ceiling on a larger crafted token instead. At
n=200000 the pre-patch rebuild runs 26-43s in every one of the six
languages while the in-place mutation stays under 0.5s, so a 4.0s ceiling
has both teeth (>6x over the fix) and wide contention headroom (>8x under
the fix). Verified by reintroducing the real O(n**2) into all six stemmers:
every language parameter fails; the clean tree passes.

The other timing regression tests are left as their existing absolute
wall-clock bounds: those quadratics are dramatic (seconds to minutes) at
their sizes, so the generous ceilings already have teeth and do not flake.

commits.message:
perf: keep the TUI off the status line render path (#575)

Claude Code re-runs this binary every couple of seconds for as long as a
session is open, so module load time is paid continuously rather than once.

src/ccstatusline.ts imports runTUI statically, which pulls ink, React and
yoga-layout into the render path even though rendering never touches them.
Making that import dynamic is not enough on its own: --outfile cannot split,
so the whole graph still gets parsed. Building with --splitting moves the TUI
into its own chunk and shrinks the entry from 3.34 MB to 21 KB.

Measured on an M-series Mac, 20 runs per data point, real payload piped in:

  before  238, 237, 238 ms/render
  after   226, 222, 220 ms/render

That is roughly 7%, and the rendered output is byte-identical. The
interactive TUI was smoke-tested under a pty and behaves the same.

scripts/replace-version.ts had to change too: with splitting the
__PACKAGE_VERSION__ placeholder lands in a chunk rather than in
dist/ccstatusline.js, so patching only the entry would have silently
shipped an unreplaced placeholder. It now patches every emitted script and
fails loudly when it finds none.

Packaging is unaffected: files is already dist/, and bin/main/exports keep
pointing at dist/ccstatusline.js. Verified the built output runs under node
as well as bun.

commits.message:
terminal: add option to disable scrollback pull on resize (#14296)

#14294

This adds a boolean flag throughout the Zig API and C API to control
whether resizing can pull scrollback back into the active area. The
default is true, which is the existing behavior.

Ptys that keep their own screen buffer without scrollback (namely
Windows ConPTY) can't pull rows back, so after a resize that pulls we
disagree with the pty about what is on screen and subsequent output
lands in the wrong place.

Row growth always appends blank rows at the bottom when pulling is
disabled.

Refs:

https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/blob/7c92ecd037476f957809d0813b14d8bc44bb071a/src/cascadia/TerminalCore/Terminal.cpp#L380-L406
https://github.com/xtermjs/xterm.js/blob/c58ea3637f3968e0e6e79cd92cf9aace7ef89ee2/src/common/buffer/Buffer.ts#L194-L197
https://github.com/wezterm/wezterm/blob/b09b56c29c1e367e598b60ca266e2cc9038751e0/term/src/screen.rs#L268-L288

embedded: route split and close C APIs through performBindingAction (#14261)

## Summary

macOS menus call `ghostty_surface_split`, `split_focus`, and
`request_close` directly, while keybinds go through
`Surface.performBindingAction`. GTK already uses that path for splits
and close. Route the embedded C APIs the same way so menus and keybinds
share one hook.

Behavior without any extra Surface hook is unchanged:
`performBindingAction` still forwards splits to the app and
`close_surface` still closes.

## Test plan

- [x] `zig build test -Demit-macos-app=false` (compiles; these C exports
have no unit test)

This change was prepared with Cursor. I reviewed the C API routing and
how it compares to GTK's existing `performBindingAction` path.

bash: detect hooks in prompt command arrays (#14266)

The delimiter-based guard treats PROMPT_COMMAND as a semicolon-separated
command list. Indexed array expansion joins elements with spaces
instead, so a hook appended after an existing element is not detected
when the integration is sourced again.

Match the full internal hook command as a substring so the guard works
for both scalar and array values. This intentionally gives up command
boundary matching; the private function name and redirection keep an
incidental match unlikely.

commits.message:
fix(audio): rebuild platform FormData bodies for the undici transport (#1580)

#1514 moved every lib/audio provider call to the npm undici package's
fetch so the pinned dispatcher is guaranteed to be honored. But the
adapters kept building multipart bodies with the platform-global
FormData — a class of Node's bundled undici — and undici's serializer
brand-checks a FormData body against its own class. A foreign FormData
fell through to the string branch and left the process as
`content-type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8` with the 17-byte literal
`[object FormData]` as the whole body: the audio bytes and every field
(including `model`) were dropped, downstream gateways fell back to
whisper-1 and answered 503, and every multipart audio request (ASR,
TTS FormData paths, voice registration/cloning) failed with a generic
internal error.

Bare Blob/File, string/JSON/Buffer and stream bodies were never
affected: undici 7.29.0 exports no File/Blob classes of its own and
its bare-body brand checks (and multipart part handling) bind the
platform classes.

Normalize the body in the transport, once, before either transport
path serializes it, so the adapters can keep the platform globals as
their public API boundary: a foreign FormData is re-created as
undici's own with every entry carried over verbatim — `append` (not
`set`) so repeated field names survive, and no filename argument so a
platform File part keeps its own name/type/lastModified. Everything
else passes through untouched.

Also drive real loopback regression tests with a platform-global
FormData (direct, with repeated field names, empty, and across a 307
redirect hop whose per-hop loop re-issues the normalized body) and a
bare Blob, asserting multipart on the wire instead of
`[object FormData]`, and update the voxcpm unit test that asserted
the buggy contract (a platform FormData at the undici boundary).

Fixes #1579

fix(audio): reuse one narration element so mobile playback survives the first segment (#1477)

On mobile browsers classroom narration plays the first segment and then goes
silent for every following one, while the lesson keeps advancing: the player
created a new HTMLAudioElement per line, and only the first line is covered by
the user's gesture, so every programmatic play() after it is refused with
NotAllowedError and the engine falls back to its reading-time timer. #651/#652
fixed the blob leak from that rejection, not the missing voice.

Keep one element per player instead:

- getAudioElement() creates it on first use and every line reuses it, so the
  element the first gesture activated stays playable for the rest of the lesson
- stopAudioElement() releases the line's state rather than the element: onended
  cleared, src removed, load() called -- a stopped line must not keep reporting
  speech it is no longer playing, nor retain narration bytes through a revoked
  object URL until the next play()
- onended is assigned rather than added: the element now outlives a single line,
  so a listener would accumulate once per segment and call the engine back
  several times for one line

tests/audio/audio-player-element-reuse.test.ts stubs the mobile policy itself

commits.message:
Merge pull request #1469 from twmb/record-reader-no-progress

kgo: error when a record consumes no input

Merge pull request #1468 from ajavanma/fix/record-reader-regexp-utf8

kgo: decode UTF-8 in regex record readers

kgo: error when a record consumes no input

A regexp field that matches the empty string, such as %v{re[a*]} on
input "bbb", succeeds without consuming anything. With that as the only
field, next never reaches EOF and never errors, so ReadRecord returns an
empty record forever. The same holds for any layout whose fields all
match empty on the input at hand.

An empty match is legitimate for one field of a record, so the check is
per record: count the bytes consumed from the bufio.Reader, and if a
record consumed none, return an error instead of the record. The count
wraps the bufio.Reader so the header handoff's inner reader is counted
too. A layout that reads nothing at all is still rejected at
construction.

The expErr rows in TestRecordReader now require an error; previously a
nil error passed, which is how this case went unnoticed.

Merge pull request #1467 from ajavanma/fix/record-reader-regexp-mismatch

kgo: return an error for regexp record reader mismatches

kgo: return an error for regexp record reader mismatches

An anchored expression can reject input before the reader encounters an
I/O error. Returning that nil error reports empty records repeatedly
without consuming input. Treat a missing match with no reader error as
a regexp mismatch while preserving EOF and real reader errors.

The error was renamed ErrMaxDecompress in #1463: the client refuses to
decompress, so the past participle described something that never
happened. The option follows, and now reads like BrokerMaxReadBytes and
FetchMaxBytes: the most bytes a batch may decompress to. Unreleased.

Merge pull request #1463 from twmb/decompress-bound

kgo: MaxDecompressedBatchBytes defaults to 1 GiB and bounds merges alone; zstd frames carry their checksum

kgo: fix the merge sweep test to observe the merge

The test slept 20ms into a merge and timed a failure sweep against a
60ms bound. Under the race detector the merge's setup alone takes 60 to
135ms (a fresh level 4 zstd encoder, a 4MB buffer), so the sweep always
ran before the merge had locked a source, and the bound only measured
scheduler noise; a loaded run failed it at 64ms.

The merge stamps each record for the merged batch as it copies it,
under the source's mu. The test now gives the second source a later
timestamp, takes the mu until the stamps show the merge 128 records in,
and checks the count is within a few chunks: a merge holding the source
across the codec stamps all 3800 before the mu is free. Stamps are read
before the sweep, since finishing a promise resets them.

kgo: write the zstd frame checksum again

8b33e43d dropped it because the record batch CRC already covers the
compressed bytes, saving 4% of encoding time. The batch CRC only exists
inside a record batch, though: a zstd blob pulled out of a batch and
written to a file for archival has only the frame checksum to verify
against later. The frame carries it again.

kgo: default MaxDecompressedBatchBytes to 1 GiB, drop the merge constant

A merged batch was capped at min(1 GiB, MaxDecompressedBatchBytes)
uncompressed, the 1 GiB an internal constant. The constant is gone: the
option alone bounds the merge, and its default is 1 GiB rather than
math.MaxInt32, so the bound is yours to raise. If you want to send 2 GiB
through Kafka in one batch, raise the option on both sides.

The merge's check is written as n <= max-uncompressed rather than
uncompressed+n <= max so that it cannot overflow a 32-bit int.

ErrMaxDecompressed is renamed ErrMaxDecompress. Neither name has been
released.

Merge pull request #1462 from twmb/kversion-features

kversion: feature levels per release

kfake: ApiVersions answers features from the kversion table

ApiVersions hand built three features gated on which request keys the
cluster advertised. It now walks the kversion table for the cluster's
version (MaxVersions, else Stable): every feature that release
supports, and every finalized level, with the levels UpdateFeatures set
on top. A level 0 feature is left out of the finalized list and min and
max both carry the level, as a real broker answers. A version below 3.3
answers no features.

UpdateFeatures validates against the same table, so metadata.version is
a known feature and a level below a feature's supported min is refused.
kfakeFeatureSpecs is gone.

TestApiVersionsSupportedFeatures pinned that capping Produce below v12
on Stable hid transaction.version; the table does not gate on keys, so
that case is now TestApiVersionsFeatureTable, which pins 4.4, 4.1, 3.9,
and 3.2 against the table.

commits.message:
Merge pull request #1570 from Altinity/issue-1568

Keep mapped object disk restores from sharing keys with the source table

Rewrite bare object keys too and keep the owner of rewritten metadata

CI of the previous commit failed in two ways.

On ClickHouse 22.8 the object keys of an S3 disk are a bare random
name without the `xxx/` directory component, and splitRestoreObjectKeys
(like the code before it) skipped such keys, so the mapped copy still
shared its objects with the source and TestRestoreMappingObjectDiskDropDst
failed with the very error it guards against. The suffix now goes onto
the only component when there is no directory.

On 26.8 every embedded backup restore failed with `Cannot open file
.../metadata/<db>/<table>.sql ... Permission denied` and its remote
leftovers cascaded into the other tests of the same pooled environment.
WriteMetadataToFile now creates the file via CreateTemp, which as root
produces a root owned file, while the in-place os.Create kept the
clickhouse owner of the existing file and its 0640 mode made it
unreadable for the server. The owner of the replaced file is now copied
onto the new one together with its mode.

Verified on 22.8 (TestRestoreMappingObjectDiskDropDst) and 26.8
(TestRestoreMappingObjectDiskDropDst, TestEmbeddedS3,
TestBwLimitEmbeddedS3).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Keep mapped object disk restores from sharing keys with the source table

A table restored next to its source with --restore-database-mapping on
the same S3 disk lost the source data on DROP DATABASE ... SYNC of the
copy (Code: 499 The specified key does not exist). Three defects in
downloadObjectDiskParts and its callers combined into that:

The idempotency guard strings.Contains(objectPath, backupName) looked
at the whole key, so a disk endpoint prefix which contains the backup
name (backup `regression` on `.../regression-test/live/`) silently
disabled the key rewrite and the copy referenced the source objects.

HardlinkBackupPartsToStorage ran before the objects were copied and the
keys rewritten, so an interrupted restore left `detached` (or the table
directory with restore_as_attach) pointing at the source keys.

The shadow metadata files are hardlinked into the restored table and
WriteMetadataToFile wrote them in place, so a second mapped restore of
the same local backup rewrote the parts of the first copy, and since
the suffix carried only the backup name both copies shared their keys.

splitRestoreObjectKeys now derives the source key from the backup key
(a suffix left by a previous restore is stripped), the destination key
carries `_<backup>_<crc32(db.table)>`, objects are copied before the
parts are linked into the table and metadata files are written via a
temporary file plus rename.

TestRestoreMappingObjectDiskDropDst covers the plain, cache-wrapped
tiered, prefix-contains-backup-name, interrupted and restore-twice
cases; all but the first two fail on master.

Verified on 26.8: TestRestoreMappingObjectDiskDropDst,
TestRestoreMapping, TestCacheDiskBackup, TestS3.

fix https://github.com/Altinity/clickhouse-backup/issues/1568
